ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Trajectory KL Regularization for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Train a variety of pre-trained diffusion models (e.g., DDM, DDPM) on text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation datasets, and fine-tune them using a KL-regularized objective with trajectory KL regularization. Compare the results to fine-tuning without KL regularization or with a marginal KL penalty computed using importance sampling. Control for impact on learning instability, sample quality, and downstream task performance.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning without KL regularization, marginal KL penalty via importance sampling
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning with trajectory KL regularization shows improved convergence and sample quality compared to no KL regularization, but may suffer from over-regularization and increased computational cost compared to marginal KL penalty.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of KL Regularization on Long-Range Dependencies in Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 1 by adding an experiment where a perturbation analysis is performed on the learned reverse process, to quantify how KL regularization affects long-range dependencies in the generated sequences. To do this, generate a set of samples with uniform random perturbations in the reverse sampling process, and measure the sensitivity of downstream task metrics (e.g., inception score, FID) to these perturbations.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning without KL regularization, marginal KL penalty via importance sampling, original trajectory KL regularization
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: The results will show that KL regularization tends to make the reverse process more robust to perturbations, but this comes at the cost of potentially over-stabilizing the process, leading to minor drops in sample quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Connection Between Reward-Shaping and KL-Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between designing reward functions and KL-regularization in diffusion model fine-tuning. In particular, analyze whether carefully designing reward functions that are shaped to penalize deviations from the reference distribution in a way that matches the KL-regularization penalty can improve fine-tuning results. This can be done by modifying the reward function design and observing the effect on the resulting fine-tuned models.
CONTROLS: KL-regularization without reward-shaping, KL-regularization with random reward-shaping
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Reward-shaping might improve fine-tuning results by reducing unexpected dependencies and making the KL-regularization penalty more effective, but may also lead to reward-seeking behavior that is not aligned with downstream tasks.

TITLE: Comparative Analysis of Rejection Sampling and Policy Gradient Methods for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning

TITLE: Leverage Denoising Process for Fine-Tuning: A Flow-Based Approach
PROPOSAL: Design and train a flow-based model that operates on the intermediate noisy states of the diffusion model, and use this model as a bridge to fine-tune the original diffusion model. This approach aims to leverage the information present in the intermediate states to improve the fine-tuning results.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning without using the denoising process, using the pre-trained flow model without fine-tuning
COST: 288000
PREDICTION: The flow-based approach will likely show improved fine-tuning results by incorporating information from the intermediate states, but may also introduce additional computational cost and potentially create over-fitting issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Regularization in Diffusion Models: Understanding the Role of the Reverse Process
PROPOSAL: Analyze the self-regularization properties of the reverse process in diffusion models, and investigate how these properties can be leveraged to improve fine-tuning results without additional regularization penalties. This can be done by studying the behavior of the model during fine-tuning, and designing experiments that modify the reverse process to encourage self-regularization.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning without modifying the reverse process, fine-tuning with additional regularization penalties
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: Self-regularization in the reverse process will be found to have a positive impact on fine-tuning results, but its role may vary depending on the specific characteristics of the model and dataset used.

TITLE: Correcting Imperfections in Pre-trained Flow Models without Explicit Rewards
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of using a variant of the flow-based approach from proposal 4, where the flow model is fine-tuned to correct imperfections in the pre-trained model using only samples from the data distribution, without explicit rewards. This can be done by modifying the loss function of the flow model to include a penalty term for deviating from the data distribution.
CONTROLS: Pre-trained flow model without fine-tuning, fine-tuning with explicit rewards
COST: 432000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach will be able to correct imperfections in the pre-trained model, but may require careful tuning of the penalty term to avoid over-fitting and ensure that the corrected model still captures the underlying structure of the data.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regulated Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a variational inference approach can be used to estimate the marginal KL divergence in KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models. Specifically, use a hierarchical multitask variational autoencoder (HMVAE) trained jointly on the pre-trained diffusion model's samples and the task reward signal to estimate the KL term. This is inspired by the original development of KL-regularized SVGD. 
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, and KL-regularized SVGD.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: The variational inference approach could succeed in stabilizing training compared to ignoring KL regularization, although the upper-bound error of the regime may cause difficulties. The accuracy might fail due to inaccurate estimation of the marginal KL term.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Marginal KL Divergence Estimation via Denoising Diffusion Process Abstraction
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel method that abstracts the denoising diffusion process into a sequence of probabilistic transitions between states, and uses a plug-in estimator on embeddings of these states to approximate the marginal KL divergence in KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models. Specifically, we will use Normalizing Flows to map the intermediate noisy states to a latent space and estimate the KL term as the difference between the learned distribution over these embeddings under the pre-trained model and those under the fine-tuned model.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the variational inference approach from proposal 1, ignoring KL-regularization, and the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: The method could be successful in providing a more accurate estimate of the marginal KL term, but it might be computationally expensive for high-dimensional data, and the requirements of the sequence of Normalizing Flows might lead to convergence issues.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization by KL-Free Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off
PROPOSAL: Propose an algorithm that replaces the KL regularization term in the original KL-regularized reward maximization objective with a KL-free exploration-exploitation trade-off term that encourages the fine-tuned model to explore the vicinity of the pre-trained model's distribution under some probability measure, while exploiting regions with high reward values. This exploration-exploitation trade-off can be achieved using a nearest neighbor search over the pre-trained model's samples.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, the variational inference approach from proposal 1, and the marginal KL divergence estimation method via denoising diffusion process abstraction from proposal 2.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: The approach might improve the stability of training by avoiding the KL regularization term, but it may lead to suboptimal performance if the exploration-exploitation trade-off is overly optimistic, and may not generalize well to tasks that benefit from the specific structure of the KL regularization term.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-Based Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Leverage the structure of diffusion models as invertible flow models to fine-tune them. Specifically, use an invertible flow model to learn a correction to the pre-trained diffusion model's inverse process, and apply this correction to the forward process to obtain a fine-tuned diffusion model.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, the variational inference approach from proposal 1, the marginal KL divergence estimation method via denoising diffusion process abstraction from proposal 2, and the KL-Regularized Reward Maximization by KL-Free Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off from proposal 3.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: This approach has the potential to utilize the structure of diffusion models effectively and achieve state-of-the-art fine-tuning results, but might require careful tuning of the flow architecture and may be sensitive to the choice of initialization for the flow parameters. Additionally, the increased number of parameters compared to the original diffusion model may lead to overfitting when fine-tuning on small datasets.

TITLE: 2. Marginal KL Divergence Estimation via Denoising Diffusion Process Abstraction
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal to use an ensemble of Normalizing Flows to better capture the complexity of the pre-trained diffusion model's distribution, and use a probabilistic neural network (PNN) to learn the weighting of the ensemble members. This can improve the accuracy of the marginal KL divergence estimate by leveraging the strengths of multiple flow-based models.

Additionally, the increased number of parameters compared to the original ensemble member may lead to overfitting when fine-tuning on small datasets.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-Shot Adapters for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel few-shot adapter architecture for fine-tuning diffusion models, where a small, specially designed adapter module is added to the pre-trained diffusion model's intermediate noisy states to correct the distribution. The adapter is trained from scratch in a few-shot setting, using the pre-trained diffusion model's parameters as a cold start. This approach can leverage domain-specific knowledge and address errors in pre-trained models without large increases in the number of parameters.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, and other existing few-shot adaptation techniques for diffusion models.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly reduce the gap between the pre-trained model and the target data distribution, especially when the adaptation dataset is small, but may struggle with extremely large adaptation datasets or when adapting to multiple tasks simultaneously.

TITLE: Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models with Stabilized Denoising Processes
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel stabilization technique for the denoising processes in diffusion models during fine-tuning, by replacing each intermediate noisy state with a probabilistic estimate, allowing the fine-tuned model to focus on more relevant regions of the input space. This can lead to improved stability and convergence in the case of ill-conditioned pre-trained diffusion models.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, the variational inference approach from proposal 1, and the KL-Regularized Reward Maximization by KL-Free Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off from proposal 3.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: This stabilization technique should improve the stability and convergence of the fine-tuning process, allowing for more accurate adaptation to the target data distribution, but may lead to suboptimal fine-tuned models if the stabilization mechanism overly penalizes the fine-tuning process for exploring the pre-trained diffusion model's distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grain-Aggregate Policy for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel policy for fine-tuning diffusion models by introducing a coarse-grained aggregation strategy that learns to aggregate high-level information from multiple policy iterations and adapt the diffusion model accordingly, leading to increased efficiency and exploration in fine-tuning. This policy uses a message passing mechanism to share information between iterations, guiding the fine-tuned diffusion model towards more optimal solutions.
CONTROLS: We will compare against policy gradient methods, ignoring KL-regularization, and the KL-Regularized Reward Maximization by KL-Free Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off from proposal 3.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: The grain-aggregate policy should improve the efficiency and exploration of the fine-tuning process, enabling faster convergence and more accurate adaptation to the target data distribution, but may require careful tuning of the message passing mechanism to prevent over-aggregation of information.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Utilizing Flow-Based Denoising Strategies for Zero-Reward Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the pre-existing structure of diffusion models, combined with flow-based denoising strategies, can be utilized to correct errors in pre-trained models without explicit reward supervision. We will focus on using these strategies to correct errors in the latent space, enabling the model to refine its output towards a more accurate representation of the target data distribution.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, other existing zero-reward adaptation techniques.
COST: 72000
PREDICTION: This approach has the potential to correct errors in pre-trained models without explicit reward supervision, but may require careful tuning of the flow-based denoising strategies to prevent over-smoothing of the latent space and maintain the characteristic distribution of the target data.

textes:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regulated Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a variational inference approach can be used to estimate the marginal KL divergence in KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models. Specifically, use a hierarchical multitask variational autoencoder (HMVAE) trained jointly on the pre-trained diffusion model's samples and the task reward signal to estimate the KL term. This is inspired by the original development of KL-regularized SVGD. 
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, and KL-regularized SVGD.
COST: 32400
PREDICTION: The variational inference approach could succeed in stabilizing training compared to ignoring KL regularization, although the upper-bound error of the regime may cause difficulties. The accuracy might fail due to inaccurate estimation of the marginal KL term.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Marginal KL Divergence Estimation via Denoising Diffusion Process Abstraction
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel method that abstracts the denoising diffusion process into a sequence of probabilistic transitions between states, and uses a plug-in estimator on embeddings of these states to approximate the marginal KL divergence in KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models. Specifically, we will use Normalizing Flows to map the intermediate noisy states to a latent space and estimate the KL term as the difference between the learned distribution over these embeddings under the pre-trained model and those under the fine-tuned model.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the variational inference approach from proposal 1, ignoring KL-regularization, and the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL.
COST: 43200
PREDICTION: The method could be successful in providing a more accurate estimate of the marginal KL term, but it might be computationally expensive for high-dimensional data, and the requirements of the sequence of Normalizing Flows might lead to convergence issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization by KL-Free Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off
PROPOSAL: Propose an algorithm that replaces the KL regularization term in the original KL-regularized reward maximization objective with a KL-free exploration-exploitation trade-off term that encourages the fine-tuned model to explore the vicinity of the pre-trained model's distribution under some probability measure, while exploiting regions with high reward values. This exploration-exploitation trade-off can be achieved using a nearest neighbor search over the pre-trained model's samples.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, the variational inference approach from proposal 1, and the marginal KL divergence estimation method via denoising diffusion process abstraction from proposal 2.
COST: 43200
PREDICTION: The approach might improve the stability of training by avoiding the KL regularization term, but it may lead to suboptimal performance if the exploration-exploitation trade-off is overly optimistic, and may not generalize well to tasks that benefit from the specific structure of the KL regularization term.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-Based Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Leverage the structure of diffusion models as invertible flow models to fine-tune them. Specifically, use an invertible flow model to learn a correction to the pre-trained diffusion model's inverse process, and apply this correction to the forward process to obtain a fine-tuned diffusion model.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, the variational inference approach from proposal 1, the marginal KL divergence estimation method via denoising diffusion process abstraction from proposal 2, and the KL-Regularized Reward Maximization by KL-Free Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off from proposal 3.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: This approach has the potential to utilize the structure of diffusion models effectively and achieve state-of-the-art fine-tuning results, but might require careful tuning of the flow architecture and may be sensitive to the choice of initialization for the flow parameters. Additionally, the increased number of parameters compared to the original diffusion model may lead to overfitting when fine-tuning on small datasets.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 2. Marginal KL Divergence Estimation via Denoising Diffusion Process Abstraction
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal to use an ensemble of Normalizing Flows to better capture the complexity of the pre-trained diffusion model's distribution, and use a probabilistic neural network (PNN) to learn the weighting of the ensemble members. This can improve the accuracy of the marginal KL divergence estimate by leveraging the strengths of multiple flow-based models.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the original ensemble member, ignoring KL-regularization, and the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL.
COST: 57600
PREDICTION: The ensemble-based approach should improve the accuracy of the marginal KL divergence estimate, but may be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of the flow architectures and PNN. Additionally, the increased number of parameters compared to the original ensemble member may lead to overfitting when fine-tuning on small datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-Shot Adapters for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel few-shot adapter architecture for fine-tuning diffusion models, where a small, specially designed adapter module is added to the pre-trained diffusion model's intermediate noisy states to correct the distribution. The adapter is trained from scratch in a few-shot setting, using the pre-trained diffusion model's parameters as a cold start. This approach can leverage domain-specific knowledge and address errors in pre-trained models without large increases in the number of parameters.
CONTROLS: We will compare against ignoring KL-regularization, the standard KL-regularized LSTM-like trajectory KL, and other existing few-shot adaptation techniques for diffusion models.
COST: 72000
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly reduce the gap between the pre-trained model and the target data distribution, especially when the adaptation dataset is small, but may struggle with extremely large adaptation datasets or when adapting to multiple tasks simultaneously.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will train a diffusion model on the CIFAR-10 dataset and then fine-tune it using KL-regularized PPO. The objective will be to maximize the expected reward while controlling the KL divergence between the fine-tuned distribution and the pre-trained reference model. We will use the DDPM model as the pre-trained reference and focus on text-to-image generation as the first domain. For rewards, we will use a simple reward function based on the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score.
CONTROLS: We will compare our KL-regularized PPO approach to ignoring the KL term and using the trajectory KL constraint as baseline methods.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: This approach should improve stability and sample quality compared to ignoring the KL term, but may suffer from the subpar results and initial value function bias seen in the trajectory KL constraint.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trajectory KL Constraint with Post-Hoc Bias Correction
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with the trajectory KL constraint for fine-tuning diffusion models and attempt to mitigate the initial value function bias problem by incorporating a post-hoc bias correction. Specifically, we will use a neural network to learn a correction term that compensates for the bias. We will apply this approach to both the DDPM model and a U-Net based diffusion model, and evaluate its performance on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bias-corrected trajectory KL constraint to the KL-regularized PPO and baseline methods from Proposal 1, as well as a naive trajectory KL constraint without bias correction.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: The bias correction should help alleviate the subpar results associated with the trajectory KL constraint, but it may introduce additional instability or require careful parameter tuning.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Best-of-N Sampling for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the application of best-of-N (BoN) sampling for fine-tuning diffusion models. Specifically, we will generate multiple samples using the pre-trained model, select the top-N samples based on their rewards, and then fine-tune the model on these selected samples. We will use the COCO dataset for image-to-image translation tasks and evaluate the performance of BoN sampling in comparison to KL-regularized PPO and other fine-tuning methods.
CONTROLS: We will compare our BoN sampling approach to KL-regularized PPO, trajectory KL constraint with post-hoc bias correction, and other fine-tuning methods on various image-to-image translation tasks.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: BoN sampling may provide a simple and effective way to fine-tune diffusion models, but it may suffer from over-reliance on the initial samples and potential mode collapse issues.

TITLE: Flow-Based Fine-Tuning for Molecular Generation
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of flow-based methods for fine-tuning pre-trained diffusion models for molecular generation tasks. Specifically, we will use a normalizing flow model as a penalty term in the KL-regularized objective to regularize the fine-tuning distribution. We will apply this approach to the ZINC database for molecule generation tasks and compare its performance to other fine-tuning methods.
CONTROLS: We will compare our flow-based fine-tuning approach to KL-regularized PPO, trajectory KL constraint with post-hoc bias correction, and best-of-N sampling on various molecule generation tasks.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: This approach may provide a powerful way to fine-tune diffusion models for molecular generation tasks, but it may require careful tuning of the flow model and may not generalize well to other tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Sampling-based KL Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a modification to the KL-regularized objective for fine-tuning diffusion models, replacing the intractable marginal KL divergence with an upper bound that can be estimated from samples drawn according to the fine-tuned and reference distributions. Specifically, we compute the KL divergence between the empirical distributions of denoising trajectory prefixes, whose lengths are determined by importance sampling of the conditional process. We compare this proposal to a baseline that relies on the trajectory KL constraint, as well as to an unregularized policy gradient method (PPO).
CONTROLS: Baseline: KL-regularized PPO; Ablations: skipping the KL term, early truncation of trajectory prefixes, importance sampling with only a fixed number of samples.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: The sampling-based KL regularization shows improved stability over the unregularized PPO while outperforming the baseline; Early truncation of prefixes degrades performance, but skipping the KL term results in unstable training dynamics.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We develop an adversarial fine-tuning framework for diffusion models. We treat the reward function as a generator G that tries to produce high-reward samples, and an adversary D that predicts sample quality. The generator and adversary engage in a zero-sum game, where the generator aims to maximize the expected reward while the adversary tries to minimize the reward. This framework allows us to leverage the multi-step generative structure of diffusion models and improve sample quality. We compare this method to the policy gradient baseline and the sampling-based KL regularization method.
CONTROLS: Baseline: PPO; Comparison: sampling-based KL regularization (proposal 1)
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: The adversarial training framework improves sample quality over policy gradient methods, and it also shows improved stability compared to the sampling-based KL regularization. However, its computational cost may lead to longer training times due to the dual gameplay.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Flow-based KL Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the structure of flow models, we propose to represent the KL divergence between the fine-tuned and reference distributions as a sequence of conditional KL divergences between successive denoising steps. For each step, we compute the conditional KL divergence as the difference between the reference and fine-tuned distributions given the input noise. This allows us to leverage the invertibility and bijective mapping properties of flow models to regularize the diffusion fine-tuning process. We compare this proposal to the sampling-based KL regularization method and the policy gradient baseline.
CONTROLS: Baseline: PPO; Comparison: proposal 1, importance sampling of individual denoising steps
COST: 4020
PREDICTION: The flow-based KL regularization improves stability over the unregularized policy gradient method and outperforms the sampling-based KL regularization. However, the special case where each step is a deterministic SDE might introduce a built-in bias if not careful in handling it.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning with Early Termination
PROPOSAL: We modify the adversarial training framework (proposal 2) to incorporate early termination of the training process when a stopping criterion is met, based on the discriminatory power of the adversary. We hypothesize that, early on, the adversary is better at distinguishing poorly generated samples, which we filter out, leading to more efficient learning and less computationally expensive optimization. We compare this extension to the original adversarial training framework (proposal 2), the sampling-based KL regularization method, and the policy gradient baseline.
CONTROLS: Baseline: PPO; Comparison: original adversarial training, proposal 1, and early truncation of trajectory prefixes
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: The early terminated adversarial training method shows faster convergence and improved sample quality over the original adversarial training, while outperforming the policy gradient baseline. It compares closely to the sampling-based KL regularization but may perform better with fewer samples due to the importance of rare cases.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Self-Consistent Reinforcement Learning for Flow Models
PROPOSAL: Building on our findings from proposal 3, we explore leveraging the structure of flow models for explicit policy correction without explicit rewards. We propose to estimate the difference between the pre-trained flow model and the target distribution by minimizing a VAE-AEs specific- distance (IminL), with test predictions in variational learning along a deterministic ODE (Beta-VAE+flow). Leveraging local estimate potential variance may enable metaphor-driven approach selection differing than record mapping comparison.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard flow model retraining; Ablations: omitting self-consistency regularization, replacing VAE-AEs with other reconstruction objectives
COST: 3240
PREDICTION: The self-consistent reinforcement learning approach shows improved sample quality over retraining the standard flow model. By controlling variational regularization learning it decreases reconstruction reward task-specific distance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: On the Connection between Best-of-N Sampling and Policy Gradient Methods for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Following the recent work on Best-of-N sampling for generative models, we investigate its relationship to policy gradient methods for fine-tuning diffusion models. We derive a novel formulation of the Best-of-N sampling objective as an approximate lower bound on the KL-regularized policy gradient objective. We then develop an algorithm that integrates these two approaches by alternating between Best-of-N sampling and policy gradient updates. We compare this integrated method to the policy gradient baseline, the sampling-based KL regularization method, and the adversarial training framework.
CONTROLS: Baseline: PPO; Comparison: integrated method with and without policy gradient updates, proposal 1 and early truncation of trajectory prefixes
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: The integrated method shows improved convergence speed and sample quality over the policy gradient baseline, and it also outperforms the sampling-based KL regularization method. However, the interplay between best-of-n sampling and policy gradients may pose challenges during the initial iterations of the algorithm, requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Local and Global Regularization Constraints for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel regularization scheme that combines both local (fine-grained) and global (coarse-grained) regularization constraints for fine-tuning diffusion models. Local constraints are based on the sampling-based KL regularization (proposal 1), while global constraints are derived from the flow-based KL regularization (proposal 3). We demonstrate the effectiveness of this combined regularization scheme in improving the convergence speed and sample quality of diffusion models. We compare this method to the sampling-based KL regularization method, the flow-based KL regularization method, and the integrated Best-of-N sampling and policy gradient method.
CONTROLS: Baseline: unregularized policy gradient; Comparison: sampling-based KL regularization, flow-based KL regularization, and integrated Best-of-N sampling and policy gradient method
COST: 6432
PREDICTION: The combined local and global regularization constraints show improved convergence speed and sample quality over individual regularization schemes and the integrated method. However, the additional regulator hyperparameter tuning may increase computational cost and lead to overfitting.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Parallelizing Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning using Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent work on parallelizing reinforcement learning algorithms, we propose to speed up the diffusion model fine-tuning process using a multi-task parallelization framework. We derive a novel formulation of the parallelization objective that takes into account the inter-task reinforcement learning dependencies between the fine-tuning of individual diffusion models. We develop an efficient algorithm to solve the parallelization problem and compare it to the sampling-based KL regularization method, the flow-based KL regularization method, and the integrated Best-of-N sampling and policy gradient method.
CONTROLS: Baseline: sequential policy gradient; Comparison: sequential policy gradient, sampling-based KL regularization, and flow-based KL regularization
COST: 7800
PREDICTION: The parallelized fine-tuning framework shows improved speedup over sequential policy gradient methods and comparable or even improved sample quality over individual regularization schemes and integrated methods. However, the inter-task dependencies may lead to increased risk of poor solution convergence in sub-optimal scenarios.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Activation Scaling on Steering Primitives
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the behavior of activation addition and directional ablation under the influence of RMS normalization. It uses a fixed set of steering primitives learned from a large dataset of contrasting examples to steer a pre-trained language model toward or away from a specific behavior (e.g., refusing a harmful request). We systematically vary the scaling of the activation by applying a set of constants scaled to the current activation norm before applying the steering primitive. The performance is measured in both accuracy and fluency on the test set. We hypothesize that the primitives interact with the normalization procedure in a way that leads to degraded performance at both weak and strong scaling, except for a narrow range around the identity scaling.
CONTROLS: 
  * Baseline 1: Using unnormalized activations for steering primitives (as in activation addition and directional ablation).
  * Baseline 2: Using point-wise normalized activations instead of RMS normalized activations.
  * Ablation 1: Not applying any scaling adjustments to the activation before steering.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: The experiment will reveal a u-shaped curve for both primitives when plotted against the scaling constants, confirming our hypothesis, and identifying a small but useful range of scaling values that provides near-optimal steering performance. This range may fail to generalize across different model sizes or complexities, and further investigations may be required to determine the underlying reasons and conditions necessary for reliable and robust behavior.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Specific Scaling Calibration for Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: This experiment extends the initial investigation by proposing a new method for adapting the scaling constants per layer, allowing for more granular control over the steering performance. We employ an automatic sub-task learning framework, where we learn a set of per-layer coefficients using a secondary task of evaluating the maneuverability of the model's activations. We measure maneuverability by learning the capability of small changes in the activation values to produce the target behavior, using a dedicated evaluation set. The secondary task provides a quantitative signal that guides the selection of layer-wise scaling factors in the range identified in the initial investigation. These factors are then used to steer the language model in a primary task of refusing harmful requests.
CONTROLS: 
  * Baseline 1: Using the layer-agnostic scaling factors from the initial investigation.
  * Baseline 2: Using a random set of layer-specific scaling factors.
  * Ablation 1: Not using the secondary task, instead directly applying a predefined array of layer-specific scaling factors selected by human inspection.
  * Ablation 2: Not using the per-layer coefficients but rather evaluating maneuverability over the entire activation vector instead of per layer.
COST: 1680
PREDICTION: The method will result in a marked improvement in steering performance, especially for behaviors with high maneuverability demands, by allowing for tailoring of the scaling factors to the specific activation properties of each layer. However, we may also see instances where this tailoring leads to overfitting of the scaling factors; the experiments should show higher robustness to variations in model architectures or sizable changes in the model's internal representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Examining Steering as a Function of Steering Strength and Ambient Activation Distribution
PROPOSAL: This theoretical investigation delves into the nature of steering as a function of steering strength and ambient activation distribution. We derive and analyze the relationship between the target behavior, steering strength, and the ambient activation distribution, focusing on how steering modifies the probability of exhibiting the target behavior. We propose and analyze the existence of a tipping point: a strength beyond which the model either completely refuses the request or complies with it, in a total and irreversible manner. We aim to derive bounds or estimates for the location of this tipping point depending on the ambient activation distribution and model properties (e.g., the range or variance of the activations).
CONTROLS: 
  * None (a fully theoretical experiment).
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This investigation is likely to reveal the existence of a tipping point, and possibly uncover its relation with the ambient activation distribution. However, it might become clear that the tipping point depends heavily on various other properties of the model and dataset, limiting the directly applicable insights and highlighting the need for additional domain-specific knowledge to accurately estimate this tipping point. It might also show that there is no clear single, universal tipping point, and steering strength may have to be adjusted on a per-application or task basis.

PROPOSAL: This experiment extends the initial investigation by proposing a new method for adapting the scaling constants per layer, allowing for more granular control over the steering performance. We employ an automatic sub-task learning framework, where we learn a set of per-layer coefficients using a secondary task of evaluating the maneuverability of the model's activations. We measure maneuverability by learning the capability of small changes in the activation values to produce the target behavior, using a dedicated evaluation set. The secondary task provides a quantitative signal that guides the selection of layer-wise scaling factors in the range identified in the initial investigation. These factors are then used to steer the language model in a primary task of refusing harmful requests.
CONTROLS: 
  * Baseline 1: Using the layer-agnostic scaling factors from the initial investigation.
  * Baseline 2: Using a random set of layer-specific scaling factors.
  * Ablation 1: Not using the secondary task, instead directly applying a predefined array of layer-specific scaling factors selected by human inspection.
  * Ablation 2: Not using the per-layer coefficients but rather evaluating maneuverability over the entire activation vector instead of per layer.
COST: 5040
PREDICTION: The method will result in a marked improvement in steering performance, especially for behaviors with high maneuverability demands, by allowing for tailoring of the scaling factors to the specific activation properties of each layer. However, we may also see instances where this tailoring leads to overfitting of the scaling factors; the experiments should show higher robustness to variations in model architectures or sizable changes in the model's internal representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Examining Steering as a Function of Steering Strength and Ambient Activation Distribution
PROPOSAL: This theoretical investigation delves into the nature of steering as a function of steering strength and ambient activation distribution. We derive and analyze the relationship between the target behavior, steering strength, and the ambient activation distribution, focusing on how steering modifies the probability of exhibiting the target behavior. We propose and analyze the existence of a tipping point: a strength beyond which the model either completely refuses the request or complies with it, in a total and irreversible manner. We aim to derive bounds or estimates for the location of this tipping point depending on the ambient activation distribution and model properties (e.g., the range or variance of the activations).
CONTROLS: 
  * None (a fully theoretical experiment).
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: This investigation is likely to reveal the existence of a tipping point, and possibly uncover its relation with the ambient activation distribution. However, it might become clear that the tipping point depends heavily on various other properties of the model and dataset, limiting the directly applicable insights and highlighting the need for additional domain-specific knowledge to accurately estimate this tipping point. It might also show that there is no clear single, universal tipping point, and steering strength may have to be adjusted on a per-application or task basis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Layer-Specific Adjustment in Activation Addition
PROPOSAL: We adapt the activation addition primitive by proposing a control parameter that adjusts the scaling factor for each layer individually, based on a learned linear mapping from minibatch norms of different activation layers to suitable coefficients.
CONTROLS: Compare the adjusted activation addition operation against (a) the original activation addition with a tunable overall scaling factor, (b) activation addition with a constant scaling factor (e.g., as used before normalization), (c) directional ablation, and (d) a robust baselines using task-based objectives to steer the model towards or away from the target behavior.
COST: 168
PREDICTION: The method with layer-specific adjustments should outperform the baselines, but the gap may be smaller than expected due to challenges in accurately modeling the activation norms for specific tasks, and the difficulty of training a stable model that captures the nuanced relationships between layer-wise activations and their respective suitable coefficients.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Absorbing Activation Encoding for Improved Steering
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the challenge that existing activation editing operations can inadvertently interact with other, unrelated features encoded in the activation representations, we introduce an absorbing activation encoding (AAE) module that embeds target features and behaviors in dedicated spaces that repel background information, facilitating coherent control of targeted behaviors while leaving other features untouched.
CONTROLS: Implement AAE in the context of the layer-specific activation addition and evaluate its effectiveness by comparing against the same baselines from Proposal 1. Assess AAE's ability to maintain general language modeling capabilities across the whole range of the steering control parameter. 
COST: 250
PREDICTION: AAE can show significant improvements in controlling targeted behaviors while reducing adversarial effects on other features, but the AAE could require careful optimization to avoid entangling its learned encodings with model-specific representations, a problem that remains an open challenge in the control of complex AI systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Activation Masking for Orthogonalizing Steering Operations
PROPOSAL: We explore incorporating learnable masks into steering operations to enable efficient suppression of target features, reducing the need for orthogonal ablation and mitigating interaction with other, unrelated features. This can be done by conditioning the activation projection onto the orthogonal complement of the feature direction, using the learnable mask to selectively zero out activation components that are likely to interact with other features.
CONTROLS: Evaluate masking with layer-specific scaling from Proposal 1, compare against directional ablation, and assess the effectiveness of masking in reducing muddle interactions for behaviors beyond refusal. 
COST: 282
PREDICTION: Activation masking with layer-specific scaling should exhibit improved performance and reduced unwanted interactions, enhancing the reliability and flexibility of steering operations. However, accurately learning and adapting the masks to different scenarios and model behaviors may be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Effects of RMS Normalization on Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: We investigate the interplay between RMS normalization and steering operations by studying how normalization affects the efficacy and expressive power of layer-specific scaling, activation masking, and absorbing activation encoding. Specifically, we aim to understand how normalization transforms activation distributions and feature interactions, and how these changes impact the accuracy and stability of steering operations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of steering operations on normalized and non-normalized activations, using both synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare against a robust baseline that optimizes for steering performance under both conditions.
COST: 330
PREDICTION: We expect RMS normalization to have a significant impact on the behavior of steering operations, and that understanding its effects could lead to better design choices for controlled activation editing. However, investigating the interplay between normalization and steering may also reveal existing performance limitations in activation steering methods, which need to be addressed through new optimisation or additional techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Expressive Power of Hierarchical Steering Operations
PROPOSAL: Building on insights from proposals 1-4, we introduce a hierarchical steering framework that recursively applies activation steering operations to achieve more complex control objectives. Specifically, we design a hierarchical structure that incrementally refines the steering direction, leveraging the strengths of layer-specific scaling, activation masking, and absorbing activation encoding.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the hierarchical steering framework against individual steering methods (Proposals 1-4), as well as against a baseline that combines individual methods heuristically.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: The hierarchical steering framework should demonstrate improved performance, as it effectively leverages the strengths of individual steering methods to achieve complex control objectives. However, the framework's performance may degrade as the hierarchy becomes increasingly deep, due to potential overfitting or loss of expressiveness.

TITLE: Introspective Activation Steering for Controlled LLM Behavior
PROPOSAL: Experiment a new introspective activation steering method that combines self-attention and attention-isolation (such as that in the AdapterHub or LiteBloch embeddings) to build a hierarchical representation of a model's behavior space from its activations. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of RMS Normalization on Activation Steering Operations
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experimental analysis to examine how activation steering operations (addition, ablation, and conditional methods) are affected by RMS normalization in a set of pre-trained LLMs. We experiment with manually setting a uniform scaling factor to mimic the normalization effect for certain layers, to better understand the role of RMS normalization on the behavior of these steering operations. Our experiments use a single downstream task (factuality on a set of test sentences) and work over three sizes of pre-trained models (small, medium, and large).
CONTROLS: We include the following baselines and ablations:
- A baseline where RMS normalization is disabled (no normalization)
- A baseline where RMS normalization is enabled but we zero-pad the initial activations to simulate shallow activations
- An ablation that removes RMS normalization but maintains the rest of the model architecture
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Our results will show that RMS normalization intensifies the effect of the steering operations for most layers, suggesting that current steering methods have a dependence on layer-specific activation scales which needs to be addressed for robust control. The ablation and zero-padded baseline may exhibit degraded performance without the benefits of re-scaled activations, pointing to the limitations of steering in the presence of normalization.

PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel activation steering primitive, called " activation dampening", which dampens the activation along a feature direction using a specially designed projection matrix. This primitive combines the benefits of both addition and ablation methods while avoiding their respective drawbacks. In contrast to ablation, it selectively attenuates the activation without removing it entirely, allowing for more nuanced control over behavior expression. Unlike addition, it doesn't require careful tuning of a scaling coefficient and can handle different activation norms across layers. We also propose a learning-based approach to estimate the optimal projection matrix for a given feature direction and model architecture, overcoming the need for manual feature extraction. We implement this novel primitive and test it on a diverse set of tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare our dampening primitive against the existing addition, ablation, and conditional methods, and also examine the stability of our primitive in the absence of RMS normalization (i.e. when the initial activations are un-normalized).
COST: 540
PREDICTION: Our results will show that activation dampening can provide a higher degree of control over behavior expression while preserving the model's coherence and general language capabilities. The primitive will exhibit robustness to varying activation norms and intercept better trades between sensitivity to certain features and the model's ability to handle unrelated information.

PROPOSAL: We extend the evaluation of our revised activation damper to multitask and multi-behavior setups, where the model is asked to express or suppress multiple behaviors simultaneously. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-learning for Adaptive Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: We explore a meta-learning approach to adaptively learn how to steer the activation in different models and across various behaviors, eliminating the need for manual feature extraction and reducing the number of training tasks required. We design a meta-training procedure that learns a set of generalizable steering rules that can be applied to novel models and behaviors. We also investigate the use of similarity metrics and distance functions to improve the compatibility between the model and the steering rule.
CONTROLS: We compare our meta-learning approach to a fine-tuning baseline where the model learns the steering rules from scratch for each task, and also examine the performance of our approach on a set of out-of-distribution tasks and behaviors.
COST: 1188
PREDICTION: Our results will show that our meta-learning approach can effectively adapt to novel models and behaviors, resulting in faster and more accurate steering performance. However, the quality of the steering rules may suffer from the limited training data and the generalization capability of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-aware Activation Steering for Safe and Robust Model Control
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel mechanism for uncertainty-aware activation steering that enables the model to acknowledge and adapt to uncertain situations when steering the behavior. This is achieved by conditioning the steering action on the model's uncertainty estimates, ensuring that the model steers more conservatively when uncertainty is high and more aggressively when the model is confident. We evaluate our approach on a set of safety-critical tasks where robust control is essential.
CONTROLS: We compare our uncertainty-aware approach to a baseline where the steering action is taken independently of the model's uncertainty estimates and also examine the impact of our approach on the model's tendency to exhibit oversteering or understeering behaviors.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Our results will show that our uncertainty-aware activation steering mechanism improves the safety and robustness of the model control, particularly in situations with high levels of uncertainty. However, the performance might trade-off in scenarios with very low uncertainty levels.

TITLE: Scalable and Interpretable Activation Steering: A Unified Framework for Model Steering
PROPOSAL: We propose a unified framework for model steering that integrates the insights and techniques developed over the course of our research, providing a scalable and interpretable solution for steering the behavior of language models. Our framework combines the benefits of activation dampening, meta-learning, and uncertainty-aware control to enable efficient and robust steering in a wide range of scenarios. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on a comprehensive set of benchmarks and illustrate its interpretability through visualizations of the steering actions.
CONTROLS: We compare our unified framework to the state-of-the-art activation steering methods, as well as to a range of ablated and modified versions of our framework to assess the contribution of individual components.
COST: 2430
PREDICTION: Our results will show that the unified framework provides a significant improvement in steering performance and interpretability, while offering a scalable solution for model steering in a variety of scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of RMS Normalization on Activation Steering Operations
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experimental analysis to examine how activation steering operations (addition, ablation, and conditional methods) are affected by RMS normalization in a set of pre-trained LLMs. We experiment with manually setting a uniform scaling factor to mimic the normalization effect for certain layers, to better understand the role of RMS normalization on the behavior of these steering operations. Our experiments use a single downstream task (factuality on a set of test sentences) and work over three sizes of pre-trained models (small, medium, and large).
CONTROLS: We include the following baselines and ablations:
- A baseline where RMS normalization is disabled (no normalization)
- A baseline where RMS normalization is enabled but we zero-pad the initial activations to simulate shallow activations
- An ablation that removes RMS normalization but maintains the rest of the model architecture
COST: 540
PREDICTION: Our results will show that RMS normalization intensifies the effect of the steering operations for most layers, suggesting that current steering methods have a dependence on layer-specific activation scales which needs to be addressed for robust control. The ablation and zero-padded baseline may exhibit degraded performance without the benefits of re-scaled activations, pointing to the limitations of steering in the presence of normalization.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Understanding Activation Steering through Regression-based Interpretability
PROPOSAL: 
Employ regression-based interpretability techniques to gain insight into how activation steering methods influence the output of a language model. The goal is to establish a connection between the editorial edits (addition, ablation, re-orbitalization) and changes in the model's behavior. A linear regression model will be trained on a set of activation edits, their corresponding target behaviors, and the resulting model outputs. This will enable the identification of critical feature interactions, which may subsequently inform the development of more targeted and nuanced steering methods.
CONTROLS: 
We will compare the performance of the regression model with various feature representations (e.g., layer-wise, token-wise, or combination of both) to assess their impact on the interpretability results. Additionally, we will contrast our approach with existing interpretability methods, such as saliency maps or feature importance charts, to determine whether the regression-based approach offers unique benefits in understanding activation steering.
COST: 43490
PREDICTION: 
The regression model is expected to successfully capture the relationships between activation edits and resulting model behaviors, potentially shedding light on the underlying dynamics of activation steering. However, interpretability results may be sensitive to the choice of feature representation and the model complexity, which could limit the generalizability of our approach.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Activation Steering under Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: 
Investigate the robustness of activation steering methods to adversarial attacks, simulating real-world scenarios where attackers may intentionally manipulate input data to disrupt model behavior. We will generate adversarial examples using various attack methods (e.g., FGSM, PGA) and evaluate the ability of activation steering to adapt to these manipulations. Specifically, we will test how well our proposed methods (Modified Continuous Activation Editing, Gradual Steering, and Enhancing Interpretability with Activation-based Embeddings) can steer the model to respond correctly to adversarial inputs while maintaining their desired behavior.
CONTROLS: 
We will compare the performance of our proposed methods with existing state-of-the-art defense mechanisms and vary the attack methods, model complexities, and evaluation metrics to assess their robustness under different conditions.
COST: 82000
PREDICTION: 
The activation steering methods are expected to demonstrate resilience to adversarial attacks but may exhibit limitations when confronted with highly targeted or sophisticated attacks. The relationship between steering strength, robustness, and model performance will be critical to understand in order to design robust activation steering solutions that balance control over model behavior with resistance to manipulation.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning with Latent Alignment
PROPOSAL: To design a neural architecture that enables efficient federated multi-task learning (FMTL) across users with heterogeneous tasks and model architectures, we propose using a differentiable meta-learnable alignment module that learns latent representations across all tasks within a single shared embedding space. We will use the unfrozen pre-trained encoder layers from each user's model as initializations and would treat the weight updates in the shared layers as a meta-learning objective. This approach decouples the adaptation of shared latents from the local model adaptation, allowing for a simple and ON/OFF control of shared parameters. The updates are conducted via a server-client iterative process, leveraging the benefits of FTL, with gradient information from all users.
CONTROLS: We compare against recently proposed methods that address model heterogeneity (Moro+, 2022; Kim+, 2023), traditional contrastive learning methods (InfoNCE, 2020), and random initialization of latent representations.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: By design, our model achieves efficient FMTL with minimal shared parameters and can effectively align representations across all tasks. It could fail if complicated multi-modal tasks are included, in which case an aggregation scheme may be required to refine the latent representations under a common space.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Beyond Contrastive Loss: Generalized Kernel Learning for Federated Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: To address the limitation of InfoNCE loss in pairwise alignment of representations, we propose a generalized kernel learning approach for federated representation alignment. We derive a diffusion-based kernel alignment loss that promotes alignment across an arbitrary number of models. This approach leverages the rich expressiveness of kernel machines to capture higher-order dependencies among representations. To make kernel learning scalable, we ensemble the kernel functions from multiple sharing pairs of models using a voting procedure. We consider both instances and tasks as the symbol of the diffuse memory retrieval for coded indices setting.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with the Gramian-based contrastive loss (Ahmad+, 2022) and a classic kernel-based method on federated multi-task learning tasks.
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: Our method achieves better alignment and faster convergence by capturing the dependencies among representations more effectively. However, scaling to very large numbers of models and tasks might become challenging, and incorporating modality embeddings might be necessary for multi-modal federated learning settings.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Modularized Federated Learning with Selective Knowledge Transfer
PROPOSAL: To enable efficient learning in large-scale federated settings, we propose a modular framework with selective knowledge transfer that aggregates knowledge from few most relevant users. This framework leverages a meta-learning-based selector to determine the appropriate subset of users to share knowledge from, based on their local task-specific and task-agnostic knowledge. We further propose a hierarchical memory-based structure to store and integrate hierarchical task-aware patterns from component subsets, rather than flat collections.
CONTROLS: We compare our framework with a recently proposed meta-learning approach (Liu+, 2022) and homogenization-based methods (Parwez+, 2022) on a range of real-world federated multi-task datasets.
COST: 2880
PREDICTION: Our modular framework significantly reduces the communication overhead and improves knowledge transfer efficiency, especially for large and diverse collaborative multi-task settings. However, identifying the optimal subset of users and handling concept drift might be non-trivial challenges.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Energy-Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning via Pruning and Quantization
PROPOSAL: In large-scale federated settings, energy consumption can be a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose an energy-efficient framework for federated multi-task learning, that leverages model pruning and quantization techniques to reduce communication overhead and energy consumption. By pruning and quantizing redundant parameters, we minimize the communicated model updates and reduce the energy required for transmission. Furthermore, we employ a dynamic sparse update strategy for efficient transmission.
CONTROLS: We compare our framework with energy-aware Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and a hybrid pruning-quantization method (Kim+, 2020) on real-world federated multi-task datasets.
COST: 3300
PREDICTION: Our framework effectively reduces communication overhead and energy consumption, making it more suitable for large-scale federated settings. However, it may suffer from balancing energy savings and accuracy degradation trade-offs due to the over-pruning or under-pruning of models.

TITLE: Anomaly Detection-Augmented FTL for Improving Robustness to Varying Model Architectures
PROPOSAL: To improve the robustness of federated learning across diverse model architectures, we add an anomaly detection module that identifies and handles task-specific anomalies that lead to sub-optimal generalization. The module detects anomalies by analyzing the similarity of model weights and the task-specific loss functions, using a combination of density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) for anomaly detection and a learned weighting function to assign a penalty to the anomalous tasks. The goal is to reduce the impact of anomalies on the overall model performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with traditional federated learning methods (FedAvg, FedProx) and a recent anomaly detection method for federated learning (Wu+, 2022) on a set of real-world federated multi-task datasets with varying model architectures.
COST: 9150
PREDICTION: Our approach significantly improves the robustness of federated multi-task learning against anomalies, achieving better accuracy and reducing the impact of outliers. However, the effectiveness of anomaly detection may suffer when the anomalies are subtle or occur infrequently.

TITLE: Hierarchical Federated Learning for Multi-Task and Multi-Modal Settings
PROPOSAL: To scale federated learning to large-scale multi-task and multi-modal settings, we propose a hierarchical framework that divides the tasks and modalities into a tree-like structure, enabling efficient transfer of knowledge and alignment of representations across different levels of the hierarchy. Each node in the hierarchy represents a specific task or modality, and the framework uses a combination of message passing and contrastive learning to align the representations at each node, while encouraged their models to share knowledge and improve the overall performance.

However, the effectiveness of our approach may depend on the choice of the hierarchy structure and the representation alignment methods used at each node, which may require careful tuning and hyperparameter selection.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning with Latent Alignment
PROPOSAL: To design a neural architecture that enables efficient federated multi-task learning (FMTL) across users with heterogeneous tasks and model architectures, we propose using a differentiable meta-learnable alignment module that learns latent representations across all tasks within a single shared embedding space. We will use the unfrozen pre-trained encoder layers from each user's model as initializations and would treat the weight updates in the shared layers as a meta-learning objective. This approach decouples the adaptation of shared latents from the local model adaptation, allowing for a simple and ON/OFF control of shared parameters. The updates are conducted via a server-client iterative process, leveraging the benefits of FTL, with gradient information from all users.
CONTROLS: We compare against recently proposed methods that address model heterogeneity (Moro+, 2022; Kim+, 2023), traditional contrastive learning methods (InfoNCE, 2020), and random initialization of latent representations.
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: By design, our model achieves efficient FMTL with minimal shared parameters and can effectively align representations across all tasks. It could fail if complicated multi-modal tasks are included, in which case an aggregation scheme may be required to refine the latent representations under a common space.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Beyond Contrastive Loss: Generalized Kernel Learning for Federated Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: To address the limitation of InfoNCE loss in pairwise alignment of representations, we propose a generalized kernel learning approach for federated representation alignment. We derive a diffusion-based kernel alignment loss that promotes alignment across an arbitrary number of models. This approach leverages the rich expressiveness of kernel machines to capture higher-order dependencies among representations. To make kernel learning scalable, we ensemble the kernel functions from multiple sharing pairs of models using a voting procedure. We consider both instances and tasks as the symbol of the diffuse memory retrieval for coded indices setting.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with the Gramian-based contrastive loss (Ahmad+, 2022) and a classic kernel-based method on federated multi-task learning tasks.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: Our method achieves better alignment and faster convergence by capturing the dependencies among representations more effectively. However, scaling to very large numbers of models and tasks might become challenging, and incorporating modality embeddings might be necessary for multi-modal federated learning settings.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Modularized Federated Learning with Selective Knowledge Transfer
PROPOSAL: To enable efficient learning in large-scale federated settings, we propose a modular framework with selective knowledge transfer that aggregates knowledge from few most relevant users. This framework leverages a meta-learning-based selector to determine the appropriate subset of users to share knowledge from, based on their local task-specific and task-agnostic knowledge. We further propose a hierarchical memory-based structure to store and integrate hierarchical task-aware patterns from component subsets, rather than flat collections.
CONTROLS: We compare our framework with a recently proposed meta-learning approach (Liu+, 2022) and homogenization-based methods (Parwez+, 2022) on a range of real-world federated multi-task datasets.
COST: 8640
PREDICTION: Our modular framework significantly reduces the communication overhead and improves knowledge transfer efficiency, especially for large and diverse collaborative multi-task settings. However, identifying the optimal subset of users and handling concept drift might be non-trivial challenges.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Energy-Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning via Pruning and Quantization
PROPOSAL: In large-scale federated settings, energy consumption can be a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose an energy-efficient framework for federated multi-task learning, that leverages model pruning and quantization techniques to reduce communication overhead and energy consumption. By pruning and quantizing redundant parameters, we minimize the communicated model updates and reduce the energy required for transmission. Furthermore, we employ a dynamic sparse update strategy for efficient transmission.
CONTROLS: We compare our framework with energy-aware Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and a hybrid pruning-quantization method (Kim+, 2020) on real-world federated multi-task datasets.
COST: 10080
PREDICTION: Our framework effectively reduces communication overhead and energy consumption, making it more suitable for large-scale federated settings. However, it may suffer from balancing energy savings and accuracy degradation trade-offs due to the over-pruning or under-pruning of models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Distributed Foundation Models
PROPOSAL: We investigate federated multi-task learning for a set of users with heterogeneous model architectures and different tasks. Each user selects a pre-trained foundation model based on their resource constraints and task requirements, and then fine-tunes it on a small local dataset. We propose a method that enables the server to capture common task-agnostic information from the users' representations and transfer this knowledge across tasks. Our approach combines contrastive learning with knowledge distillation, which allows for the alignment of representations across all users, regardless of the number of users. We experiment with across a range of datasets including Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, as well as ImageNet and CIFAR-10, each with a diverse set of tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a simple federated averaging method, where each user trains a model separately and shares the weights with the server. We also experiment with a vanilla knowledge distillation method without contrastive learning.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method outperforms the baseline and vanilla knowledge distillation method on Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, and achieves comparable performance on ImageNet and CIFAR-10. However, the approach might struggle with large numbers of users due to the increased communication cost of contrastive learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Agnostic Similarity Measures for Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We investigate the reliability of model-agnostic similarity measures for representation alignment in the context of federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we examine the centered kernel alignment (CKA) and its variants, as well as the recently proposed Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD) similarity measure. We design experiments to test the robustness of these similarity measures against varying degrees of task similarity, model differences, and representation sparsity. Our evaluation framework involves training multiple models on Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, and then applying each similarity measure to compute alignment scores between these models.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of each similarity measure against a proposed surrogate loss function that uses a pre-trained clustering model to cluster representations.
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that OGD outperforms CKA on Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, particularly in scenarios with varying degrees of task similarity, while the CKA variants struggle in these cases due to their sensitivity to model differences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach for federated multi-task learning that adapts to new tasks and users without explicit task identity. Our method employs a meta-learner that takes in representations from various users and fine-tunes these representations to adjust for task- and user-specific differences. We experiment with this meta-learner as a component of our federated multi-task learning framework proposed earlier (Federated Multi-Task Learning with Distributed Foundation Models) and compare its performance on a diverse set of tasks from the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository (UCI) datasets and the ImageNet dataset.
CONTROLS: We examine the impact of different meta-learner architectures (e.g., a simple multi-layer perceptron) and learning objectives (e.g., inception score) on the adaptability of our federated multi-task learning approach.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our meta-learning approach significantly improves the adaptability of our federated multi-task learning framework, yielding state-of-the-art performance on the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository (UCI) datasets and competitive performance on ImageNet. However, its computational cost may limit its application to scenarios with limited data.

TITLE: Non-Uniform Federated Calibration for Robust Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate a non-uniform federated calibration approach to improve the robustness of federated multi-task learning. Our method divides the users into clusters based on their representations and task differences, and then adjusts the local learning rates and regularization strengths of each cluster to optimize the shared knowledge transfer. We apply this approach to a variety of heterogeneous tasks on the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, with each user selecting a pre-trained foundation model and then fine-tuning it on a small local dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare our non-uniform federated calibration approach against a uniform federated calibration method and a simple federated averaging baseline.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our non-uniform federated calibration approach significantly improves the robustness of federated multi-task learning, yielding improved performance on ImageNet and competitive performance on CIFAR-10. However, its sensitivity to the choice of clustering algorithm and hyperparameters may limit its applicability in practice.

TITLE: Experimental Analysis of Privacy-Aware Techniques for Federated Learning
PROPOSAL: We design an experimental analysis to investigate the effectiveness of various privacy-aware techniques for federated learning in the context of federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we evaluate differential privacy, Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC), and Homomorphic Encryption (HE) techniques for protecting user data while enabling knowledge transfer. We experiment with these techniques on a diverse set of tasks from the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, with each user selecting a pre-trained foundation model and then fine-tuning it on a small local dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of each privacy-aware technique against a simple federated averaging method with no privacy protection.
COST: 4800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that differential privacy is the most effective method for protecting user data while minimizing the impact on knowledge transfer. However, the approaches may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, particular to the degree of differential privacy required for each application.

TITLE: Federated Collaborative Learning for Multi-Modal Data
PROPOSAL: We propose a framework for federated collaborative learning for multi-modal data. Our approach involves redefining the representation alignment and knowledge transfer mechanisms to accommodate multiple modalities. We apply this framework to a diverse range of multi-modal tasks, including predictive maintenance, healthcare, and computer vision. Specifically, we experiment with the integration of sensor data and images for predictive maintenance on a dataset of industrial machinery, and evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in transferring knowledge across different modalities and tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our framework against federated multi-task learning methods that assume a single modality and against multi-modal federated learning methods that assume a homogeneous architecture.

PREDICTION: Our results suggest that our framework significantly improves the performance of federated collaborative learning for multi-modal data, enabling the effective transfer of knowledge across different modalities and tasks. However, the approach may require a significant increase in computational resources due to the complexity of multi-modal data integration.
