Our approach involves designing a decentralized architecture that enables parallel processing of multiple tasks and models. Specifically, we experiment with this architecture on a large-scale dataset of multiple image classification tasks and natural language processing tasks. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in scaling federated learning to large-scale multi-task settings while maintaining training efficiency.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our framework against conventional federated learning methods for single tasks and against large-scale multi-task learning methods that assume a centralized architecture.
COST: 170000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that our scalable federated learning framework significantly improves the training efficiency and adaptability of federated learning for large-scale multi-task settings, enabling faster convergence and better knowledge transfer. However, the approach may require careful tuning of the decentralized architecture to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Distributed Foundation Models
PROPOSAL: We investigate federated multi-task learning for a set of users with heterogeneous model architectures and different tasks. Each user selects a pre-trained foundation model based on their resource constraints and task requirements, and then fine-tunes it on a small local dataset. We propose a method that enables the server to capture common task-agnostic information from the users' representations and transfer this knowledge across tasks. Our approach combines contrastive learning with knowledge distillation, which allows for the alignment of representations across all users, regardless of the number of users. We experiment with across a range of datasets including Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, as well as ImageNet and CIFAR-10, each with a diverse set of tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a simple federated averaging method, where each user trains a model separately and shares the weights with the server. We also experiment with a vanilla knowledge distillation method without contrastive learning.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method outperforms the baseline and vanilla knowledge distillation method on Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, and achieves comparable performance on ImageNet and CIFAR-10. However, the approach might struggle with large numbers of users due to the increased communication cost of contrastive learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model-Agnostic Similarity Measures for Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We investigate the reliability of model-agnostic similarity measures for representation alignment in the context of federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we examine the centered kernel alignment (CKA) and its variants, as well as the recently proposed Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD) similarity measure. We design experiments to test the robustness of these similarity measures against varying degrees of task similarity, model differences, and representation sparsity. Our evaluation framework involves training multiple models on Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, and then applying each similarity measure to compute alignment scores between these models.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of each similarity measure against a proposed surrogate loss function that uses a pre-trained clustering model to cluster representations.
COST: 7200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that OGD outperforms CKA on Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) and ACE 2005 datasets, particularly in scenarios with varying degrees of task similarity, while the CKA variants struggle in these cases due to their sensitivity to model differences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach for federated multi-task learning that adapts to new tasks and users without explicit task identity. Our method employs a meta-learner that takes in representations from various users and fine-tunes these representations to adjust for task- and user-specific differences. We experiment with this meta-learner as a component of our federated multi-task learning framework proposed earlier (Federated Multi-Task Learning with Distributed Foundation Models) and compare its performance on a diverse set of tasks from the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository (UCI) datasets and the ImageNet dataset.
CONTROLS: We examine the impact of different meta-learner architectures (e.g., a simple multi-layer perceptron) and learning objectives (e.g., inception score) on the adaptability of our federated multi-task learning approach.
COST: 10800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our meta-learning approach significantly improves the adaptability of our federated multi-task learning framework, yielding state-of-the-art performance on the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository (UCI) datasets and competitive performance on ImageNet. However, its computational cost may limit its application to scenarios with limited data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-Uniform Federated Calibration for Robust Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate a non-uniform federated calibration approach to improve the robustness of federated multi-task learning. Our method divides the users into clusters based on their representations and task differences, and then adjusts the local learning rates and regularization strengths of each cluster to optimize the shared knowledge transfer. We apply this approach to a variety of heterogeneous tasks on the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, with each user selecting a pre-trained foundation model and then fine-tuning it on a small local dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare our non-uniform federated calibration approach against a uniform federated calibration method and a simple federated averaging baseline.
COST: 9000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our non-uniform federated calibration approach significantly improves the robustness of federated multi-task learning, yielding improved performance on ImageNet and competitive performance on CIFAR-10. However, its sensitivity to the choice of clustering algorithm and hyperparameters may limit its applicability in practice.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISION of Federated Multi-Task Learning with Distributed Foundation Models
PROPOSAL: We extend our earlier federated multi-task learning with distributed foundation models (FedM-TL-DFM) approach to incorporate a robust loss function that aggregates the knowledge transfer across user-specific models. Specifically, we combine our earlier contrastive learning with knowledge distillation framework with a new robust loss function that estimates the uncertainty of each user's model. This enables the server to effectively capture the shared task-agnostic information across user models, while also accounting for the uncertainty of individual user models. We apply this revised approach to a wide range of tasks on the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, and compare its performance against our earlier FedM-TL-DFM and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: In addition to our earlier baselines (federated averaging and vanilla knowledge distillation), we also compare against a model-agnostic meta-learning approach with a robust loss function.
COST: 16200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised FedM-TL-DFM approach significantly improves the robustness and reliability of federated multi-task learning, yielding improved performance on ImageNet and competitive performance on CIFAR-10. However, the approach may require a significant increase in computational resources due to the complexity of the robust loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Analysis of Privacy-Aware Techniques for Federated Learning
PROPOSAL: We design an experimental analysis to investigate the effectiveness of various privacy-aware techniques for federated learning in the context of federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we evaluate differential privacy, Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC), and Homomorphic Encryption (HE) techniques for protecting user data while enabling knowledge transfer. We experiment with these techniques on a diverse set of tasks from the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, with each user selecting a pre-trained foundation model and then fine-tuning it on a small local dataset.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of each privacy-aware technique against a simple federated averaging method with no privacy protection.
COST: 14400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that differential privacy is the most effective method for protecting user data while minimizing the impact on knowledge transfer. However, the approaches may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, particular to the degree of differential privacy required for each application.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISION of Non-Uniform Federated Calibration for Robust Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We refine our earlier non-uniform federated calibration approach to incorporate a mechanism for adjusting the weights of each cluster based on the confidence of the knowledge transfer. Specifically, we introduce a clustering-weight learning module that predicts the confidence of each cluster and adjusts the weights accordingly. This refinement enables the server to effectively capture the shared task-agnostic information across user models while also accounting for the uncertainty of individual user models. We apply this revised approach to a wide range of tasks on the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets, and compare its performance against our earlier approach and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: In addition to our earlier baselines (uniform federated calibration and simple federated averaging), we also compare against a model-agnostic meta-learning approach with confidence-based clustering.
COST: 21600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised non-uniform federated calibration approach significantly improves the robustness and reliability of federated multi-task learning, yielding improved performance on ImageNet and competitive performance on CIFAR-10. However, the approach may require a significant increase in computational resources due to the additional clustering-weight learning module.

TITLE: Federated Collaborative Learning for Multi-Modal Data
PROPOSAL: We propose a framework for federated collaborative learning for multi-modal data. Our approach involves redefining the representation alignment and knowledge transfer mechanisms to accommodate multiple modalities. We apply this framework to a diverse range of multi-modal tasks, including predictive maintenance, healthcare, and computer vision. Specifically, we experiment with the integration of sensor data and images for predictive maintenance on a dataset of industrial machinery, and evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in transferring knowledge across different modalities and tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our framework against federated multi-task learning methods that assume a single modality and against multi-modal federated learning methods that assume a homogeneous architecture.
COST: 21600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that our framework significantly improves the performance of federated collaborative learning for multi-modal data, enabling the effective transfer of knowledge across different modalities and tasks. However, the approach may require a significant increase in computational resources due to the complexity of multi-modal data integration.

TITLE: Asymmetric Federated Learning for Heterogeneous Tasks and Models
PROPOSAL: We propose an asymmetric federated learning framework for heterogeneous tasks and models. Our approach involves designing an adaptive learning rate mechanism that dynamically adjusts the update frequency of each user based on the quality of their local model. Specifically, we experiment with this mechanism on a diverse range of tasks and models, including image classification and natural language processing. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in adapting to heterogeneous tasks and models while maintaining training efficiency.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our framework against asymmetric federated learning methods that assume homogeneous tasks and models.
COST: 32400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results suggest that our asymmetric federated learning framework significantly improves the adaptability and efficiency of federated learning for heterogeneous tasks and models, enabling better knowledge transfer and faster convergence. However, the approach may require careful tuning of the adaptive learning rate mechanism to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Heterogeneous Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an extensive, large-scale experiment to explore the robustness of heterogeneous federated multi-task learning across various real-world datasets and user settings. We'll use five popular model architectures for fine-tuning and five diverse tasks typically found in remote health monitoring and advertisement systems. Our goal is to compare the tasks' effectiveness when paired with different pre-trained foundation models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa, distilBERT) and various user settings (different levels of noisy labels, heterogeneous local dataset sizes, etc.). We'll assess model performance using conventional metrics (accuracy, precision, recall) as well as model interpretability metrics (feature importance, SHAP values), while guaranteeing the users' privacy by applying local differential privacy methods.
CONTROLS: (1) IID case with each user given the same model architecture and task; (2) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (3) Ablated version without local differential privacy
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The results will show that rotating users' fine-tuning tasks can improve the convergence rate, further analysis on noisy labels may discover beneficial noise injected by descent causes better hidden patterns captured in rep followers to real users; its effectiveness may degrade when users have very low or very high noisy labels in their dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Model Architecture Mismatch on Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We'll explore the effect of model architecture mismatch on the performance of federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we'll conduct experiments where each user has a different model architecture (e.g., linear, CNN, transformer) and is fine-tuning a pre-trained foundation model on a different task. We'll investigate how the performance of federated multi-task learning varies when the server aggregates knowledge from users with highly mismatched architectures. We'll use a range of real-world datasets and model architectures, and assess model performance using a combination of accuracy, precision, recall, and AUC-ROC metrics.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (2) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (3) Ablated version without knowledge distillation; (4) Comparison with the previously proposed Gramian-based contrastive loss
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: This will reveal that users operate in significantly different loss and comfort levels of architectures when training on challenging tasks, phenomenal knowledge loss from architecturally mismatched models, but, results change altogether if task complexity are reordered after discovery.

PREDICTION: This will reveal that users with mismatched architectures are highly sensitive to shift in architecture which decelerate learning rates of various exact task compositions involved; consolidation of knowledge increases performance based on loss landscapes usually independently w.r.t. mismatch; precision will be less consistent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gramian-Based Contrastive Loss: Convergence Analysis and Optimization
PROPOSAL: We'll provide a theoretical analysis of the Gramian-based contrastive loss, a recently proposed approach for aligning representations produced by multiple models in federated multi-task learning. Our goal is to establish a convergence guarantee for this approach and provide insights into its optimization properties. We'll assume that the models have a smooth, Lipschitz-continuous manifold representation, and use tools from nonlinear dynamical systems to analyze the convergence of the Gramian-based contrastive loss.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: InfoNCE loss; (2) Comparison with other alignment losses; (3) Case study with 3 and 5 users
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: This will show the convergence of the Gramian-based contrastive loss in multiple users with certain convergence rates, under different conditions related to the manifold representation of the models' features, particularly when there is too narrow or very large manifold dimension.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning with Model Distillation and Pruning
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a novel federated multi-task learning approach that combines model distillation and pruning to improve the efficiency of knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models. Our method will use a novel proxy distillation network to transfer knowledge from the globally trained model to each user's local model, and then prune the local model to reduce the computational overhead. We'll demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using multiple real-world datasets and model architectures.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (2) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (3) Comparison with other knowledge distillation and pruning methods
COST: 28800
PREDICTION: This will show that the proposed approach significantly improves the efficiency of federated multi-task learning, with improved model accuracy and reduced communication overhead, but may also lead to over-distillation and under-pruning if not properly adapted.

Our method will utilize a TF-IDF-based feature selection mechanism to align task-agnostic features across heterogeneous models. We'll demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using multiple real-world datasets and model architectures, and evaluate its performance using conventional metrics (accuracy, precision, recall) as well as model interpretability metrics (feature importance, SHAP values).
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (2) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (3) Ablated version without TF-IDF feature selection
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: This will show that aligning task-agnostic features successfully helps generalised learning significant enhance representation embedding in heterogenuous environment of multi-task settings than relying solely on via distillation approaches - but it will also present challenges such as dealing with the embedding space, particularly when entity-specific features play significant roles.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Model Architecture Mismatch on Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We'll extend our previous experiment to include a deeper investigation of the impact of model architecture mismatch on federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we'll explore how the performance of federated multi-task learning varies when the users have highly mismatched architectures, as well as the effect of task complexity on the performance. We'll use a combination of accuracy, precision, recall, and AUC-ROC metrics to evaluate the performance of federated multi-task learning under different mismatched architectures and task complexities.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (2) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (3) Ablated version without knowledge distillation; (4) Comparison with the previously proposed Gramian-based contrastive loss; (5) Evaluation under different task complexities
COST: 28800
PREDICTION: This will reveal that users with mismatched architectures are highly sensitive to shift in architecture which decelerate learning rates of various exact task compositions involved; consolidation of knowledge increases performance based on loss landscapes usually independently w.r.t. mismatch; precision will be less consistent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gramian-Based Contrastive Loss: Convergence Analysis and Optimization
PROPOSAL: We'll provide a theoretical analysis of the Gramian-based contrastive loss, a recently proposed approach for aligning representations produced by multiple models in federated multi-task learning. Our goal is to establish a convergence guarantee for this approach and provide insights into its optimization properties. We'll assume that the models have a smooth, Lipschitz-continuous manifold representation, and use tools from nonlinear dynamical systems to analyze the convergence of the Gramian-based contrastive loss.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: InfoNCE loss; (2) Comparison with other alignment losses; (3) Case study with 3 and 5 users
COST: 43200
PREDICTION: This will show the convergence of the Gramian-based contrastive loss in multiple users with certain convergence rates, under different conditions related to the manifold representation of the models' features, particularly when there is too narrow or very large manifold dimension.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Gramian-Based Contrastive Loss: Convergence Analysis and Optimization
PROPOSAL: We'll extend our previous theoretical analysis of the Gramian-based contrastive loss by investigating the impact of the manifold dimensionality ratio on its convergence properties. Specifically, we'll analyze how the manifold dimensionality ratio affects the convergence rate of the Gramian-based contrastive loss, and provide insights into its optimization properties in high-dimensional spaces.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: InfoNCE loss; (2) Comparison with other alignment losses; (3) Case study with 3 and 5 users; (4) Focus on large manifold dimensionality ratio (above 10)
COST: 64800
PREDICTION: This will reveal that manifold dimensionality ratio plays a significant role in the convergence rate and optimization properties of the Gramian-based contrastive loss, particularly in high-dimensional spaces; optimal convergence rates and stability are observed at medium manifold dimensionality ratios, but high manifold dimensionality ratio pose major complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning with Model Distillation and Pruning
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a novel federated multi-task learning approach that combines model distillation and pruning to improve the efficiency of knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models. Our method will use a novel proxy distillation network to transfer knowledge from the globally trained model to each user's local model, and then prune the local model to reduce the computational overhead. We'll demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using multiple real-world datasets and model architectures.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (2) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (3) Comparison with other knowledge distillation and pruning methods
COST: 86400
PREDICTION: This will show that the proposed approach significantly improves the efficiency of federated multi-task learning, with improved model accuracy and reduced communication overhead, but may also lead to over-distillation and under-pruning if not properly adapted.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning with Model Distillation and Pruning
PROPOSAL: We'll extend our previous proposal to include a more comprehensive analysis of the impact of different pruning strategies on the efficiency and effectiveness of federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we'll compare the performance of our proposed proxy distillation network with different pruning strategies (e.g., L1, L2, lottery ticket pruning) and evaluate their impact on model accuracy, communication overhead, and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (2) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (3) Comparison with other knowledge distillation and pruning methods; (4) Ablated version without pruning
COST: 129600
PREDICTION: This will reveal that the choice of pruning strategy significantly impacts the effectiveness and efficiency of federated multi-task learning, with L1 and lottery ticket pruning showing the best trade-offs between model accuracy and computational overhead, but may also lead to the loss of important features and knowledge if not properly adapted.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Defending Federated Multi-Task Learning Against Unauthorized Model Access and Knowledge Extraction
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate the security risks associated with federated multi-task learning and propose novel defense mechanisms to prevent unauthorized model access and knowledge extraction. Specifically, we'll design and implement a secure multiparty computation-based framework to securely aggregate knowledge across users and protect against malicious users.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (2) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (3) Comparison with existing secure multi-party computation methods
COST: 172800
PREDICTION: This will show that the proposed defense mechanisms are effective in preventing unauthorized model access and knowledge extraction, but may also introduce additional overhead and complexity, requiring careful trade-offs to ensure practicality.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Defending Federated Multi-Task Learning Against Unauthorized Model Access and Knowledge Extraction
PROPOSAL: We'll extend our previous proposal to include a more in-depth analysis of the trade-offs between security, efficiency, and effectiveness in federated multi-task learning. Specifically, we'll investigate the impact of the proposed defense mechanisms on model accuracy, communication overhead, and computational efficiency, and provide guidelines for practitioners to balance these competing factors.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Federated averaging on IID data; (2) Baseline: Homogeneous IID case; (3) Comparison with existing secure multi-party computation methods; (4) Ablated version without defense mechanisms
COST: 259200
PREDICTION: This will reveal that the proposed defense mechanisms can effectively balance security, efficiency, and effectiveness, but may also introduce additional complexity and overhead, requiring careful consideration of the trade-offs in different scenarios and settings.

PROPOSAL: We will adapt and extend our recent federated distillation method [WWW 2022] to directly handle task heterogeneity and allow users to choose different architectures, simultaneously incorporating knowledge distillation and contrastive learning to enable robust and high-quality sharing of information without sharing local data.

TITLE: Theoretical Foundation for Joint Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We will develop a theoretical framework to justify the Gramian-based contrastive loss [ICML 2022], and further extend it to handle an arbitrary number of models, and provide a bound on its performance over the shared representation space, thereby providing a theoretically grounded approach for joint representation alignment.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bounds against state-of-the-art results in [WWW 2022] for pairwise alignment, and verify our analysis using synthetic experiments.
COST: 6000

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Federated Multi-Task Learning with Self-Erasing based Model Alignment
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptive federated multi-task learning approach that adapts model architecture and dimensionality during the training process, and leverages self-erasing to align representations across users. In each round, users send their representations, and the server aggregates and aligns them via a contrastive loss that adapts to the feature spaces of the users. While adapting architectures, we minimize the distance between user feature spaces.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to recent methods like KGCL and Fed-CL, and also to a random architecture space search baseline that randomizes model dimensions and data modalities.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: Our method should achieve the best results in terms of model adaptation and feature space alignment, as well as reducing the domain gap between users. It might fail if self-erasing is not effective in aligning feature spaces, or if the adaptation process gets stuck in a suboptimal region of the architecture space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Knowledge Graph Based Federated Learning for Heterogeneous Tasks
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel knowledge graph based federated learning approach that leverages graph neural networks to align representations across users with different tasks, modeling potential relationships between tasks. We regularize the alignment process with a knowledge graph loss function that encourages shared common sense knowledge across tasks, while preserving task-specific information.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to recent knowledge distillation based methods like FedDistill and graph neural network methods like GNN-Fed, as well as a random graph construction baseline.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: Our method should achieve state-of-the-art results in terms of alignment and knowledge transfer across heterogeneous tasks, as well as improving task-agnostic performance. It might fail if the relationship modeling between tasks does not properly capture the underlying structure, or if the regularization does not effectively balance common sense and task-specific knowledge.

TITLE: Sequential Label Correction
PROPOSAL: Introduce a sequential label correction approach where noisy labels are iteratively corrected during training. Each iteration will involve selecting a subset of noisy labels to correct based on their influence on the model's prediction, and then updating the model on the corrected subset. This process can be repeated multiple times, allowing the model to adapt to the corrected labels and improve its performance. We will use the toughest instance-dependent noise scenario as the main experiment setting and use a regularized training loss during iterations.
CONTROLS: 1. Noisy label correction from uncertainty-based method, 2. Standard training without label correction, 3. Different iteration numbers for sequential label correction
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to provide further improvements over the uncertainty-based method, as the model adapts to corrected labels multiple times. However, it may require a careful tuning of parameters to balance the tradeoff between overcorrection and undercorrection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Model for Noisy Labels
PROPOSAL: We propose an evaluation of the robustness of the recently introduced Co-teaching++ algorithm [] against noisy labels. Co-teaching++ is a self-learning method that progressively refines the clean and noisy samples through an iterative cross-teacher training process. We compare it with the original Co-teaching algorithm and a more recent Meta Detach Label Learning (MDLL) algorithm. The experiments are run on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 5% and 20% symmetric noise, and various metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and mean squared error are used to evaluate the performance.
CONTROLS: We compare Co-teaching++ with the original Co-teaching and Meta Detach Label Learning (MDLL).
COST: 330
PREDICTION: Co-teaching++ is expected to outperform the other two methods in terms of accuracy and robustness on both datasets. However, its performance might degrade at higher noise levels, particularly when the label noise distribution is instance-dependent. 

It is worth noting that due to the self-learning nature of Co-teaching++, the result could also be noisy if not converged properly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Instance-Dependent Noise Correction using Graph Structure
PROPOSAL: We propose to design and evaluate a graph-based approach to correct noisy labels in the presence of instance-dependent noise. The method represents the data samples using a graph, where the edge weights capture the similarity between samples and the likelihood of label noise correlation. We then use a personalized PageRank algorithm to identify and corrected the noisy labels based on the local and global structure of the graph. The experiments are run on real-world datasets such as Yelp Restaurant Reviews and Amazon Product Reviews with noisy labels and a variety of assessment metrics including accuracy and label noise correlation.
CONTROLS: A comparison is made with the state-of-the-art label correction method, via self-training with noisy supervision or its variant ViaBoost [].
COST: 832.876
PREDICTION: The graph-based approach is expected to significantly improve the label correction accuracy and quality of the resulting models. However, its performance may be compromised by datasets with very complex or instance-dependent noise, requiring more computational resources for graph construction and the personalized PageRank algorithm.

The graph construction process is expected to be more expensive than ViaBoost.

TITLE: Active Label Correction Exploration using Bayesian Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage Bayesian optimization to actively explore different label correction possibilities and identify the most effective ones for noise correction. The Bayesian optimization framework is used to search for the optimal label correction strategy by evaluating different combinations of clean and noisy samples. The goal is to find a label correction strategy that balances the trade-off between over-correcting and under-correcting the noisy labels. The experiments are run on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 5% and 20% symmetric noise.
CONTROLS: A comparison is made with the state-of-the-art label correction method, Meta Detach Label Learning (MDLL), and also with the graph-based approach.
COST: 1345.6
PREDICTION: The Bayesian optimization-based approach is expected to effectively explore different label correction possibilities and identify the most effective ones for noise correction. However, its performance might be affected by the quality of the initial search space and the choice of surrogate model used in the Bayesian optimization framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Noisy Labels: Exposing a New Perspective
PROPOSAL: We propose to explore the potential of transfer learning in mitigating the effects of noisy labels. We hypothesize that, by pre-training a model on a clean dataset and fine-tuning it on a noisy dataset, we can transfer the knowledge learned from the clean dataset and improve the robustness of the model to noisy labels. We also investigate the effects of label noise on pre-trained models and design a new method to select relevant features and fine-tune the pre-trained model to adapt to noisy labels. The experiments are run on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 5% and 20% symmetric noise.
CONTROLS: A comparison is made with the state-of-the-art transfer learning methods and the previous label correction approaches.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach is expected to provide a new perspective on mitigating the effects of noisy labels. However, it might be challenging to pre-train a model on a clean dataset and fine-tune it on a noisy dataset without degrading the performance on clean data, which might add extra computational costs due to multiple training epochs.

TITLE: Label Corruption Frequency (LCF) Analysis for Noisy Label Mitigation
PROPOSAL: We propose to analyze and understand the distribution of label corruption frequencies (LCF) for different datasets and noise levels, which is crucial for designing effective noisy label mitigation methods. We investigate the relationship between LCF and various model performance metrics, such as accuracy and robustness, and design a method to estimate the optimal LCF for noisy label mitigation. The experiments are run on various datasets with noisy labels.

However, the estimation of optimal LCF might require additional computational resources and the choice of performance metrics might significantly impact the results. The overall contribution of this research is to provide a deeper understanding of the noisy label mitigation problem and facilitate the design of more effective methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Model for Noisy Labels
PROPOSAL: We propose an evaluation of the robustness of the recently introduced Co-teaching++ algorithm [] against noisy labels. Co-teaching++ is a self-learning method that progressively refines the clean and noisy samples through an iterative cross-teacher training process. We compare it with the original Co-teaching algorithm and a more recent Meta Detach Label Learning (MDLL) algorithm. The experiments are run on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 5% and 20% symmetric noise, and various metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and mean squared error are used to evaluate the performance.
CONTROLS: We compare Co-teaching++ with the original Co-teaching and Meta Detach Label Learning (MDLL).
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Co-teaching++ is expected to outperform the other two methods in terms of accuracy and robustness on both datasets. However, its performance might degrade at higher noise levels, particularly when the label noise distribution is instance-dependent. 

It is worth noting that due to the self-learning nature of Co-teaching++, the result could also be noisy if not converged properly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Instance-Dependent Noise Correction using Graph Structure
PROPOSAL: We propose to design and evaluate a graph-based approach to correct noisy labels in the presence of instance-dependent noise. The method represents the data samples using a graph, where the edge weights capture the similarity between samples and the likelihood of label noise correlation. We then use a personalized PageRank algorithm to identify and corrected the noisy labels based on the local and global structure of the graph. The experiments are run on real-world datasets such as Yelp Restaurant Reviews and Amazon Product Reviews with noisy labels and a variety of assessment metrics including accuracy and label noise correlation.
CONTROLS: A comparison is made with the state-of-the-art label correction method, via self-training with noisy supervision or its variant ViaBoost [].
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: The graph-based approach is expected to significantly improve the label correction accuracy and quality of the resulting models. However, its performance may be compromised by datasets with very complex or instance-dependent noise, requiring more computational resources for graph construction and the personalized PageRank algorithm.

The graph construction process is expected to be more expensive than ViaBoost.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Instance-Dependent Noise Correction using Graph Structure
PROPOSAL: We modify the previous approach by incorporating more sophisticated graph embedding techniques, such as Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) or Graph Attention Network (GAT), to enhance the representation of samples and the structure of the graph. The goal is to leverage the hierarchical information in the graph more effectively to detect and correct noisy labels. The experiments remain the same as before.
CONTROLS: A comparison is made with the previous graph-based method and ViaBoost, with ablation studies on the different graph embedding techniques.
COST: 3500
PREDICTION: The improved graph-based approach is expected to provide better label correction accuracy and noise robustness. However, its performance might be sensitive to the choice of graph embedding technique and hyperparameter tuning, which may add extra computational costs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Coreset-based Sample Selection
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of a model trained on a reduced set of samples selected using a coreset approach to one trained on the full dataset. The coreset is constructed by iteratively adding the samples most informative for classification, and the dataset is assumed to be partially labeled with noisy labels. We will use a classification task on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a corruption ratio of 20%, compared to a baseline model trained on the full dataset without any filtering or selection.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: model trained on full dataset, 2) Noisy Labels Only: model trained on fully corrupted dataset, 3) Random Subset: model trained on a random subset of samples selected without considering any noise or informative value.
COST: 125000
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to improve robustness to noisy labels, especially when the amount of corrupted data is relatively small, but may struggle in scenarios with a large amount of corrupted data or with highly instance-dependent noise.

TITLE: Active Learning-based Label Correction Method
PROPOSAL: This experiment explores the application of active learning techniques to selectively correct noisy labels in the training dataset. The method will first identify ambiguous samples using uncertainty estimates from a pre-trained model, and then query human annotators to correct the labels of the most uncertain samples. The corrected labels will be used to fine-tune the model, and the resulting performance will be compared to a baseline model trained on the original dataset with noisy labels. We will use a classification task on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a corruption ratio of 5% compared to a baseline model trained on the fully corrupted dataset.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: model trained on full dataset with noisy labels, 2) Random Label Correction: model trained on noisy dataset with randomly corrected labels.
COST: 150000
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to improve the accuracy of the model in noisy data regimes, but the effectiveness may depend on the quality of the human annotators and the amount of ambiguous samples.

TITLE: Investigation of Confidence-weighted Loss Functions for Noisy Labels
PROPOSAL: This experiment evaluates the effect of confidence-weighted loss functions on the robustness of deep neural networks trained on noisy label datasets. The idea is to use the model's confidence estimates to downweight the loss contributions from samples that are likely to be mislabeled. We will implement this using the Mean Teacher loss and compare its performance to the standard cross-entropy loss on a classification task on the CIFAR-100 dataset with a corruption ratio of 10% compared to a baseline model trained on the fully corrupted dataset.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: model trained on full dataset with noisy labels and standard cross-entropy loss, 2) Mean Teacher without noise, 3) Standard ERM with confidence threshold.
COST: 184500
PREDICTION: The confidence-weighted loss functions are likely to improve the model's robustness to noisy labels, but may not be effective in scenarios with highly instance-dependent noise or when the noise is spatially coherent within classes.

TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Coreset-based Sample Selection
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the performance of a model trained on a reduced set of samples selected using a coreset approach to one trained on the full dataset. The coreset is constructed by iteratively adding the samples most informative for classification, and the dataset is assumed to be partially labeled with noisy labels. We will use a classification task on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a corruption ratio of 20%, compared to a baseline model trained on the full dataset without any filtering or selection.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: model trained on full dataset, 2) Noisy Labels Only: model trained on fully corrupted dataset, 3) Random Subset: model trained on a random subset of samples selected without considering any noise or informative value.
COST: 375000
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to improve robustness to noisy labels, especially when the amount of corrupted data is relatively small, but may struggle in scenarios with a large amount of corrupted data or with highly instance-dependent noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Learning-based Label Correction Method
PROPOSAL: This experiment explores the application of active learning techniques to selectively correct noisy labels in the training dataset. The method will first identify ambiguous samples using uncertainty estimates from a pre-trained model, and then query human annotators to correct the labels of the most uncertain samples. The corrected labels will be used to fine-tune the model, and the resulting performance will be compared to a baseline model trained on the original dataset with noisy labels. We will use a classification task on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a corruption ratio of 5% compared to a baseline model trained on the fully corrupted dataset.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: model trained on full dataset with noisy labels, 2) Random Label Correction: model trained on noisy dataset with randomly corrected labels.
COST: 450000
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to improve the accuracy of the model in noisy data regimes, but the effectiveness may depend on the quality of the human annotators and the amount of ambiguous samples.

PROPOSAL: This experiment evaluates the effect of confidence-weighted loss functions on the robustness of deep neural networks trained on noisy label datasets. The idea is to use the model's confidence estimates to downweight the loss contributions from samples that are likely to be mislabeled. We will implement this using the Mean Teacher loss and compare its performance to the standard cross-entropy loss on a classification task on the CIFAR-100 dataset with a corruption ratio of 10% compared to a baseline model trained on the fully corrupted dataset.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: model trained on full dataset with noisy labels and standard cross-entropy loss, 2) Mean Teacher without noise, 3) Standard ERM with confidence threshold.

PREDICTION: The confidence-weighted loss functions are likely to improve the model's robustness to noisy labels, but may not be effective in scenarios with highly instance-dependent noise or when the noise is spatially coherent within classes.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Term Event-RGB Fusion for Dense Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes an online learning framework, Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN), to achieve high-frame-rate semantic segmentation. Given an RGB frame $I_t$ and the corresponding event stream $\mathcal{E}_{t-\Delta t \to t+\delta t}$, ERFN first extracts a compact representation of the event stream using a spatiotemporal attention mechanism. The extracted event representation is then fused with $I_t$ through a feature pyramid network. The fused features are fed into a time-dilated convolutional neural network to generate a sequence of dense semantic predictions at arbitrary timestamps within the perceptual gap.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: RGB-only semantic segmentation model; Baseline 2: Event-only semantic segmentation model.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: ERFN is expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving, drone navigation, and quadruped robot navigation benchmarks, with a notable improvement in segmentation accuracy at arbitrary timestamps. However, it may struggle in highly dynamic scenes and long prediction intervals due to the limited contextual information in a single past RGB frame.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Coherence Awareness for Event-RGB Alignment
PROPOSAL: This experiment introduces a temporal coherence awareness module to enhance the fusion of events and RGB frames. By learning the temporal dependencies between events and RGB frames, the module can better align the event representation with the RGB context, leading to more accurate predictions. The module is integrated with the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) proposed in Proposal 1. A new skip connection is added to leverage the temporal coherence information in both forward and backward frames.
CONTROLS: Revision of Proposal 1 (ERFN without the additional module).
COST: 500
PREDICTION: The addition of temporal coherence awareness is expected to further improve the performance of ERFN, especially in scenes with high motion and occlusions. However, it might increase the risk of overfitting to the temporal dynamics in the training data, affecting its generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semantic Localization with Adversarial Events
PROPOSAL: Inspired by adversarial training, this experiment introduces an adversarial event generator to simulate adversarial events that might appear in real-world scenes. The goal is to enhance the robustness of the Event-RGB Fusion Network (ERFN) to such events and improve its ability to predict accurate semantic padding even in the absence of clear RGB information. The adversarial event generator is trained to produce events that mislead the model, and the model is trained to be resilient to these events.
CONTROLS: Revision of Proposal 2 (ERFN with the addition of temporal coherence awareness).
COST: 729.17
PREDICTION: By adding adversarial events, the model is expected to produce more robust predictions, especially in scenes with high occlusions or missing RGB information. However, the addition of the adversarial generator might increase the computational cost and require additional fine-tuning to achieve optimal results.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Event-`RGB Conditional Random Fields
PROPOSAL: This experiment introduces a conditional random field (CRF) to model the uncertainty of event-based features and RGB information. The CRF is designed to capture the spatial and temporal dependencies between events and RGB values, allowing the model to output uncertainty maps that can be used for probability-based dense semantic segmentation. The proposal is based on a novel loss function that combines the standard cross-entropy loss with a weighted sum of the mean squared error and the mean absolute error between the model's predictions and the ground truth values.
CONTROLS: Revision of Proposal 3 (ERFN with the addition of adversarial events).
COST: 1036.8
PREDICTION: By incorporating the uncertainty-aware CRF, the model is expected to produce more accurate uncertainty maps and achieve better performance under varying lighting conditions, occlusions, and viewpoint changes. However, the computational cost of the CRF might be significant, affecting the overall performance and real-time processing capabilities of the model.

TITLE: Multi-Agent Hierarchical Reasoning for Event-RGB Fusion
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a multi-agent hierarchical reasoning framework for event-RGB fusion, which leverages a hierarchical attention mechanism to recursively reason about the relationships between events and RGB features at multiple scales and abstraction levels. The framework allows the model to focus on the most informative events and RGB features, leading to improved semantic segmentation performance.

PREDICTION: The multi-agent hierarchical reasoning framework is expected to improve the model's ability to reason about complex scenes and relationships between events and RGB features. However, the increased complexity of the model might lead to overfitting or require additional regularization techniques to prevent overparameterization.

The goal is to demonstrate the effectiveness of these components when combined into a single model.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: RGB-only semantic segmentation model; Baseline 2: Event-only semantic segmentation model; Revision of Proposal 2 (ERFN with the addition of temporal coherence awareness); Revision of Proposal 3 (ERFN with the addition of adversarial events); Revision of Proposal 4 (ERFN with the uncertainty-aware CRF).
COST: 4200

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Temporal Coherence Awareness for Event-RGB Alignment
PROPOSAL: This revised experiment introduces a more robust and efficient implementation of temporal coherence awareness for Event-RGB alignment. Specifically, we propose to utilize a temporal convolutional network (TCN) to learn the temporal dependencies between events and RGB frames, instead of a traditional convolutional neural network (CNN). This modification aims to improve the model's ability to capture long-range temporal dependencies and enhance its robustness to occlusions and viewpoint changes.
CONTROLS: Revision of Proposal 2 (ERFN); Revision of Proposal 3 (ERFN with the addition of adversarial events); Revision of Proposal 4 (ERFN with the uncertainty-aware CRF).
COST: 3300
PREDICTION: By utilizing the TCN-based temporal coherence awareness, the model is expected to improve its accuracy and robustness under various temporal scenarios. However, the performance might degrade if the TCN layer fails to capture the essential temporal relationships between events and RGB frames.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Event-`RGB Conditional Random Fields
PROPOSAL: This revised experiment introduces a multi-resolution version of the uncertainty-aware conditional random field (CRF) to better capture the spatial and temporal dependencies between events and RGB values at different scales. Specifically, we propose to use a crisscross Apollo pattern to combine features extracted from different resolution spaces, allowing the model to capture more precise uncertainty relationships between events and RGB features.
CONTROLS: Revision of Proposal 1 (long-term event-RGB fusion for dense semantic segmentation); Revision of Proposal 2 (temporal coherence awareness for event-RGB alignment); Revision of Proposal 3 (semantic localization with adversarial events).

PREDICTION: By incorporating the multi-resolution CRF, the model is expected to produce more accurate uncertainty maps and achieve better performance under varying lighting conditions, occlusions, and viewpoint changes. However, the additional feature transformation and CRF layers might increase the computational cost and memory requirements.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a multi-agent hierarchical reasoning framework for event-RGB fusion, which leverages a hierarchical attention mechanism to recursively reason about the relationships between events and RGB features at multiple scales and abstraction levels. The framework allows the model to focus on the most informative events and RGB features, leading to improved semantic segmentation performance.
CONTROLS: Revision of Proposal 1 (long-term event-RGB fusion for dense semantic segmentation); Revision of Proposal 2 (temporal coherence awareness for event-RGB alignment); Revision of Proposal 3 (semantic localization with adversarial events).

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a meta-learning framework for event-RGB fusion, which learns a dynamic attention mechanism that adapts to the characteristics of the input data and the task at hand. The framework uses meta-learning to adapt the attention weights and selection strategy, allowing the model to focus on the most informative events and RGB features in a dynamic and task-dependent manner.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-Camera Assisted RGB Predictive Segmentation
PROPOSAL: 
We will adapt a graph neural network model (GNN) that fuses RGB and event stream information to predict dense semantic maps at any timestamp within the perceptual gap. We'll modify the graph node and edge structure to handle the spatial and temporal features of the event stream, and incorporate causal masks to enforce temporal causality.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to a standard RGB-only graph neural network model as a baseline.
- Ablate the event stream to evaluate its contribution to segmentation accuracy.
- Compare to a state-of-the-art RGB-event fusion model that doesn't enforce causality or anytime prediction.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect improved segmentation accuracy compared to RGB-only and non-causal RGB-event fusion methods. However, challenging cases in highly dynamic scenes may still cause errors, particularly if objects move swiftly or objects reappear after being occluded.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-Triggered Temporal Aggregation
PROPOSAL: 
We propose to incorporate event-triggered temporal aggregation (ETTA) to selectively aggregate spatial features from the RGB frame and event stream features over time. ETTA will identify important events and compute temporal aggregations accordingly, focusing on regions with high motion or changes, thereby capturing the dynamic nature of the scene. This will be applied to the node updates of the GNN in Event-Camera Assisted RGB Predictive Segmentation (proposal 1).
CONTROLS: 
- Control for the trade-off between the degree of temporal aggregation and the computational cost of aggregating event stream features.
- Compare with a baseline that applies uniform temporal aggregation across the entire image.
- Evaluate the contribution of ETTA to the overall predictive segmentation accuracy.
COST: 5200
PREDICTION: With the incorporation of ETTA, we expect improved predictive segmentation accuracy in dynamic scenes, particularly in areas with significant motion changes. However, potential over-aggregation in regions of low motion may introduce errors.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Event-Camera Assisted RGB Predictive Segmentation (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: 
We refine the GNN model in Event-Camera Assisted RGB Predictive Segmentation (proposal 1) by introducing a spatial attention module to selectively weigh the contributions of event stream features and RGB features at different spatial locations. This will enable better information transfer between the two modalities, potentially capturing spatial dependencies between high-motion regions and improving overall predictive accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with the original GNN model as a baseline.
- Ablate the spatial attention module to evaluate its contribution.
- Compare with a graph-attention-based GNN model that adapts weights for the entire graph, rather than using spatial attention.
COST: 5500
PREDICTION: With the addition of spatial attention, we expect enhanced predictive segmentation accuracy, especially in high-motion regions where accurate spatial dependencies are critical. Challenges may arise when the spatial attention weights are difficult to learn, such as in very sparse or highly occluded event stream regions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Occurrence Guided Dropout
PROPOSAL: 
We propose Occurrence Guided Dropout (OGD), a novel dropout strategy tailored for event streams. OGD will selectively drop nodes or edges in the GNN model based on the occurrence of salient events in the event stream, allowing the model to focus on the most informative features and reduce overfitting. This will be integrated into the GNNs in proposal 1 and 2.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with standard dropout as a baseline.
- Ablate OGD to evaluate its contribution.
- Evaluate the trade-off between the degree of dropout and the model's predictive accuracy.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: With OGD, we expect reduced overfitting and improved model robustness, particularly in scenarios with high event noise or sparse event data. However, aggressive dropout may also lead to underfitting if the model drops critical information.

TITLE: Multitask Learning for Event-Camera and RGB-Frame Understanding
PROPOSAL: 
We will train the models in proposal 1-5 jointly on both event-camera and RGB-frame datasets, with a multitask learning objective that encourages the models to leverage the complementary strengths of both modalities. Specifically, we will task the models to predict segmentation, depth, and optic flow from both event-camera and RGB-frame data.
CONTROLS:

- Ablate individual tasks (segmentation, depth, and optic flow) to evaluate their contribution.
- Evaluate the trade-off between multitask learning and monotasking in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.
COST: 21000
PREDICTION: With multitask learning, we expect improved predictive accuracy and robustness across both event-camera and RGB-frame modalities, particularly in scenarios with high event noise orRGB-frame occlusions. However, the added complexity of multitask learning may also lead to increased computation time or overfitting if not regularized properly.

TITLE: Event RGB Fusion for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Implement a neural network based approach, called Event RGB Fusion Network (ERFNet), that fuses sparse event streams with a single RGB frame to predict dense, semantically accurate pixel-level labels at any arbitrary timestamp within the perceptual gap. ERFNet will learn to effectively merge the static contextual information from the RGB frame with the temporal information from the event stream, using a two-branch architecture with a novel event-resampling module that gineralizes past work and an attention-based module that selectively combines event features with RGB features.
CONTROLS: We include ablations: a) removing the event-resampling module and b) replacing the attention-based module with a standard conv-bn-relu layer. We also compare ERFNet with state-of-the-art multi-modal fusion approaches and RGB-only baseline models using metrics such as mIoU, mF1 score and ASE.
COST: 16.5
PREDICTION: We expect ERFNet to outperform the ablated variants and compared methods by a notable margin, especially in highly dynamic scenes. However, we also acknowledge that ERFNet may struggle with longer prediction intervals, leading to a decrease in accuracy over time.

TITLE: Temporal Consistency Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a temporal consistency evaluation protocol to investigate the performance of ERFNet in predicting segmentations at varying time offsets within the perceptual gap. This will involve generating a range of synthetic events at different time intervals between two consecutive RGB frames and evaluating ERFNet's ability to produce consistent segmentations across these intervals. Specifically, we will measure the segmental F1 score, precision, and recall at different time offsets to better understand ERFNet's performance under temporal variations.

PREDICTION: We expect ERFNet to exhibit notable improvements in temporal consistency when predicting segmentations at small time offsets (e.g., 5ms), while starting to degrade at larger offsets (e.g., 20ms), indicating the potential limitations of the current fusion mechanism when dealing with increasing time spans.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: RGB-Event Fusion with Masked Transformers for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to predict dense semantic maps from low-frame-rate RGB streams and temporally dense event data. This method leverages a masked transformer architecture that learns to selectively attend to relevant event timestamps and RGB locations, following our modified version of Roomba, selectable or "maskable" transformer architecture. This attention mechanism enables the model to utilize event information from a target time window to inform its RGB-driven predictions, preventing catastrophic forgetting as dynamic scenes evolve over time.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Model: Video semantic segmentation on a standard RGB video dataset to evaluate performance at the same frame rate, and (2) RGB-only Masked Transformer: remove the event conditioning from our proposed model to evaluate how well it performs on static scenes.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: This method should improve upon previous RGB-event fusion models by effectively addressing the anytime prediction challenge, given its ability to selectively attend to event information. However, it may struggle in highly dynamic scenes with rapidly changing conditions or with limited training data from diverse driving scenarios where a wide variety of relevant events may occur.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: RGB-Event Fusion with Masked Transformers for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to predict dense semantic maps from low-frame-rate RGB streams and temporally dense event data. This method leverages a masked transformer architecture that learns to selectively attend to relevant event timestamps and RGB locations, following our modified version of Roomba, selectable or "maskable" transformer architecture. This attention mechanism enables the model to utilize event information from a target time window to inform its RGB-driven predictions, preventing catastrophic forgetting as dynamic scenes evolve over time.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Model: Video semantic segmentation on a standard RGB video dataset to evaluate performance at the same frame rate, and (2) RGB-only Masked Transformer: remove the event conditioning from our proposed model to evaluate how well it performs on static scenes.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: This method should improve upon previous RGB-event fusion models by effectively addressing the anytime prediction challenge, given its ability to selectively attend to event information. However, it may struggle in highly dynamic scenes with rapidly changing conditions or with limited training data from diverse driving scenarios where a wide variety of relevant events may occur.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Enhancing RGB-Event Fusion with Temporal Consistency Loss
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the RGB-Event Fusion with Masked Transformers, we propose incorporating a temporal consistency loss (TCL) term into the objective function. TCL assesses the consistency between predictions made on consecutive time windows, leveraging the temporally dense event data to provide reliable guidance on the dynamic scene's evolution. By minimizing TCL, the model encourages generating coherent predictions even when faced with rapidly changing scenarios.
CONTROLS: (1) RGB-Event Fusion with Masked Transformers only, (2) TCL with a simple baseline matching each time window's prediction to the next one in the sequence, and (3) STL (Structured Time Loss) Rx: enjoying pre-computed accumulated distortions aggregated from several future time-ste step by step for Compensation to prove robustness, before being evaluated.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: The addition of TCL should significantly improve the performance of the RGB-Event Fusion model, particularly in high dynamic scenes. However, the model may still struggle with extreme scene dynamics, and it will be crucial to balance the weight of TCL in the overall loss function to avoid over-fitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-Cloud: A Multi-modal Fusion Framework for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception
PROPOSAL: To address the problem, we will develop a multi-modal fusion framework, called Event-Cloud, that effectively merges the rich semantic context of the past RGB frame with the temporally dense event stream. Event-Cloud employs a novel event-inspired attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most relevant events that could have occluded or misled the past RGB frame. This attention will be combined with a hierarchical graph neural network architecture, allowing for efficient modeling of complex scene structures and object interactions. By leveraging both the spatial and temporal context available in the event stream, Event-Cloud will generate accurate and dense semantic predictions within the perceptual gap.
CONTROLS: A baseline multi-modal fusion approach using a simple sum fusion strategy, and an ablation study of the event-inspired attention mechanism.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: We expect Event-Cloud to significantly improve segmentation accuracy within the blind interval, with a performance boost of at least 15% compared to the baseline multi-modal fusion approach, especially in highly dynamic scenes. However, the method might struggle with extreme occlusions or significant changes in scene context, compromising its ability to generate accurate predictions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: CAMemb: A Novel Approach for Event-RGB Merging using Boosting from CAMs
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the concept of Class Activation Mapping (CAM), we propose CAMemb, a novel method that leverages the strengths of both event and RGB data to produce accurate and dense semantic predictions at any arbitrary timestamp within the perceptual gap. CAMemb uses a generative neural network architecture to combine the top-down attention maps from a CAM-inspired module applied on events with an appearance-based RGB representation. This fusion process is carried out using adversarial training for better context encoding, safely maintaining accuracy and robustness regarding assumed boundary jump presence.
CONTROLS: A baseline approach that fuses the event and RGB features using a simple concatenation method, and an ablation study of the adversarial training process.
COST: 2079

PREDICTION: We expect CAMemb to achieve competitive results with Event-Cloud, but with the potential advantage of being more interpretable and less prone to overfitting. However, its performance on highly dynamic scenes might be negatively affected due to the limitations of the CAM-inspired module in capturing spatial contexts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Event-Driven Capsule Networks for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the concept of capsule networks, we propose an event-driven capsule network (EDCN) architecture that integrates spatial and temporal information from event streams to make robust and dense semantic predictions. Each event-driven capsule represents a 3D shape or an object part, and the routing between capsules is learned through an iterative process that favors coherent and meaningful representations. The EDCN architecture is particularly well-suited for high-temporal-resolution event streams, enabling accurate predictions at high frame rates.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the standard semantic segmentation benchmark, and an ablation study to evaluate the impact of the event-driven capsule architecture.
COST: 3600

PREDICTION: We expect EDCN to demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on high-frame-rate semantic perception tasks, with significant improvements in handling object occlusions and rapid movement. However, the EDCN architecture might be computationally expensive due to the complexity of the capsule routing mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-Cloud: A Multi-modal Fusion Framework for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Perception
PROPOSAL: To address the problem, we will develop a multi-modal fusion framework, called Event-Cloud, that effectively merges the rich semantic context of the past RGB frame with the temporally dense event stream. Event-Cloud employs a novel event-inspired attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most relevant events that could have occluded or misled the past RGB frame. This attention will be combined with a hierarchical graph neural network architecture, allowing for efficient modeling of complex scene structures and object interactions. By leveraging both the spatial and temporal context available in the event stream, Event-Cloud will generate accurate and dense semantic predictions within the perceptual gap.
CONTROLS: A baseline multi-modal fusion approach using a simple sum fusion strategy, and an ablation study of the event-inspired attention mechanism.
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: We expect Event-Cloud to significantly improve segmentation accuracy within the blind interval, with a performance boost of at least 15% compared to the baseline multi-modal fusion approach, especially in highly dynamic scenes. However, the method might struggle with extreme occlusions or significant changes in scene context, compromising its ability to generate accurate predictions.

TITLE: CAMemb: A Novel Approach for Event-RGB Merging using Boosting from CAMs
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the concept of Class Activation Mapping (CAM), we propose CAMemb, a novel method that leverages the strengths of both event and RGB data to produce accurate and dense semantic predictions at any arbitrary timestamp within the perceptual gap. CAMemb uses a generative neural network architecture to combine the top-down attention maps from a CAM-inspired module applied on events with an appearance-based RGB representation. This fusion process is carried out using adversarial training for better context encoding, safely maintaining accuracy and robustness regarding assumed boundary jump presence.
CONTROLS: A baseline approach that fuses the event and RGB features using a simple concatenation method, and an ablation study of the adversarial training process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Key-Image Exploration for Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the role of sampling strategies in personalized 3D generation, using a sampling strategy based on exploring regions of interest corresponding to key-views of the subject. We will adopt the popular Class-Based Viewpoint Estimation approach, mapping X, Y, Z camera poses to viewpoint codes, and exploit this ordering to prioritize viewpoints, assigning higher probabilities to viewpoints that require higher-resolution rendering. In the experiments, we will fine-tune different pre-trained networks (e.g., Meta-Dream, DALL-E, DALL-E Mini) trained on coarse-to-fine resolution 3D models, using this sampling strategy on the test subjects and datasets (e.g. dataset 3 with 2000+ 3D subjects; dataset 4 with several dozen videos of 3D subjects).
CONTROLS: We will compare our sampling strategy against a random sampling strategy and the existing identity-preserving view-aware spatial-sampling method.
COST: 210
PREDICTION: This strategy will mitigate systematic errors, but may only work for 3D subjects observable from multiple viewpoints, and may have difficulty addressing subject identities preserved across specific body parts (e.g., ears, horns, legs). Overall, we expect a moderate improvement by about 10-15% over the baseline view-aware spatial-sampling method in terms of the just noticeable difference of the identity error.

TITLE: Identity-Preserving Multi-View Diffusion Model with Temporal Consolidation
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the Multi-View Diffusion Model (MVDM) to incorporate temporal consolidation of views. This will involve finetuning a 4D generation model to generate a target subject and appending a 3D diffusion module. The diffusion module simulates the implantation of target subject's view under 2D consistency regularizer and uses temporal consolidation loss for  reconstructed sequences from the front and side views that are observed to predict the view the model is hallucinating and utilize the rich visual information from these multiple views and motion patterns to hallucinate the missing views accurately. By doing so, the model can capture identity information from different viewpoints and angles, making it a potentially more effective method for hallucinating novel views.
CONTROLS: We will compare this approach to the basic MVDM that only uses spatial transformations to predict novel views and evaluate its performance on dataset 6 with 170 subjects and complex rotational viewpoint transformations.
COST: 2408
PREDICTION: By leveraging temporal consolidation, we expect the proposed approach to achieve a 25% reduction in the identity error at novel views, especially in complex rotations, and perform significantly better than the traditional MVDM in many cases. However, this could come at the cost of significant increases in computational complexity and latency due to the additional 4D-to-3D diffusion module.

TITLE: Extending Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose adapting a 4D diffusion model by conditioning its number of steps on a learned subject-specific latent encoding, derived from the input video. This subject-specific diffusion model will take in a video of a specific subject, infer the latent code from the input, and adapt its number of steps based on this code, to hallucinate novel viewpoints that accurately preserve the subject's identity and appearance.
CONTROLS: We compare against the current state-of-the-art 4D generation models that use class-agnostic one-step diffusion, as well as ablation studies on the effect of the subject-specific latent encoding and the number of steps in the diffusion process.
COST: 1276.2
PREDICTION: This proposal should give us competitive results with existing 4D models while better capturing the subject's identity with novel viewpoints, but may struggle to handle complex scenes with multiple subjects.

TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Subject-Driven 3D/4D Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training scheme to improve the robustness of subject-driven 3D/4D generation models against potential attacks or noise in the input data. The model is trained to minimize the difference between the generated assets and the real assets, while an adversary aims to maximize this difference.
CONTROLS: We compare against the state-of-the-art 3D/4D generation models and evaluate the impact of the adversarial training scheme on the quality and robustness of generated 3D/4D assets.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the robustness of subject-driven 3D/4D generation models, but the added complexity of the adversarial training scheme might lead to increased computational requirements and risk of overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework that trains the subject-driven 3D generation model to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, such as 3D reconstruction, texture synthesis, and normal estimation. This framework aims to improve the robustness and generalizability of the model by leveraging the shared features and learning multiple tasks jointly.
CONTROLS: We compare against the state-of-the-art 3D generation models and evaluate the impact of multi-task learning on the quality and robustness of generated 3D assets.
COST: 3750
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the robustness and generalizability of subject-driven 3D generation models, but the added complexity of multi-task learning might lead to increased computational requirements and risk of overfitting.

textes:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Extending Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose adapting a 4D diffusion model by conditioning its number of steps on a learned subject-specific latent encoding, derived from the input video. This subject-specific diffusion model will take in a video of a specific subject, infer the latent code from the input, and adapt its number of steps based on this code, to hallucinate novel viewpoints that accurately preserve the subject's identity and appearance.
CONTROLS: We compare against the current state-of-the-art 4D generation models that use class-agnostic one-step diffusion, as well as ablation studies on the effect of the subject-specific latent encoding and the number of steps in the diffusion process.
COST: 3840
PREDICTION: This proposal should give us competitive results with existing 4D models while better capturing the subject's identity with novel viewpoints, but may struggle to handle complex scenes with multiple subjects.
