ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Conservative Approaches for Subject-Driven 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose using a series of refinement networks that iteratively refine the generated 3D asset based on a consistency loss that ensures the identity of the subject is preserved across multiple views, in a subject-specific 3D transformation-diffusion model. Each refinement network will be trained to correct the hallucinations of novel viewpoints in a conservative manner, to maintain the subject's appearance within specific tolerance thresholds.
CONTROLS: We compare against the state-of-the-art 3D generation models and evaluate the effect of the number of refinement iterations on the quality of the generated 3D assets, with and without the proposed consistency loss.
COST: 5760
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve the preservation of subject identity in novel viewpoints, but the added complexity of the refinement networks might lead to increased computational requirements.

alia

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: REVISED Conservative Approaches for Subject-Driven 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: We modify the refinement networks to incorporate both cycle consistency and adversarial losses to further improve the realism and identity preservation of the generated 3D assets. Additionally, we explore the use of a subject-specific prior, learned from few-shot precedent images, to guide the refinement process and enforce consistency across different views of the same subject.
CONTROLS: We continue to compare against the state-of-the-art 3D generation models, with a focus on understanding the impact of the additional losses and the subject-specific prior on the quality of generated 3D assets.
COST: 7200 (initial proposal was revised to include additional components)
PREDICTION: This revised approach should provide state-of-the-art results on subject-driven 3D generation, but the increased complexity of the loss functions and the prior may require significant computational resources to converge.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Font-averaged personalization in 3D/4D generation
PROPOSAL: Train the state-of-the-art 4D generation model, NudeNet [1], using a novel training objective that averages the output features over multiple fonts (Arial, Times New Roman, etc.) of the text prompts. This encourages the model to extract more abstract features of the subject, potentially preserving identity across viewpoints.
CONTROLS: (1) Train NudeNet on the original training objective; (2) Use only a subset of fonts.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Improved identity preservation for unseen viewpoints, but might suffer from reduced photorealism due to the abstract feature extraction.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Riding the wave of differential privacy
PROPOSAL: Propose a new personalization method by incorporating differential privacy into the score distillation process of multi-view diffusion models. Introduce noise to the distillation objective, ensuring that the model's predictions of novel views are private and robust against identity-preserving attacks. This adaptation may help correct biases in the training data and improve identity preservation.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline multi-view diffusion model without differential privacy; (2) Experiment with different noise schedules.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Improved identity preservation due to reduced vulnerabilities to identity-preserving attacks, but might come at the expense of increased computational requirements for training.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Mean teacher with identity constraints
PROPOSAL: Implement a mean teacher mechanism to improve the personalization quality of 3D/4D generation. Train a teacher model using a standard 3D/4D generation objective, and then use the teacher's output to regularize the student model, which is trained with identity constraints (e.g., requiring the generated views to preserve the subject's appearance).
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline teacher-student architecture without identity constraints; (2) Experiment with different teacher-student architectures and identity constraints.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Improved personalization quality through the regularization of the student model, but might come at the expense of increased computational requirements for maintaining the teacher and student models.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Subject-driven meta-learning for 3D/4D generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a subject-driven meta-learning framework for 3D/4D generation. Train a meta-model to learn how to adapt 3D/4D generation models to specific subjects, using a fixed set of image and video examples. This adaptable model can then be fine-tuned for various subjects with a minimal number of examples.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline 3D/4D generation without meta-learning; (2) Experiment with different meta-learning architectures and adaptation protocols.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Improved adaptability and reduced training requirements for 3D/4D generation on specific subjects, but might suffer from overfitting and reduced generative quality for unseen subjects.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Physics-informed HoX embeddings for 3D/4D generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce physics-informed HoX (Hidden Input-Output) embeddings to incorporate physical constraints into the 3D/4D generation process. Train the HoX embeddings using a domain-specific physics model, and then use these embeddings to regularize and constrain the 3D/4D generation output, improving its plausibility and faithfulness.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline 3D/4D generation without HoX embeddings; (2) Experiment with different physics models and HoX architectures.
COST: 1320
PREDICTION: Improved plausibility and faithfulness of 3D/4D generation through physics-informed constraints, but might come at the expense of increased computational requirements and potential brittleness of the physics models.

TITLE: Self-supervised personalization through temporal coherence
PROPOSAL: Develop a self-supervised personalization approach for 3D/4D generation through temporal coherence. Train a model to predict the next frame in a 3D/4D sequence, with the goal of learning a personalization-free and subject-agnostic representation that can be fine-tuned for specific subjects using a minimal amount of labeled data.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline 3D/4D generation without self-supervised learning; (2) Experiment with different prediction architectures and temporal coherence losses.
COST: 1620
PREDICTION: Improved adaptability and reduced labeling requirements for 3D/4D generation on specific subjects, but might suffer from overfitting and reduced generative quality for sequences with complex temporal dynamics.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Context-Aware Multi-View Personalization
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we extend the popular text-to-image diffusion model, DALL-E, to generate 3D/4D assets with personalized views. We use a novel multi-modal fusion approach to incorporate the subject-specific image/video input into the model's context, allowing it to infer appearance cues for unobserved viewpoints. We also deploy a novel modality-agnostic evaluation metric, the Identity-Preserving Score (IPS), to assess the model's ability to preserve the subject's identity across views.
CONTROLS: We compare our method, CAP (Context-Aware Personalization), against two strong baselines: a state-of-the-art 4D generation model (DeepVoxels) and a personalized 3D model (Subject-GAN) finetuned on a limited dataset.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect CAP to significantly outperform the baselines in IPS, with a 10-20% improvement, and achieve state-of-the-art results for personalized 3D/4D generation. The method might fail to generalize to subjects with complex textures or non-repeating patterns due to its reliance on image/video input.

TITLE: Context-Aware Multi-View Personalization
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we extend the popular text-to-image diffusion model, DALL-E, to generate 3D/4D assets with personalized views. We use a novel multi-modal fusion approach to incorporate the subject-specific image/video input into the model's context, allowing it to infer appearance cues for unobserved viewpoints. We also deploy a novel modality-agnostic evaluation metric, the Identity-Preserving Score (IPS), to assess the model's ability to preserve the subject's identity across views.
CONTROLS: We compare our method, CAP (Context-Aware Personalization), against two strong baselines: a state-of-the-art 4D generation model (DeepVoxels) and a personalized 3D model (Subject-GAN) finetuned on a limited dataset.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect CAP to significantly outperform the baselines in IPS, with a 10-20% improvement, and achieve state-of-the-art results for personalized 3D/4D generation. The method might fail to generalize to subjects with complex textures or non-repeating patterns due to its reliance on image/video input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Personalized 4D Generation with Face Alignment
PROPOSAL: We finetune the most recent state-of-the-art 4D video-to-3D model, VIBE, on a synthetic dataset of animals videos with frontal face views. The model is augmented with a face alignment network (Facenet), which can detect and align faces across different views. We leverage this alignment information to guide the pose-invariant feature extraction and refinement stages of VIBE, and thus, generate more realistic and consistent animated 3D assets with preserved identities.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to an ablation study of the Facenet-augmented VIBE model without facial alignment and to a baseline model, ShapeNet+, also finetuned on the same synthetic dataset but without the face alignment guidance.
COST: 1,764 GPU-h
PREDICTION: By leveraging the facial alignment, we expect to achieve better identity preservation and consistency in the generated 3D poses, as well as a reduction in errors in color and appearance for novel views. However, the model might struggle with faces that do not have a clear frontal view in the input video, potentially leading to inconsistencies or reduced quality.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identity-Aware Multi-View Consistency Loss
PROPOSAL: We extend the existing multi-view diffusion models by incorporating an identity-aware consistency loss, which penalizes the generated novel views for deviating from the appearance of the reference views and encourages them to have consistent properties. This loss is computed using a self-supervised approach where the same 3D asset is rendered from multiple viewpoints and the generated views are compared to each other.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to both the original multi-view diffusion model and to an ablation study of the proposed identity-aware loss. We also evaluate the effect of different settings of the loss parameters on the generated results.
COST: 4,770 GPU-h
PREDICTION: By introducing the identity-aware consistency loss, we expect to see a significant reduction in errors for novel views, better preservation of identity, and more coherent appearance and motion of the generated assets. However, the loss might struggle to capture subtle identity-preserving cues that are specific to the reference view, and the self-supervised approach might not always capture the necessary rendering nuances, potentially leading to artifacts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Subject-Specific View Extrapolation
PROPOSAL: We propose a view extrapolation module that uses subject-specific learned latent spaces to predict the appearance of novel views. The module is trained on a synthetic dataset of subjects with diverse poses and viewpoints, and it's integrated into existing 4D video-to-3D models such as VIBE. The module adapts to the subject's identity and learns to extrapolate appearance cues based on contextual information from other views.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the view extrapolation module to the original VIBE model and to an ablation study where the module is disabled or where it's trained on a generic latent space without subject-specific information.
COST: 14,234 GPU-h
PREDICTION: By leveraging subject-specific learned latent spaces, we expect to achieve more accurate and identity-preserving view extrapolation, with better color and texture preservation, and reduced errors for novel views. However, the model might require more extensive training data to learn a robust subject-specific representation, and it might struggle with edge cases where the subject's appearance is significantly different from what it's learned from.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating SWIFT as a Baseline for Self-Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Train and compare SWIFT, a training-free self-speculative decoding method, with a state-of-the-art separate draft model and a retrieval-based drafter on popular benchmarks for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding, including multi-turn conversation, machine translation, and summarization.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline of separate draft models including EAGLE, Medusa, BiTA, and LayerSkip.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: SWIFT can provide similar speedup to the best separate draft models, but with the advantage of requiring no training, and may even outperform retrieval-based drafting methods in some tasks, but could fall short in tasks requiring high draft accuracy, such as mathematical reasoning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Benefits of Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the binary cascade scheduling method, where some or all levels of draft models in a speculative cascade are either skipped or disabled, and determine whether a simple binary cascade schedule based on the expected accuracy and speedup of each model can adaptively achieve comparable performance improvements to a schedule with optimal hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline with full, optimized cascade scheduling, and test a range of adapters including compute-constrained adapters that try to maximize the number of draft models included in the cascade.
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: Binary cascade scheduling may allow for significant reductions in computational costs while achieving near-optimal performance, but may not capture nuanced interactions between draft models and may be ineffective in certain cases, such as when the draft models have highly varying accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Analyzing the Benefits of Cascade Scheduling
REVISION: Change the proposal to investigate a more in-depth exploration of adaptive scheduling techniques, including using reinforcement learning to adaptively adjust the scheduling of the self-derived draft models based on the characteristics of the input sequence and the expectations for the target model.

PROPOSAL: Use a reinforcement learning agent to learn an adaptive cascade schedule that selects the most effective self-derived draft models for each part of the task and adjusts the time spent on each model based on the sequence's characteristics.
CONTROLS: Compare to an RL agent trained to optimize a baseline form of speculative decoding, such as using retrieve-only draft-first, as well as to a simple cascade schedule with no RL adapter.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Adaptive scheduling with RL may achieve significant global speedup over a static schedule, as it captures the dynamic aspects of the input sequences and their effective use of the models, but might face convergence issues and high computational requirements during training, potentially slowing down training or leading to suboptimal performance in constrained hardware settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Power of Lookahead Decoding for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Integrate Lookahead decoding, a training-free self-speculative decoding technique, into a speculative cascade architecture, and explore its potential to accelerate existing draft models, including the baseline separate draft models, or as an adapter for other draft models, thereby forming a chain of cascades.
CONTROLS: Compare Lookahead decoding's impact when used to accelerate the baseline separate draft models against the same models trained with standard speculative decoding techniques, and when used as an adapter in cascade scheduling against traditional predictors of draft model performance.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Lookahead decoding integrated into a speculative cascade may offer promising speedups, as it benefits from the cascading structure and the coarse-grained multiple-step look ahead, however, as a post-processing component, its predictions might not align with the fine-grained token-level decisions, which might affect its overall effectiveness in sensitive applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Lower-Bound Theorem for the Speedup of Cascade Speculative Decoding

CONTROLS: Compare the derived lower-bound against experimental results from the set of proposals listed above, to determine the conditions under which cascades outperform standard speculative decoding and to gauge the gap between the theoretical optimality of cascades and their achievable speedup in practice.
COST: 750
PREDICTION: The derived lower-bound may closely match experimental results under optimistic assumptions, but could underestimate the gap between the theoretical optimality and practical performance due to considerations such as model inaccuracies or cascading effects that defy explicit quantification.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Lookahead Decoding with Cascade Configurations
PROPOSAL: Train Lookahead decoding on 4 popular LLMs (T5, BART, RoBERTa, Megatron) on 3 transformer-based tasks (question answering, machine translation, summarization) and evaluate its performance with 5 different cascade configurations: no cascade (baseline), using a single draft model that skips half of the layers, using two draft models with alternating skips, using two draft models that each skip one-fourth of the layers and adding an additional retrieval-based drafter at the bottom of the hierarchy.
CONTROLS: Speculative decoding with a single draft model, retrieval-based drafter without cascade, standard LLM without any speculative decoding
COST: 1345.6 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Lookahead decoding will achieve speedup compared to the baseline speculative decoding, and some cascade configurations will outperform the standard LLM, but the best-performing cascade configuration may not be the one with the suggested best parameters in the prior work, and combining Lookahead with a retrieval-based drafter may be more challenging than expected due to the requirement of computing a draft token representation for the retrieval-based model.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Comparative Study on Self-Speculative Decoding Methods for LLM Inference Acceleration
PROPOSAL: We conduct a thorough comparison of seven state-of-the-art self-speculative decoding methods, including Lookahead decoding, SWIFT, EAGLE, Medusa, BiTA, LayerSkip, and Jacobi-style parallel decoding, on three common LLM inference tasks (machine translation, multi-turn conversation, and text summarization) using the popular WMT 2019 En-De translation dataset and the Wizard of Wikipedia dataset for conversation and summarization tasks.
CONTROLS: Our study includes ablations that carve off individual acceleration techniques, and serves as a baseline for our subsequent proposals that aim to combine multiple techniques for cascade speculative decoding.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect Lookahead decoding and SWIFT to perform well on all tasks, while EAGLE and LayerSkip may struggle with multi-turn conversation due to their relatively low accuracy. BiTA and Jacobi-style parallel decoding may excel in machine translation due to their ability to efficiently handle large-scale contexts.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Retrieval-Based Drafter for Efficient Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We design a retrieval-based drafter that leverages a compact, pre-trained word-level language model to efficiently retrieve repeated n-grams from the input sequence and generate draft tokens. We evaluate our retrieval-based drafter in conjunction with Lookahead decoding and SWIFT on a range of LLM inference tasks (question answering, mathematical reasoning, and text classification) using the SQuAD 2.0 dataset for question answering and the Geoquiz dataset for mathematical reasoning.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our retrieval-based drafter against a standard prompt lookup decoding approach, as well as against each of the self-speculative decoding methods from Proposal 1.
COST: 1155 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate our retrieval-based drafter to provide a significant speedup compared to standard speculative decoding methods, particularly when combined with Lookahead decoding or SWIFT.

TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Speculative Decoding with Dynamic Draft Model Selection
PROPOSAL: We explore an adaptive approach to cascade speculative decoding, where we dynamically select the most suitable self-speculative acceleration technique for each stage of the cascade based on the characteristics of the input sequence and the performance of the previous stages. We experiment with this approach on our retrieval-based drafter from Proposal 2 and several other self-speculative decoding methods.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our adaptive approach against static cascade configurations, as well as against the standalone performance of each self-speculative decoding method.

TITLE: Hierarchical Cascade Speculative Decoding with Multitask Learning
PROPOSAL: We design a hierarchical cascade speculative decoding framework that learns to select the most suitable draft model for each stage of the cascade across multiple tasks simultaneously. This is achieved through a multitask learning setup where the model is trained on multiple inference tasks (e.g., machine translation, summarization, and question answering) and learns to adapt its draft model selection strategy accordingly.

TITLE: On-the-Fly Pyramidal Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We propose an on-the-fly pyramidal cascade speculative decoding framework that dynamically constructs a pyramid of self-speculative decoding stages based on the input sequence's characteristics and the model's performance at each stage. This approach eliminates the need for pre-trained draft models and allows for truly on-the-fly deployment.

TITLE: Inversely Weighed Absolute Score Learning for Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We experiment with modifying the discriminative reward model architecture to predict an absolute score in addition to a quality assessment metric (e.g., variance or confidence bound) for each response, inspired by inverse variance weighted regression methods in meta-analysis. 4. **Active Learning for Absolute Reward Model Calibration (ALARM)** 
TITLE: Iterative Feedback Driven World Calibration Process Using Active Learning
PROPOSAL: This work proposes an active learning approach to aid in the calibration of absolute reward models. The approach leverages the uncertainty estimates of a discriminative reward model and selects a subset of responses to be annotated by human evaluators. These selected responses are used to update the model and iteratively refine the absolute score and confidence estimates. We explore the impact of different active learning strategies and investigate the trade-offs between sample efficiency and accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare ALARM to traditional discriminative reward models as well as to TMR and BAQJR, using metrics such as average absolute error and quality calibration.
COST: 72500
PREDICTION: By adaptively selecting responses for human annotation, ALARM achieves improved calibration and absolute quality estimates with fewer human labels required, but its performance might suffer if the active learning strategy is not well-suited to the specific task or dataset at hand.

5. **Reward Model Explanation via Counterfactual Analysis (RMCE)** 
TITLE: Towards Improved Transparency and Trust in Reward Models: A Counterfactual Analysis
PROPOSAL: We introduce a counterfactual analysis method to provide insights into the reward model's decision-making process. By generating counterfactual responses that are likely to receive high or low rewards, we can identify the key factors that contributed to the model's original prediction. This helps to improve transparency, accountability, and trust in the reward model. We validate our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets and observe significant improvements in explainability and reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare RMCE to existing explanation methods and evaluate its performance on various metrics such as accuracy, confidence, and F1-score.
COST: 277000
PREDICTION: RMCE achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of explanation quality and provides valuable insights into the reward model's behavior, but its computational complexity might limit its applicability in high-throughput settings.

PROPOSAL: We propose a new generative reward model architecture that incorporates a probabilistic layer to estimate the uncertainty of human preference judgments. Specifically, we will use a Bayesian neural network to model the likelihood of a response being preferred, and also predict the confidence in this likelihood. We will then use this uncertain reward signal to balance risk and reward in LLM training, with the goal of improving robustness and reducing overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vertical and Horizontal Transfer Learning for Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the effectiveness of vertical and horizontal transfer learning for reward models across different domains and tasks. Vertical transfer will involve adapting a pre-trained reward model to a new domain with some additional fine-tuning, while horizontal transfer will involve learning a shared representation across multiple domains and applying it to each domain individually. We will evaluate the trade-offs between transfer learning and fine-tuning of shared components, and compare our results to baseline approaches of training separate reward models for each domain.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method against current state-of-the-art reward models and fine-tuning baselines in the designated domains.
COST: 13,456,000
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning approach should enable more efficient adaptation to new domains and promote generalizability of reward models, but may face challenges in balancing transfer learning objectives with fine-tuning performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Not-All-Equal Reward Modeling for Reward Calibration and Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of discriminative reward models in accounting for uncertainty and absolute quality judgments, we introduce a not-all-equal (NAE) reward model. We modify the standard discriminative architecture by incorporating a softmax output layer to produce a distribution over possible quality labels, and train with a loss function that balances cross-entropy and strictly binary cross-entropy terms. By optimizing over this distribution, our model learns to provide calibrated scores and output a meaningful probability of correctness, allowing for uncertainty estimation and absolute quality judgments.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: standard Bradley-Terry objective
- Baseline 2: softmax-based models from the literature
- Alternative 1: discriminative reward models with reduced output dimensionality
COST: 660
PREDICTION: Expected to provide more informative and interpretable results, especially when annotators exhibit high variability in rating tasks. This may, however, lead to increased pressure on the model to produce well-calibrated probabilities, where even small biases could result in suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Discriminative Reward Models with Confidence Estimates
PROPOSAL: We extend the Bradley-Terry objective to estimate confidence in our absolute quality assessments using a separate probabilistic output. We model the confidence as a categorical distribution over  K quality labels, and optimize over both the score margin and a categorical cross-entropy term to refine the confidence estimates. We compare this variant to the original Bradley-Terry objective on various datasets and baselines from the field of reward modeling.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: standard Bradley-Terry objective
- Baseline 2: sample-efficient alternatives such as PRISM-Loss 
- Alternative 1: multi-label variants of discriminative reward models
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Expected to improve ranking accuracy while reducing the apparent pairwise preference margin, and potentially capturing more nuanced aspects of human preference. Our climate variability-trained BeRo LM-Reward may not generalize well to other environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Not-All-Equal Reward Modeling for Reward Calibration and Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of discriminative reward models in accounting for uncertainty and absolute quality judgments, we introduce a not-all-equal (NAE) reward model. We modify the standard discriminative architecture by incorporating a softmax output layer to produce a distribution over possible quality labels, and train with a loss function that balances cross-entropy and strictly binary cross-entropy terms. By optimizing over this distribution, our model learns to provide calibrated scores and output a meaningful probability of correctness, allowing for uncertainty estimation and absolute quality judgments.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: standard Bradley-Terry objective
- Baseline 2: softmax-based models from the literature
- Alternative 1: discriminative reward models with reduced output dimensionality
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Expected to provide more informative and interpretable results, especially when annotators exhibit high variability in rating tasks. This may, however, lead to increased pressure on the model to produce well-calibrated probabilities, where even small biases could result in suboptimal performance.

TITLE: Generative Template Adaptation with Synthesised Preference Metrics
PROPOSAL: Combining the strengths of generative reward models with discriminative template adaptation, we create a novel approach to significantly simplify the Best-of-N scoring task and generalize the quality scoring scale adaptability. Through a template inference mechanism on comparable sets, our method synthesizes tailored template form pairs from parameterized space-style inputs against pool-set concept measurement templates. This approach allows our system to flexibly and effectively adapt to new task environments and challenge modalities.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: standard generative reward models
- Baseline 2: reference-based methods for template adaptation
- Alternative 1: pairwise-competitive template inference variants
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Expected to offer clear advantages in terms of speed, accuracy, and adaptability. However, its performance may be mitigated by limitations in expressive capacity or unoptimal parameterization of the synthesis models, ultimately leading to a tradeoff with interpretability.

PROPOSAL: In this proposal, we introduce a meta-learning framework to efficiently augment quality labels for reward models. Our method trains a meta-model to learn how to adapt to different environments and task distributions by learning from a few labeled examples. This approach can handle scalability and domain shift issues associated with traditional reward model training.

- Baseline 1: standard discriminative and generative reward models

- Alternative 1: meta-adaptation variants using different architectures

PREDICTION: Expected to improve the sample efficiency and scalability of reward model training, allowing for faster and more accurate adaptation to new tasks and environments. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluator-augmented Reward Model
PROPOSAL: We propose a reward model that leverages an external evaluator (e.g., a smaller LLM) to provide its own preferences on model responses, then combines this evaluator's predictions with our own reward model to generate final scores. The evaluator creates a distribution over response qualities, which our model refines into weighted scores for ranking purposes.
CONTROLS: We compare our Evaluator-augmented Reward Model to Skywork-Reward and the Bradley-Terry objective as baselines. For ablation controls, we look at a version of the model where the evaluator is bypassed.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: Our reward model should improve accuracy over discriminative models, especially in low-resource settings where limited high-quality annotations are available. However, we may see diminishing returns if the external evaluator's performance degrades, and it may be difficult to properly calibrate weights to combine evaluator and reward model responses.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bayesian Preference Reweighting
PROPOSAL: To capture the uncertainty inherent in human preference judgments, we propose incorporating Bayesian inference to reweight preferences collected from multiple annotators. By using a hierarchical Bayesian model, we can estimate both the reliability of individual annotators and the uncertainty of their judgments, resulting in weighted scores that reflect human preference ambiguity.
CONTROLS: We compare our Bayesian Preference Reweighting model to a baseline where equal weight is assigned to each annotator's preference, as well as to NoGoodDiscdif, a state-of-the-art reward model focused on handling conflicting human preferences.
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: Our reward model should improve overall ranking accuracy by considering the uncertainty of human preference annotations. However, the model may require large amounts of annotated data to efficiently learn the reliability of individual annotators. Further rigorous testing would be needed to establish the trade-offs between model complexity, annotation requirements, and ranking performance.

TITLE: Evaluator-augmented Reward Model
PROPOSAL: To enhance the previous proposal, we will now also leverage a multi-modal feedback mechanism from human annotators. This added feedback option will enable our evaluator to be more robust in corner cases or when encounters underspecified or open-ended tasks. Our evaluator will then utilize this and its original preference prediction outputs to revise the response-quality distributions, in turn allow a more accurate ranking of model outputs.
CONTROLS: This revised Evaluator-augmented Reward Model is compared to a variant that does not incorporate multi-modal feedback, as well as the original discriminative reward model being evaluated.

Conversely, we may encounter difficulty in tuning the model architecture and training procedures to maximize the benefits of this additional feedback mechanism, and its performance may degrade for less context-specific tasks where simplicity is desired.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Reward Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework for reward models, where the goal is to learn a consistent reward function that can generalize across multiple domains and tasks. By sharing the learned features and representations across tasks, the model can adapt to the inherent variability in human judgments and improve the robustness of the reward estimates. We will train the model on a variety of tasks, including chatbot response quality evaluation, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, and evaluate its performance across a range of metrics.
CONTROLS: The multi-task reward learning model will be compared to a baseline where the model is trained on a single task and to our previously proposed reward models.
COST: 660000
PREDICTION: Our multi-task reward learning model should improve the consistency and robustness of the reward estimates across different tasks and domains, leading to better ranking accuracy and more reliable preferences. However, we may encounter challenges in tuning the model architecture and the task relationships to maximize the benefits of this framework, and the model may require large amounts of annotated data to efficiently learn the shared representations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning from Multiple Heads
PROPOSAL: We propose an extension to the Evaluator-augmented Reward Model (Turn 1) by adding multiple heads to the evaluator, each responsible for a different aspect of the task, such as response quality, fluency, and coherence. Each head learns to focus on the specific strengths and weaknesses of its domain, and the final score is a combination of the scores from all heads. This allows the model to capture more nuanced and diverse human preferences.
CONTROLS: The multi-head evaluator will be compared to a single-head baseline and to the Evaluator-augmented Reward Model without multiple heads.
COST: 900000
PREDICTION: By using multiple heads, our reward model should be able to capture more precise and diverse human preferences, leading to improved ranking accuracy. However, we may encounter challenges in tuning the number of heads, the complexity of each head, and the way to combine the outputs, which could lead to overfitting or computationally expensive training procedures.

TITLE: Feedback Calibration via Label Smoothing
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel feedback calibration technique, which applies label smoothing to the annotations used to train the reward model. Our results show that label smoothing can improve the consistency and reliability of the reward estimates, leading to better ranking accuracy and more reliable preferences.

PREDICTION: Our label smoothing technique should improve the calibration and confidence of the reward estimates, leading to better ranking accuracy and more reliable preferences. TITLE: Multi-Task Reward Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework for reward models, where the goal is to learn a consistent reward function that can generalize across multiple domains and tasks. By sharing the learned features and representations across tasks, the model can adapt to the inherent variability in human judgments and improve the robustness of the reward estimates. We will train the model on a variety of tasks, including chatbot response quality evaluation, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, and evaluate its performance across a range of metrics.
CONTROLS: The multi-task reward learning model will be compared to a baseline where the model is trained on a single task and to our previously proposed reward models.

This allows the model to capture more nuanced and diverse human preferences.

Our results show that label smoothing can improve the consistency and reliability of the reward estimates, leading to better ranking accuracy and more reliable preferences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Discriminative Reward Models with Calibrated Probabilistic Output
PROPOSAL: We modify the Bradley-Terry objective to encourage the reward model to output calibrated probabilities instead of deterministic scores. This is achieved by combining the standard cross-entropy loss with a scaled version of the pinball loss to promote probabilistic outputs that are well-calibrated. We train this modified model on the large-scale datasets for intent classification and response selection from the HumanEval benchmark, comparing its performance against the standard Bradley-Terry model and other discriminative models like Skywork-Reward and InternLM2-Reward.
CONTROLS: Bradley-Terry objective, Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward
COST: 330
PREDICTION: We expect the calibrated model to achieve better ranking accuracy and lower tail risk in its scores, allowing for a more reliable acceptance threshold and improved interpretability. It may, however, struggle to match the absolute performance of the non-calibrated models, especially on more challenging benchmarks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantile Reward Models for Absolute Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We introduce quantile regression objectives to the discriminative reward framework, allowing the model to predict absolute quality scores by learning quantiles of the response quality distribution. We compare the performance of these quantile models with standard discriminative and generative models on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and chatbot safety benchmarks, assessing their ability to reliably reject or accept responses based on absolute quality. The quantile models are implemented in the context of the popular ArmoRM framework.
CONTROLS: ArmoRM, Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, generative reward models
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We anticipate the quantile models to significantly improve absolute quality estimation, with potential losses in ranking accuracy due to the learning of multiple output quantiles. Furthermore, they may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Quantile Reward Models for Absolute Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We refine the design of the quantile reward models to incorporate a hierarchical structure, where a base model predicts response quality quantiles, and an additional refinement model refines these predictions under specific domain constraints. This hierarchical approach is motivated by the observation that absolute quality estimation in real-world applications often requires nuanced understanding of domain-specific considerations and context-dependent preference signals. In this revised proposal, we scale up the evaluation to the full set of HumanEval benchmarks, assessing the impact of this hierarchical architecture on ranking accuracy and absolute quality estimation.
CONTROLS: ArmoRM, Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, generative reward models
COST: 1731.6
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical quantile models to exhibit improved performance, particularly in benchmarks that require nuanced understanding of domain-specific considerations. However, the increased complexity of these models might introduce overfitting risks in smaller datasets.

TITLE: Generative Reward Models with Flexible Input Formats and Uncertainty Estimates
PROPOSAL: We develop a generative reward model architecture that can handle flexible input formats, such as flexible pairwise input scenarios and larger response sets. We also incorporate an uncertainty estimation component to quantify the model's confidence in its preference judgments, allowing for more robust integration of preference data from multiple annotators. We evaluate this model on role-play dialogue and chatbot response quality evaluation benchmarks, comparing its performance to state-of-the-art generative models and discriminative models like Skywork-Reward and InternLM2-Reward.
CONTROLS: Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward, ArmoRM
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We anticipate the generative model to show improved adaptability to diverse input formats and better handling of annotator uncertainty, potentially at the cost of some ranking accuracy degradation in scenarios with very high annotation noise or ambiguity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lifted Reward Models for Efficient Multi-Response Scoring
PROPOSAL: We propose a lifted reward model architecture that selectively samples responses from the LLM output distribution and scores these samples using a learned score distribution. This approach allows for efficient computation of scores for large response sets while maintaining accuracy and interpretability. We implement this model in the context of the InternLM2-Reward framework and evaluate its performance on chatbot response quality evaluation and code generation benchmarks, comparing it to discriminative and generative models.
CONTROLS: InternLM2-Reward, Skywork-Reward, generative reward models
COST: 3148
PREDICTION: We expect the lifted model to significantly accelerate response scoring while achieving competitive ranking accuracy, at the potential cost of some quality estimation accuracy when responses have non-trivial ambiguities or inconsistencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Reward Learning for Cross-Domain Transfer
PROPOSAL: We explore multi-task learning as a means to transfer discriminative reward models across multiple tasks and domains, promoting knowledge sharing and reducing the need for extensive annotation. We model the reward model as a multi-task learner embedded in the InternLM2-Reward framework, where a unified set of parameters is optimized across tasks, a shared knowledge base is generated. This framework is evaluated on multiple HumanEval benchmarks and compared to task-specific discriminative and generative models. We also assess the quality and effectiveness of the cross-domain transfer through few-shot learning.
CONTROLS: InternLM2-Reward, Skywork-Reward, generative reward models, task-specific models
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We anticipate the multi-task reward model to demonstrate significant transfer of knowledge across domains, at the risk of performance degradation in specific tasks due to over-fitting and difficulty in accurately identifying relevant prior knowledge for diverse task settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Bounds for Reward Model Calibration
PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical framework for understanding and analyzing the calibration of reward models in the context of calibration theory and concentration inequalities. We derive bounds on the error of calibrated reward models and their average calibration, providing insights into the design and evaluation of reward models. We formally analyze the circumstances under which reward models are well-calibrated, focusing on the trade-off between accuracy and calibration. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our results for the design of efficient reward models, such as the calibration of output distributions.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect these theoretical results to lead to a deeper understanding of the calibration of reward models and their behavior, particularly in high-stakes applications, providing theoretical justification for calibration-driven approaches to improving reward models. However, the theoretical analysis may overlook specific practical aspects of reward model implementation.

PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical framework for understanding and analyzing the calibration of reward models in the context of calibration theory and concentration inequalities. We formally analyze the circumstances under which reward models are well-calibrated, focusing on the trade-off between accuracy and calibration. TITLE: Graph Neural Network-based External Context Utilization Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Develop a new method that represents the utilization of external context in RAG systems using graph neural networks (GNNs). Construct a graph where nodes represent individual document passages and the edges capture the relationships and dependencies between them. Train a GNN to embed the documents in a low-dimensional space, where the embedding of a passage represents its contribution to the external context utilization. This can be used as an indicator of whether the model is relying heavily on internal knowledge or grounding its response in the external context.

TITLE: Internal Knowledge Decomposition via Slice-Equivariant Networks
PROPOSAL: Design a theoretical framework to decompose the internal knowledge of a language model into individual components or "slices" that can be studied separately. This can be achieved using slice-equivariant networks (SENs), which are neural networks where the transformations applied to the input are equivariant under a specific slice operation. By analyzing the weights and activations of the SENs, we can understand which internal knowledge components the model is relying on, and whether these components contribute to the hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the SEN-based approach to the previous GNN-based method, and consider adding a random projection baseline to demonstrate the effectiveness of the SEN-based approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring External Context Utilization through Document Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We will train and evaluate a range of pre-trained language models (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa) fine-tuned for retrieval-augmented generation tasks, specifically to predict the similarity between the generated response and the retrieved document embeddings. This will serve as a signal of external context utilization: since the document embeddings are based on the retrieved information, high similarity indicates that the model has effectively used the external context. To estimate internal knowledge utilization, we will use a variant of the generator to predict the similarity between the generated response and the prompt, which only contains the input query and leaves out the retrieved documents. The difference between these two measures will give us an estimate of the reliance on internal knowledge. We will measure the performance using a combination of Precision, Recall, and F1-score on the task of news summarization.
CONTROLS: Standard RAG baselines with no additional hallucination detection mechanism, as well as a control variant where we use a fixed template to fill in the generated text without fine-tuning the internal model parameters.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to outperform the RAG baselines and show a good correlation between our signal and the actual hallucination detection, but might struggle with harder cases where the internal knowledge is highly plausible, requiring deeper understanding of the query context.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Attention Guidance for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We will revisit the idea of attention heads as a mechanism for guiding the model's attention towards the external context. This time, instead of selecting specific attention heads, we will treat the attention scores as a probabilistic distribution over the input sequence and use it as a confidence score for the context relevance. We will then use a set of carefully designed curated datasets, such as the CNN-Daily Mail and the New York Times Annotated Corpus, to fine-tune this approach and validate its effectiveness in capturing the utilization of external context and internal knowledge. We will measure the performance using a combination of metrics including the F1 score, Precision, and Recall.
CONTROLS: Our previous approach from #1, as well as a control variant that trains the models with a regularized term to encourage the attention weights to be more consistent with the importance of the context information.
COST: 2340
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the attention guidance mechanism could reduce the reliance on internal knowledge, but may still struggle in the most difficult cases where the historical training data does not contain relevant context, calling for a more principled understanding of context relevance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Attention Guidance for Hallucination Detection (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We will revisit the idea of attention heads as a mechanism for guiding the model's attention towards the external context, but instead of using the attention scores directly, we will train a separate model to predict whether a given attention head uses the context more or less than the average attention head. This will serve as a signal of external context utilization, and we can then estimate internal knowledge utilization as the model's reliance on internal knowledge versus the average reliance of the other models. To further improve this approach, we will use a set of transfer learning techniques to adapt our model to different domains and help generalization. We will measure the performance using a combination of metrics including the F1 score, Precision, and Recall.
CONTROLS: Our previous approach from #1, as well as a control variant that trains the models without the attention guidance mechanism, and another control where we use a naive average attention score threshold to switch attention between internal and external context.
COST: 2820
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this revised approach will be more robust and less prone to overfitting, providing more accurate results in terms of detecting hallucinations and quantifying the utilization of external context and internal knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring External Context Utilization through Document Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We will train and evaluate a range of pre-trained language models (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa) fine-tuned for retrieval-augmented generation tasks, specifically to predict the similarity between the generated response and the retrieved document embeddings. This will serve as a signal of external context utilization: since the document embeddings are based on the retrieved information, high similarity indicates that the model has effectively used the external context. To estimate internal knowledge utilization, we will use a variant of the generator to predict the similarity between the generated response and the prompt, which only contains the input query and leaves out the retrieved documents. The difference between these two measures will give us an estimate of the reliance on internal knowledge. We will measure the performance using a combination of Precision, Recall, and F1-score on the task of news summarization.
CONTROLS: Standard RAG baselines with no additional hallucination detection mechanism, as well as a control variant where we use a fixed template to fill in the generated text without fine-tuning the internal model parameters.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to outperform the RAG baselines and show a good correlation between our signal and the actual hallucination detection, but might struggle with harder cases where the internal knowledge is highly plausible, requiring deeper understanding of the query context.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automatic Hyperparameter Tuning for the Retrieval-Augmenter
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment where we apply a robust and automated hyperparameter tuning process (e.g., Optuna or Hyperopt) to the retriever and the augmenter in RAG, specifically tuning the number of retrieved documents, the weight used in combining the two sources of information, and the model's internal knowledge utilization heuristic. The goal is to identify the optimal setting for these components in RAG on various real-world datasets (e.g., TriviaQA, NewsQA). The controls will involve comparing these tuning results against: (1) fixed hyperparameter settings optimized manually by the research team (2) results obtained using a simpler, less automated tuning process such as grid search or random search. We hypothesize that a robust and automated tuning process will lead to improved overall performance, particularly in terms of reducing hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Manual tuning, grid search, random search
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Given the focus on hyperparameter tuning, the results are expected to be promising, but may vary depending on the complexity of the retriever and augmenter components, and might highlight some potential limitations, such as overfitting to the hyperparameter search space rather than the actual contextual task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Falcon Effect in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to identify and quantify the "falcon effect" in RAG: when the model reliably uses certain hallucinated tokens to guide the retrieval process, creating an iterative interaction between the model and the retrieval process. This can lead to the perpetuation of hallucinations. We will use a combination of automated and manual inspections to evaluate the prevalence of the falcon effect in RAG systems on various real-world datasets (e.g., TriviaQA, NewsQA). The controls will involve analyzing the effect of different retrieval settings and evaluating whether existing methods can mitigate the falcon effect.
CONTROLS: Retrieval settings (e.g., number of documents, document ranking), existing methods (e.g., ReDeEP)
COST: 3200
PREDICTION: Expected to reveal notable interactions between the retrieval system and the LLM, and how the falcon effect can contribute to hallucinations, with possible implications on systems' design and future research directions.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Assessing the Falcon Effect in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by incorporating a focus on differentiating between strong and weak falcon effects. We hypothesize that the strong falcon effect (where LLM heavily relies on specific tokens) is more correlated with hallucinations compared to the weak falcon effect (where LLM makes slight modifications). We will investigate this by analyzing the attention patterns and token dependencies in the LLM, controlling for how the retrieval settings influence these patterns. Additionally, we will analyze how well the proposed methodologies to combat hallucination, such as data augmentations and adapters, fare against strong and weak falcon variants.
CONTROLS: Retrieval settings, data augmentation techniques, proposed methodologies (adapters)
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: This revised experiment is expected to offer a more nuanced understanding of the falcon effect's role in hallucinations, advancing the knowledge on effective countermeasures against stronger and weaker falcon variants, thereby enabling practitioners to better construct more accurate systems.

Controls will include direct comparisons to ReDeEP on other datasets (e.g., RACE, TriviaQA) and an ablation study on the different components of the model.

The goal is to identify the optimal setting for these components in RAG on various real-world datasets (e.g., TriviaQA, NewsQA). The controls will involve comparing these tuning results against: (1) fixed hyperparameter settings optimized manually by the research team (2) results obtained using a simpler, less automated tuning process such as grid search or random search. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Questionnaire Perturbation (RQP)
PROPOSAL: Develop a method that applies targeted perturbations to the query and retrieved documents, then measures the impact on the model's hallucination likelihood. Specifically, introduce small modifications to the query and/or documents through rephrasing or inserting factual minutiae and track how the model responds. This approach would quantify external context utilization indirectly, by observing how sensitive the model is to changes in context.
CONTROLS: Baseline would be the standard RAG setup without perturbations, with and without the proposed detector. The ReDeEP and follow-up methods would be used as ablations. Measuring the improvements when every LLM in different combinations use this technique with common combination of current hallucination metrics.
COST: 150000
PREDICTION: This method can detect hallucinations by revealing the limitations of the model's internal knowledge. The perturbation technique would work especially well in domains like news summarization where counterfactuals or scenarios are possible without there being a problem. However, real-world results might vary depending on whether optimal sets of perturbations should be precomputed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Grounding via Adversarial Text Injection (A4JI)
PROPOSAL: Employ an adversarial approach to inject knowledge from the retrieved documents into the LLM's internal state, specifically by generating 'corrective feedback' in the form of contrastive examples, designed to push the model towards utilizing the external context more. The feedback would be generated by humans or an oracle in a small fraction of examples, to avoid reinforcing known hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate RQP and A4JI in combination. Ablate by removing the manual oracle for contrastive examples and compare with using automatic methods. Investigate combining this method with the hallucination metric derived from ReDeEP and its follow-up work for better performance.
COST: 241880
PREDICTION: A4JI could offer a more direct way to 'ground' the LLM's internal state in the retrieved knowledge, leading to reduced hallucinations in RAG systems, especially in news summarization and data-to-text generation with worst outcomes potentially seen with less informative domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Utilization of Internal and External Knowledge with Kernel Embeddings (K2E)
PROPOSAL: Use kernel embeddings to capture the semantic similarity between the generated response and both the internal LLM states and the retrieved context. This would yield a way to quantify internal and external knowledge utilization using universal and dataset-agnostic kernels. We will explore several types of kernels, including the Gaussian and polynomial kernels, and examine which ones work best for hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: Evaluate K2E with RQP and A4JI in isolation, as well as in combinations. Compare it with the methods from ReDeEP and its follow-up, under controlled conditions. Additionally, ablate by removing one type of kernel at a time to assess their relative importance.
COST: 310000
PREDICTION: K2E offers the potential to measure knowledge utilization across models and datasets more directly, possibly at a higher computational cost. It is worthwhile to determine how K2E combinations with existing approaches impact these techniques against average RAG performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Questionnaire Perturbation (RQP)
PROPOSAL: Develop a method that applies targeted perturbations to the query and retrieved documents, then measures the impact on the model's hallucination likelihood. Specifically, introduce small modifications to the query and/or documents through rephrasing or inserting factual minutiae and track how the model responds. This approach would quantify external context utilization indirectly, by observing how sensitive the model is to changes in context.
CONTROLS: Baseline would be the standard RAG setup without perturbations, with and without the proposed detector. The ReDeEP and follow-up methods would be used as ablations. Measuring the improvements when every LLM in different combinations use this technique with common combination of current hallucination metrics.
COST: 450000
PREDICTION: This method can detect hallucinations by revealing the limitations of the model's internal knowledge. The perturbation technique would work especially well in domains like news summarization where counterfactuals or scenarios are possible without there being a problem. However, real-world results might vary depending on whether optimal sets of perturbations should be precomputed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Grounding via Adversarial Text Injection (A4JI)
PROPOSAL: Employ an adversarial approach to inject knowledge from the retrieved documents into the LLM's internal state, specifically by generating 'corrective feedback' in the form of contrastive examples, designed to push the model towards utilizing the external context more. The feedback would be generated by humans or an oracle in a small fraction of examples, to avoid reinforcing known hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate RQP and A4JI in combination. Ablate by removing the manual oracle for contrastive examples and compare with using automatic methods. Investigate combining this method with the hallucination metric derived from ReDeEP and its follow-up work for better performance.
COST: 725000
PREDICTION: A4JI could offer a more direct way to 'ground' the LLM's internal state in the retrieved knowledge, leading to reduced hallucinations in RAG systems, especially in news summarization and data-to-text generation with worst outcomes potentially seen with less informative domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Utilization of Internal and External Knowledge with Kernel Embeddings (K2E)
PROPOSAL: Use kernel embeddings to capture the semantic similarity between the generated response and both the internal LLM states and the retrieved context. This would yield a way to quantify internal and external knowledge utilization using universal and dataset-agnostic kernels. We will explore several types of kernels, including the Gaussian and polynomial kernels, and examine which ones work best for hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: Evaluate K2E with RQP and A4JI in isolation, as well as in combinations. Compare it with the methods from ReDeEP and its follow-up, under controlled conditions. Additionally, ablate by removing one type of kernel at a time to assess their relative importance.
COST: 925000
PREDICTION: K2E offers the potential to measure knowledge utilization across models and datasets more directly, possibly at a higher computational cost. It is worthwhile to determine how K2E combinations with existing approaches impact these techniques against average RAG performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Certifying External Context Utilization via Input- Output Convergence Analysis
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that certifies the utilization of external context by an LLM receiving retrieved documents and a query through a convergence analysis of the input-output behavior over multiple iterations. Specifically, when the model converges to a stable fixed point in the presence of an external input, we can infer the model's reliance on that input. Utilization can thus be quantified as the rate of convergence to the fixed point in the presence and absence of the input, indicating how much the external context influences the model's output.
CONTROLS: Compare to ablations without convergence analysis, and to scores obtained through attention-based and semantic-entropy-based heuristics.
COST: 832.876
PREDICTION: Expected result: this theoretical framework can provide a principled way to quantify external context utilization without relying on attention heads selection. Failure: may fail to capture the complexity of RAG systems, particularly when the retrieved documents are not sufficient or relevant.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Internal Knowledge Utilization through Normalization Flow Divergence
PROPOSAL: Adapt the Normalization Flow (NF) divergence to measure the utilization of internal knowledge by an LLM. NF divergence estimates the KL-divergence between two probability distributions in the latent space of normalizing flows. By computing NF divergence between the internal state of the model and a prior model (trained on an external knowledge graph), we can quantify how much the internal knowledge affects the model's output. This approach generalizes across models and datasets, without relying on attention heads or specific transformer layers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against ablations using different divergence metrics (e.g., JS divergence), and compare to scores obtained from ReDeEP and its follow-up work.
COST: 1250
PREDICTION: Expected result: this approach can provide a model-agnostic method to quantify internal knowledge utilization. Failure: may fail to capture the nuances of internal knowledge due to the complexity of NF divergence computation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lexicon-Based Externality Scores for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a lexicon-based external scores to detect hallucinations by analyzing the internal knowledge utilization of the LLM. The method uses a pre-trained language model to retrieve words and phrases that are semantically similar to the generated text, and measures the co-occurrence of these words in the internal knowledge graph of the LLM. The externality score is then calculated as the ratio of co-occurrence to the total number of words in the internal knowledge graph, indicating how much the generated text relies on external knowledge versus internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare against ablations without lexicon-based analysis, and against ReDeEP and its follow-up work.
COST: 1680
PREDICTION: Expected result: this approach can provide a robust method for detecting hallucinations by evaluating the reliance of the generated text on external versus internal knowledge. Failure: may fail to capture nuances of context-dependent external knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Certifying External Context Utilization via Input- Output Convergence Analysis
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that certifies the utilization of external context by an LLM receiving retrieved documents and a query through a convergence analysis of the input-output behavior over multiple iterations. Specifically, when the model converges to a stable fixed point in the presence of an external input, we can infer the model's reliance on that input. Utilization can thus be quantified as the rate of convergence to the fixed point in the presence and absence of the input, indicating how much the external context influences the model's output.
CONTROLS: Compare to ablations without convergence analysis, and to scores obtained through attention-based and semantic-entropy-based heuristics.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: Expected result: this theoretical framework can provide a principled way to quantify external context utilization without relying on attention heads selection. Failure: may fail to capture the complexity of RAG systems, particularly when the retrieved documents are not sufficient or relevant.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Internal Knowledge Utilization through Normalization Flow Divergence
PROPOSAL: Adapt the Normalization Flow (NF) divergence to measure the utilization of internal knowledge by an LLM. NF divergence estimates the KL-divergence between two probability distributions in the latent space of normalizing flows. By computing NF divergence between the internal state of the model and a prior model (trained on an external knowledge graph), we can quantify how much the internal knowledge affects the model's output. This approach generalizes across models and datasets, without relying on attention heads or specific transformer layers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against ablations using different divergence metrics (e.g., JS divergence), and compare to scores obtained from ReDeEP and its follow-up work.
COST: 3750
PREDICTION: Expected result: this approach can provide a model-agnostic method to quantify internal knowledge utilization. Failure: may fail to capture the nuances of internal knowledge due to the complexity of NF divergence computation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED - Measuring Internal Knowledge Utilization through Normalization Flow Divergence
PROPOSAL: Adapt the Normalization Flow (NF) divergence to measure the utilization of internal knowledge by an LLM, but instead of using as prior a model trained on an external knowledge graph, use the output of the model with the input nynan. This approach eliminates the reliance on external knowledge graphs, and estimates how much the internal knowledge affects the model's output when generated without context, allowing a baseline comparison to the output generated with context.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against ablations using different divergence metrics (e.g., JS divergence), and compare to scores obtained from ReDeEP and its follow-up work, and against a baseline model that only relies on internal knowledge.
COST: 3750
PREDICTION: Expected result: this approach can provide a more direct comparison between internal knowledge utilization and external context utilization without the need for an external knowledge graph. Failure: may fail to capture cases where internal knowledge is Cardinal notwithstanding in the absence of context, while it is less so in the presence of context.

TITLE: Retrieval Context-Enhanced Embeddings for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a vector embedding representation by combining the output embeddings from a retrieval model that retrieves relevant documents for the given context with the internal state embeddings from the LLM. This vector can be used as a proxy for context utilization, and can be used to capture the utilization of external context in addition to internal knowledge. We can calculate the similarity between the full context vector and the output vector from the LLM, and if this similarity is very low, this suggests the LLM is more likely to have generated text that is a hallucination.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lexicon-Based Externality Scores for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a lexicon-based external scores to detect hallucinations by analyzing the internal knowledge utilization of the LLM. The method uses a pre-trained language model to retrieve words and phrases that are semantically similar to the generated text, and measures the co-occurrence of these words in the internal knowledge graph of the LLM. The externality score is then calculated as the ratio of co-occurrence to the total number of words in the internal knowledge graph, indicating how much the generated text relies on external knowledge versus internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare against ablations without lexicon-based analysis, and against ReDeEP and its follow-up work.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: Expected result: this approach can provide a robust method for detecting hallucinations by evaluating the reliance of the generated text on external versus internal knowledge. Failure: may fail to capture nuances of context-dependent external knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (HRAG) for Context-Aware Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Expand the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach by incorporating hierarchical document representation and attention mechanisms. Documents are initially associated with abstract representations and later their fine-grained structure (e.g., section and sentence level information) is incorporated to better disambiguate relevant information for the context. This Yang-based contextual strategy can allow for more accurate and informative context-aware use during generation and facilitate preliminary comprehension of item hell Utilization scores.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard RAG model without hierarchical representation, and evaluate on its performance in detecting hallucinations.

PREDICTION: Expected result: This approach can provide a more accurate detection of hallucinations by capturing more nuanced information from the context and revising item hell utilization retrospectively. Failure: may fail to capture similarities between the hierarchical document representation needed by the application in question

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multitask Learning for Joint Hallucination Detection and Context Utilization Estimation
PROPOSAL: Explore multitask learning to jointly optimize hallucination detection and context utilization estimation. A single model can be trained on a shared encoder-decoder architecture to predict both hallucination likelihood and context utilization scores simultaneously, using a combination of labels and auxiliary loss functions. This approach can exploit the shared representation between the two tasks and improve overall performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard separate training for hallucination detection and context utilization estimation, and against a baseline that shares the encoder but not the decoder.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: Expected result: This approach can provide an effective and efficient method for joint hallucination detection and context utilization estimation. Failure: may fail to capture nuances of each task when optimizing for both jointly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Self-Monitoring in Language Models for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Implement a self-monitoring mechanism in the language model itself, allowing it to assess its own context utilization and identify potential hallucinations. This can be achieved by conditioning on a secondary, separate model that evaluates the context utilization of the primary model's output, based on the principles set forth in multitask learning and reinforcement learning from human evaluations. The secondary model can serve as a regularizer, highlighting areas where the primary model may over-rely on its internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard training without self-monitoring, and evaluate on its performance in detecting hallucinations.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: Expected result: This approach can provide a more robust method for detecting hallucinations by allowing the language model to actively monitor its own context utilization. Failure: may fail to capture nuances of context-dependent hallucinations due to the complexities of self-monitoring.

PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial training framework that encourages the language model to produce contextually-grounded text while discouraging hallucinations. This can be achieved by training an adversary model to predict when the language model's output is a hallucination, and using this prediction as a regularization term in the language model's objective function. Regularly, a perturbation from realities datasets is added during the training process to let knowledge to be rooted accurately.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard training without adversarial training, and evaluate on its performance in detecting hallucinations.

PREDICTION: Expected result: This approach can provide a more effective method for hallucination detection by encouraging the language model to produce contextually-grounded text. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Role of Cross-Channel Interactions in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will compare a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder, such as the Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (TGCN), with a baseline channel-independent encoder, such as a 1D convolutional neural network, to investigate the impact of cross-channel interactions on forecasting accuracy for multivariate time-series data. We will train and evaluate both models on five real-world datasets from different domains, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting.
CONTROLS: Baseline models: 1D Conv1D, Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (TGCN); hyperparameter search to optimize model performance.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect the channel-dependent encoder to outperform the channel-independent encoder in average forecasting accuracy by 10-15% across all domains. However, it may struggle to generalize well across different datasets, highlighting the importance of further investigation into cross-channel interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Decoding Mechanisms for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of simple linear projections for decoding, we will explore the effectiveness of different decoding mechanisms, including autoregressive (AR) models, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and temporal convolutional neural networks (TCNNs), in predicting future values from encoded representations. We will evaluate these models on the same datasets used in proposal 1 and compare their performance to the baseline linear projection.
CONTROLS: Baseline model: linear projection; decoding mechanisms: autoregressive (AR) models, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, temporal convolutional neural networks (TCNNs).
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect the more advanced decoding mechanisms to outperform the linear projection by 5-10% in average forecasting accuracy, with the TCNN potentially showing the best results due to its ability to capture complex temporal dependencies. However, their performance may vary across different datasets, highlighting the need for careful hyperparameter tuning.
