textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effectiveness of self-supervised pretraining, inspired by BERT, as a way to learn strong temporal representations and cross-channel interactions in a channel-dependent encoder. We will design a pretraining objective that involves masking a subset of temporal segments and training the encoder to reconstruct the masked portions, and then transfer the learned representations to a downstream forecasting task.
CONTROLS: Baseline model: linear projection; pretraining objective: masked segment reconstruction; fine-tuning objective: standard supervised forecast loss; hyperparameter search to optimize model performance.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: We expect the self-supervised pretraining to improve the performance of the channel-dependent encoder in the downstream forecasting task by 5-15% in average forecasting accuracy, by providing a strong inductive bias for learning temporal representations and cross-channel interactions. However, the extent of the performance gains may depend on the quality of the pretraining task and require careful hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Different Pretraining Objectives for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of different pretraining objectives, including masked segment reconstruction with attention (proposed in proposal 3), causal forecasting, and next-step forecasting, on the performance of the channel-dependent encoder in the downstream forecasting task. We will compare the effectiveness of these objectives in terms of average forecasting accuracy and analyze the learned representations to identify the underlying patterns and relationships.
CONTROLS: Baseline model: linear projection; pretraining objectives: masked segment reconstruction with attention, causal forecasting, next-step forecasting; fine-tuning objective: standard supervised forecast loss; hyperparameter search to optimize model performance.
COST: 3654
PREDICTION: We expect the results to reveal that different pretraining objectives are suited for different types of temporal dependencies and relationships, and that the best pretraining objective may vary depending on the specific task and dataset. However, the results may also reveal that the pretraining objectives are less effective than expected, highlighting the need for continued investigation and refinement.

TITLE: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effectiveness of self-supervised pretraining, inspired by BERT, as a way to learn strong temporal representations and cross-channel interactions in a channel-dependent encoder. We will design a pretraining objective that involves masking a subset of temporal segments and training the encoder to reconstruct the masked portions, and then transfer the learned representations to a downstream forecasting task.
CONTROLS: Baseline model: linear projection; pretraining objective: masked segment reconstruction; fine-tuning objective: standard supervised forecast loss; hyperparameter search to optimize model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Masking-and-Reconstruction for Encoder Training in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to compare the masking-and-reconstruction objective used for encoder training to supervised learning objectives directly applied to forecasting. We will use two variants of this objective: (1) replacing the reconstruction task with a linear regression task that directly predicts future values from encoded representations of past values, and (2) leveraging techniques from out-of-distribution learning to evaluate how well the encoder generalizes to unseen temporal patterns. We will compare the performance of these variants to BERT-inspired pretraining in combination with MAE training.
CONTROLS: Vanilla BERT-inspired pretraining-fine-tuning pipeline, specifically using the aforementioned pretraining objective followed by MAE-based fine-tuning. Baseline models for each variant that train the encoder using only supervised objectives.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect that directly training the encoder using a supervised task will lead to better performance on multivariate forecasting tasks than pretraining followed by fine-tuning. However, the proposals for leveraging OOD learning techniques may lead to increased overfitting and potentially lower performance overall, highlighting the trade-offs in the choice of pretraining objective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessor Attention Mechanisms for Capturing Cross-Variable Dependencies
PROPOSAL: To address the limitation of channel-dependent encoders that can capture but not consistently exploit cross-variable dependencies, we propose introducing Assessor Attention mechanisms into channel-independent encoders. These mechanisms would enable the assessment of variable importance and adaptively modulate channel attention according to the task's needs. We would investigate whether the resulting models outperform both channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders on multivariate forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: Original channel-independent encoders (MLP), channel-dependent encoders (GCN), various ablated encoders incorporating Assessor Attention mechanisms in different capacities.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect the Assessor Attention mechanisms to enable the capture of complex cross-variable dependencies and improve forecasting performance. However, their proposal might still require additional regularization techniques to control overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED: Evaluating Masking-and-Reconstruction for Encoder Training in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will extend our comparison of masking-and-reconstruction for encoder training by introducing an adaptive masking scheme that dynamically adjusts the masking rate based on the encoder's performance during training. This adaptive masking scheme will be compared to both fixed masking rates and other state-of-the-art pretraining objectives. We will also evaluate the gain in performance achieved through combining masking-and-reconstruction with other pretraining methods.
CONTROLS: Fixed masking schemes with static masking rates, existing pretraining objectives using grid-searched masking rates; Comparison against a well-tuned Random Forest Regressor baseline
COST: 800
PREDICTION: This extension may allow us to identify when adaptive masking is beneficial and can improve forecasting performance beyond what fixed masking schemes or other pretraining objectives provide. However, we risk making it more challenging to interpret the performance gain from the adaptive masking since the masking rate is no longer constant throughout training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simplified Linear Decoding for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to simplify the prediction process in multivariate time-series forecasting models by introducing a Lightweight Linear Decoder, which will be trained to directly predict future values from the encoded representations of past values. We aim to assess whether this simplified decoder can match or surpass the performance of existing complex decoding mechanisms, such as linear regression or more advanced neural network-based predictors.
CONTROLS: Comparison against existing decoding methods: linear regression, a simple MLP, and/or the decoder from the Hierarchical Modeling for Multivariate Time-Series Data approach. Ablated decoder setups exploring the impact of decoder type, attention mechanism, and dimensionality reduction.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect the Lightweight Linear Decoder to be competitive with or even surpass existing decoding methods, resulting in improved forecasting performance and reduced computational costs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable and Adaptable Encoder for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop an Encoder type that is both scalable and adaptable for use in multivariate time-series forecasting tasks. This will be achieved by introducing a dynamic layer modulus selection strategy and a concatenation of channel-wise feed-forward neural networks and recurrent neural networks to handle varying temporal scales. We aim to evaluate the performance of this Encoder on a diverse set of forecasting tasks and scenarios.
CONTROLS: Comparison against fixed layer modulus setups, competing state-of-the-art Encoders, and an Ablated version that evaluates the influence of only increasing the number of layers, the number of recurrent units per layer and the model size.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect this scalable and adaptable Encoder to demonstrate improved forecasting performance, robustness to changes in data quality, and efficiency with regard to computational resources, making it suitable for real-world applications.

TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Enabling Domain Adaptation in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage multi-task learning to enable domain adaptation in multivariate time-series forecasting tasks. By jointly training the Encoder, Decoder, and other components on multiple related tasks, we aim to capture shared representations across different domains, improving the model's ability to generalize to unseen domains and adapting to changes in the environment.
CONTROLS: Comparison against single-task learning, competing state-of-the-art multi-task learning methods for domain adaptation, and ablated experiments evaluating the influence of specific components on domain adaptation performance.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning to enable significant improvements in domain adaptation performance, enabling the model to learn more generalizable representations that can be effectively transferred across different domains, resulting in more robust and accurate forecasting performance.

PROPOSAL: Propose a novel joint training framework that integrates encoding, decoding, and training of multivariate time-series forecasting models. Specifically, we propose to extend the popular ATTN-CNN-TCN model by adding a cross-channel attention mechanism to the encoder, a non-linear decoder with a mixture of experts, and a novel training objective that aligns with the model's architectural design.
CONTROLS: We compare our joint training framework against the following baselines: 1) ATTN-CNN-TCN with a simple linear projection decoder, 2) ATTN-CNN-TCN with a masking-and-reconstruction pretraining objective, and 3) a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder with a separate decoding and training procedure.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Our proposed joint training framework should outperform the controls in terms of forecasting accuracy on the real-world benchmarks, with significant improvements in capturing complex temporal structures and cross-channel dependencies. Potential failure points include the computational cost of the proposed cross-channel attention mechanism and the non-linear decoder, which may require careful optimization and regularization.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Encoding and Decoding Multivariate Time-Series with Transformers
PROPOSAL: We design a new transformer-based architecture, MVT-Trans, to effectively capture both channel-independent and channel-dependent temporal dependencies within input signals. MVT-Trans consists of a novel channel-dependent encoder, which learns separate temporal embeddings for each channel using a shared transformer encoder, and a linear time-invariant (LTI) decoder, which directly predicts future values from the encoded representations. We explore different training objectives, including masked reconstruction, one-step forecasting, and multi-step forecasting, to evaluate the effectiveness of MVT-Trans in various settings.
CONTROLS: We compare MVT-Trans to channel-independent transformers (e.g., Transformer-XL), channel-dependent transformers (e.g., TCN), and state-of-the-art models (e.g., GRU4Rec) on five real-world datasets from weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting.
COST: 8328.76
PREDICTION: MVT-Trans achieves state-of-the-art results on most datasets, especially in weather forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting, indicating the effectiveness of its channel-dependent encoding mechanism and LTI decoder. However, in certain scenarios where temporal dependencies are extremely complex (e.g., traffic flow forecasting), MVT-Trans may struggle to adapt and require additional technical innovations.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Effective Channel-Dependent Encoding for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a new self-attention mechanism, MVT-SelfAttn, that learns both channel-independent and channel-dependent temporal relationships within input signals. MVT-SelfAttn is designed to adaptively attend to relevant channels and temporal slots, capturing complex interactions between variates. We integrate MVT-SelfAttn into the encoder of MVT-Trans and explore its effectiveness on five real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare the updated MVT-Trans (encoder with MVT-SelfAttn) to the original MVT-Trans, channel-independent baselines (e.g., Transformer-XL), and state-of-the-art models (e.g., GRU4Rec) on the five real-world datasets.
COST: 16800
PREDICTION: MVT-SelfAttn improves the performance of MVT-Trans on datasets with complex cross-channel interactions (e.g., traffic flow forecasting), demonstrating its ability to effectively capture nuanced relationships between variates. Its performance may, however, degrade on datasets with simpler patterns (e.g., weather forecasting).

TITLE: Joint Training of Encoders and Decoders for Multivariate Time-Series
PROPOSAL: We propose a joint training framework for multivariate time-series forecasting models that optimizes both the encoder and decoder simultaneously using an objective function that balances reconstruction accuracy and prediction performance. This framework encourages the model to learn temporally coherent representations of past signals and to reconstruct past values accurately, leading to improved forecasting accuracy. We adapt this framework to MVT-Trans model and evaluate its performance on five real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare the joint training framework to the traditional pretraining-finetuning pipeline used in MVT-Trans, as well as to other state-of-the-art models (e.g., TASEP) that use joint training approaches.
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: Joint training framework significantly improves the performance of MVT-Trans on most datasets, especially in scenarios where the encoder and decoder need to be in sync with each other (e.g., traffic flow forecasting and solar power generation forecasting). However, it may lead to overfitting on certain datasets with limited training data (e.g., electricity transformer temperature forecasting).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Encoding and Decoding Multivariate Time-Series with Transformers
PROPOSAL: We design a new transformer-based architecture, MVT-Trans, to effectively capture both channel-independent and channel-dependent temporal dependencies within input signals. MVT-Trans consists of a novel channel-dependent encoder, which learns separate temporal embeddings for each channel using a shared transformer encoder, and a linear time-invariant (LTI) decoder, which directly predicts future values from the encoded representations. We explore different training objectives, including masked reconstruction, one-step forecasting, and multi-step forecasting, to evaluate the effectiveness of MVT-Trans in various settings.
CONTROLS: We compare MVT-Trans to channel-independent transformers (e.g., Transformer-XL), channel-dependent transformers (e.g., TCN), and state-of-the-art models (e.g., GRU4Rec) on five real-world datasets from weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: MVT-Trans achieves state-of-the-art results on most datasets, especially in weather forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting, indicating the effectiveness of its channel-dependent encoding mechanism and LTI decoder. However, in certain scenarios where temporal dependencies are extremely complex (e.g., traffic flow forecasting), MVT-Trans may struggle to adapt and require additional technical innovations.

MVT-SelfAttn is designed to adaptively attend to relevant channels and temporal slots, capturing complex interactions between variates. We integrate MVT-SelfAttn into the encoder of MVT-Trans (proposal 1) and explore its effectiveness on five real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare the updated MVT-Trans with MVT-SelfAttn to the original MVT-Trans and channel-independent baselines (e.g., Transformer-XL) on the five real-world datasets.

PREDICTION: MVT-SelfAttn improves the performance of MVT-Trans on datasets with complex cross-channel interactions (e.g., traffic flow forecasting), demonstrating its ability to effectively capture nuanced relationships between variates. Its performance may, however, degrade on datasets with simpler patterns (e.g., weather forecasting).

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Cross-Channel Dependencies via Shared Gated Recurrent Units
PROPOSAL: Modify the existing channel-independent encoder architecture by incorporating shared gated recurrent units (GRUs) to capture cross-channel dependencies. At each GRU layer, each variate shares its GRU cell with other variates, allowing for the joint modeling of temporal dynamics and cross-variable interactions.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original channel-independent encoder and an ablation where GRUs are replaced with separate GRUs for each variate.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This modification could lead to improved performance in multivariate time-series forecasting, especially in domains like electricity consumption forecasting and solar power generation forecasting, as it enables the model to capture relationships between different variates. However, it might struggle in domains with a large number of variables or complex cross-variable interactions, leading to increased computational costs and reduced generalizability.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Cross-Channel Dependencies via Shared Gated Recurrent Units
PROPOSAL: Modify the existing channel-independent encoder architecture by incorporating shared gated recurrent units (GRUs) to capture cross-channel dependencies. At each GRU layer, each variate shares its GRU cell with other variates, allowing for the joint modeling of temporal dynamics and cross-variable interactions.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original channel-independent encoder and an ablation where GRUs are replaced with separate GRUs for each variate.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This modification could lead to improved performance in multivariate time-series forecasting, especially in domains like electricity consumption forecasting and solar power generation forecasting, as it enables the model to capture relationships between different variates. However, it might struggle in domains with a large number of variables or complex cross-variable interactions, leading to increased computational costs and reduced generalizability.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating Non-Linear Decoder Architectures for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Design and compare different non-linear decoder architectures, such as transformers, tree-based models, or graph neural networks, to improve prediction quality from encoded representations. Specifically, test a transformer-based decoder with three different attention mechanisms (scaled dot-product, local attention, and product quaternion attention).
CONTROLS: Compare with the conventional linear decoder and a baseline model that uses a channel-independent encoder and a linear decoder.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: A non-linear decoder could significantly improve forecasting accuracy, especially in domains with complex temporal patterns, such as traffic flow forecasting and electricity transformer temperature forecasting. However, it might require more training data and computational resources to converge, and may not generalize well to domains with simple temporal dynamics.

ACTION: REVISE 1

CONTROLS: Compare with the original shared GRU layers without weighted variate importance and an ablation with shared GRUs but without the weighted weights mechanism.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: The weighting mechanism could enhance the model's ability to capture complex relationships between variables, leading to improved performance in multivariate time-series forecasting. PREDICTION: The auxiliary tasks could improve the model's ability to learn temporal dynamics and adapt to the specific forecasting task, leading to better performance in domains like weather forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Information Gain of Views in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a series of ablation experiments using SimCLR on the CIFAR-10 dataset, where we vary the number and type of augmentations applied to each view while measuring the mutual information between them using the Kulback-Leibler divergence (KLD).
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline of standard SimCLR with default augmentations, and also examine the influence of data augmentation complexity by comparing different augmentation types (e.g., color jittering vs. crops).
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that increasing the diversity of augmentations applied to each view increases the mutual information between them, but that this improvement will saturate at a certain point due to leakage and nonspecificity; we also anticipate difficulties in accurately estimating the KLD due to the poor quality of the student model's representations early in training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Diversity via Dynamic Augmentation Scheduling
PROPOSAL: We will modify the MOCO framework to use a dynamic augmentation scheduling approach, where the difficulty of augmentations applied to each view is gradually increased as the model learns more complex representations, measured using a validation set accuracy threshold. Augmentation difficulty will be quantified by measuring the Jensen-Shannon divergence between views.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline MOCO implementation with static augmentations, and also examine the influence of scheduling aggressiveness by allowing for different rates of augmentation increase.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect that adaptive augmentation difficulty scheduling will lead to improved representation learning in comparison to the static scheduling approach, particularly as the model is trained for longer periods, as the augmentation schedule will allow the model to adapt to its emergent capabilities. However, we may encounter challenges in calibrating the schedule, and finding the optimal rate of augmentation increase.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Semantic Invariance and Representational Expressivity
PROPOSAL: We will design an information-theoretic framework for characterizing the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity in contrastive learning, using the Riemannian manifold framework to analyze the geometry of feature spaces. We will define a measure of "feature variability" as the minimum-distance-mean distance between views and use the mutual information between views as a proxy for representational expressivity.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline of standard contrastive loss and examine the influence of different contrastive objectives on the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity can be characterized in a principled way using our framework, but that existing contrastive objectives may not achieve optimal balance due to their limitations in modeling semantic coherence. However, we may encounter difficulties in calibrating the trade-off parameters, and in visualizing the geometry of the feature space.

TITLE: Representation Quality Metric (RQM) Development
PROPOSAL: We will develop a representation quality metric (RQM) to evaluate the quality of the model's representations, by using a combination of similarity-based measures (e.g. clustering accuracy, inter-class variance) and information-theoretic measures (e.g. entropy, mutual information).
CONTROLS: We will evaluate RQM on a set of baseline models, including those trained with different contrastive objectives, and examine the influence of different RQM variants on the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that RQM will serve as a useful tool for evaluating representation quality, but that its performance may be sensitive to the choice of similarity and information-theoretic measures, and may require careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Contrastive Augmentation Strategies Using a Novel Benchmark
PROPOSAL: We propose a new real-world benchmark, "Dynamic Views" (DV), in which we collect multiple, systematically varied views of the same instance (e.g., images with varying lighting, orientation, and cropping). We will use DV to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of different augmentation strategies, including on-the-fly data augmentation, augmentation cascades, and learning-based data augmentation, under both large-batch and small-batch settings.
CONTROLS: We will compare these strategies to established baselines (e.g., SimCLR's standard augmentation) on DV, as well as on a held-out set of real-world benchmarks (e.g., Cifar-10, ImageNet).
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Our results should provide meaningful insights into the strengths and weaknesses of various augmentation strategies and identify opportunities for improvement. However, we may find that existing augmentations, despite their heuristic nature, perform surprisingly well on certain tasks, and our findings may not generalize to entirely new environments or domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Meta-Parametric Augmentations
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive contrastive learning framework that dynamically generates meta-parametric augmentations at training time, using a learned meta-learner to optimize these parameters based on the input data. This approach allows for on-the-fly adaptation of augmentations to the specific instance or subset of instances at hand. We will leverage the "Dynamic Views" benchmark (proposed in turn 2) to evaluate the performance of our adaptive framework.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive framework to state-of-the-art contrastive learning baselines (e.g., SimCLR, MoCo) on the "Dynamic Views" benchmark, as well as on a held-out set of real-world benchmarks.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Our adaptive framework should greatly improve performance on instances or subsets of instances that are challenging for traditional augmentations, and enable more efficient adaptation to new environments or tasks. However, we may encounter difficulties in handling very complex or distractor-rich augmentations, which could introduce new modes of failure.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Meta-Parametric Augmentations
PROPOSAL: We extend the adaptive contrastive learning framework of our previous proposal (turn 3) by incorporating catastrophic forgetting prevention and dynamic reduction of augmentations. During training, the framework maintains a short-term memory of previously learned knowledge to mitigate forgetting during the adaptation process. Additionally, it adaptively adjusts the number of augmentations per instance to avoid overfitting and improve efficiency. We evaluate the improved framework using the "Dynamic Views" benchmark and a selection of held-out real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We compare our improved adaptive framework to state-of-the-art contrastive learning baselines (e.g., SimCLR, MoCo), as well as our own modified Meta-Cyclic Augmentation strategy (proposed in turn 4).
COST: 5200
PREDICTION: Our revised adaptive framework should exhibit improved robustness to catastrophic forgetting and reduced risk of overfitting, enabling it to more effectively adapt to novel environments and tasks. However, the increased complexity of our framework may introduce additional challenges and failpoints, such as slower learning or higher memory requirements.

TITLE: Theoretical Limits of Adaptive Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to theoretically analyze the limits of adaptive contrastive learning, deriving bounds on the performance of adaptive frameworks like ours in terms of the metrics studied in the information-theoretic analysis (proposed in turn 1). Our goal is to understand the fundamental trade-offs between adaptability, representation capacity, and overfitting prevention. We will pose our analysis in the regime where the number of augmentations adapts based on the input data, using tools from information theory and optimization.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bounds to the performance of the state-of-the-art adaptive framework (proposed in turn 5) to assess the practical relevance of our theoretical analysis.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Our theoretical bounds should provide fundamental insights into the behavior of adaptive contrastive learning, revealing the inherent trade-offs between adaptability, capacity, and overfitting prevention. However, our bounds may be overly pessimistic or unrealistic, failing to capture the practical success of specific adaptive implementations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Progressive Contrastive Learning for Small-Batch Regimes
PROPOSAL: We propose a new approach to progressive contrastive learning that incrementally increases the batch size and complexity of augmentations as the model learns. This involves using a probabilistic method to control the batch size, allowing the model to adapt to changing difficulty levels. We will evaluate our approach on a variety of real-world benchmarks, comparing it to state-of-the-art contrastive learning baselines and our own adaptive framework (proposed in turn 3).
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to SimCLR and MoCo, two widely-used contrastive learning frameworks.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Our progressive approach should enable effective contrastive learning in small-batch regimes, introducing adaptability and flexibility to current methods. However, we may struggle with determining the best way to adjust the batch size and augmentation complexity for specific tasks and datasets, leading to suboptimal performance in certain cases.

In each step, AACL chooses a subset of the data distribution's "easy" augmentations (i.e., augmentations that preserve semantic content) to construct informative views, dynamically adjusting the augmentation complexity to balance invariance and expressivity.
CONTROLS: We compare AACL against SimCLR, MoCo, and two ablations: one where AACL only uses a fixed augmentation strategy and another where AACL only expands the augmentation complexity, without adjusting it.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: AACL is expected to outperform the baselines and ablations in settings where the data has limited view diversity. AACL may struggle when the data contains many highly semantically preserving augmentations.

PROPOSAL: We enhance the AACL framework to include a dynamic representational expansion mechanism, allowing AACL to autonomously adapt its representational capacity to the instance in question. PROPOSAL: We evaluate the performance of AACL in small-batch settings (e.g., batch size of 32) using the CIFAR-100 and SVHN datasets. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Contrastive Learning Framework with Relative Augmentation (iCRL)
PROPOSAL: We introduce the iCRL framework, an information-theoretic extension to AACL. iCRL computes relative augmentation scores, which measure the amount of new information an augmentation provides for each instance. We propose to use these scores as a regularization term within AACL, making the augmentation strategy aware of the relative informativeness of different augmentations.
CONTROLS: We compare iCRL against AACL and additional baselines, using CIFAR-100 and SVHN as benchmark datasets.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: iCRL is expected to outperform AACL in datasets where augmentations vary significantly in informativeness, thanks to its adaptive augmentation strategy. However, iCRL may be computationally expensive in cases where the augmentation space contains an extremely large number of options.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling Strategies for Efficient Contrastive Learning with AACL and iCRL
PROPOSAL: We investigate efficient sampling strategies for contrastive learning with AACL and iCRL, particularly in small-batch settings. We propose two novel sampling schemes: 1) Informativeness-aware sampling, selecting instances based on their relative augmentation scores, and 2) Hard-negative mining, identifying challenging instances for contrastive learning. Both strategies aim to maintain a diverse yet informative set of instances for training.
CONTROLS: We evaluate these sampling strategies against random sampling, comparing performance on CIFAR-100 and SVHN.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We expect both sampling strategies to improve training efficiency and reduce noise in the contrastive learning objective. However, the informativeness-aware sampling method may not be effective for datasets with highly variable instance difficulties.

TITLE: Expanding Representation Capacity with SpecZoo: A Data-Driven Method for Augmentation Design
PROPOSAL: We introduce SpecZoo, a data-driven method for designing augmentations that expand representation capacity under AACL and iCRL. SpecZoo utilizes clustering and sparse-coding techniques to identify informative features and augmentations that enhance view diversity.
CONTROLS: We compare SpecZoo against the augmented randomization and human-engineered augmentation methods on standard contrastive learning benchmarks, and evaluate its impact on representational capacity using information-theoretic metrics.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: SpecZoo is expected to improve representation capacity and informativeness of learned representations, across various reference datasets. However, SpecZoo may become overly specialized to the specific feature distribution of the training data, failing to generalize to unseen augmentations or data.

CONTROLS: We compare SpecZoo with iterative refinement against the baseline SpecZoo, and against human-engineered augmentation methods, on various reference datasets.

PROPOSAL: Analyze the information-theoretic structure of contrastive learning objectives using tools from mutual information and information bottleneck principles. Specifically, derive a lower bound for the mutual information between augmented views of an instance, and experimentally validate this bound using the STL-10 dataset with the SimCLR framework.
CONTROLS: STL-10, SimCLR, InfoNCE loss as baseline, ablation study on different augmentation strategies
COST: 2430
PREDICTION: Expected to show that current augmentations are suboptimal (due to poor trade-off between transformation complexity and semantic preservation), and identify engines for improvement in view-design methods. It might fail to provide lower bounds that are tight in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Expansion for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop an algorithmic framework for adaptive view expansion, leveraging online learning and active sampling to iteratively augment each instance with views that maximize the information gain estimated using the lower bound from Proposal 1. Evaluate the efficacy of this approach on ImageNet with MoCo, and compare to static augmentation strategies.
CONTROLS: ImageNet, MoCo, static augmentation as baseline, ablation study on different sampling strategies
COST: 4,020
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved representation capacity, reduced batch size requirements, and improved small-batch performance. It may fail to converge to optimal view expansions in certain regimes.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Scaling Properties of Contrastive Learning Batches
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scaling properties of contrastive learning batches using spectral clustering and kernel theory, analyzing how batch size affects the learned representation space's dimensionality, spectrum, and effective capacity. Identify critical batch sizes that correspond to phase transitions in the learned representation. Evaluate on ImageNet with MoCo, and compare to the adaptive view expansion approach from Proposal 2.
CONTROLS: ImageNet, MoCo, static batch sizes as baseline, ablation study on different kernel and clustering methods
COST: 3,451
PREDICTION: Expected to show how batch size affects representation capacity and identify optimal batch sizes for different representation requirements. It might fail to recognize batch size's impact on semantic invariance.

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: Develop a principled approach to designing augmentations by leveraging the information gain bounds from Proposal 1, optimizing for either mutual information or the new information contributed to the model by each augmentation. Implement and evaluate this approach on a range of benchmark datasets, including STL-10 and CIFAR-10, comparing to both standard SimCLR and the adaptive view expansion method from Proposal 2.
CONTROLS: STL-10 and CIFAR-10, SimCLR and adaptive view expansion as baseline, ablation study on different optimization objectives and metrics
COST: 5,613
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved representation quality and semantic coherence when using principled augmentations, with a potential failure in adapting well to domain-specific datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Semantic Invariance in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the learned representation space's geometry and manifold structure relate to semantic invariance, using techniques such as Laplace embeddings and diffusion maps to visualize and analyze the learned representations. Specifically, evaluate the representational similarity between views of the same instance and its variability across different instances. Use the STL-10 dataset and the SimCLR framework.
CONTROLS: STL-10, SimCLR, ablation study on different embedding and visualization methods
COST: 7,238
PREDICTION: Expected to shed light on how contrastive learning achieves semantic invariance, and identify potential failure points in the learned representation space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mitigating Domain Shift in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of domain shift on contrastive learning, evaluating how the method generalizes to new, unseen domains. Specifically, design domain shift simulations on the Office-Caltech dataset, comparing the performance of SimCLR and the adaptive view expansion method from Proposal 2. Additionally, develop a fusion architecture integrated with both methods to leverage their respective strengths in adapted domains.
CONTROLS: Office-Caltech dataset, SimCLR and adaptive view expansion as baseline, ablation study on different fusion architectures
COST: 9,512
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved generalizability by leveraging augmented views and adaptive expansion, while potential challenges arise in identifying robust representation patterns across diverse domains.

CONTROLS: STL-10 and synthetic data, ablation study on different spectral clustering methods and hyperparameters

PREDICTION: Expected to shed light on the mechanism underlying contrastive learning's representation capacity, while potential challenges arise in translating the theoretical connection to practical insights on improving representation quality.

TITLE: Evaluating Contrastive Learning with Semi-Supervised Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We adapt a semi-supervised meta-learning framework (ALIS, Lambert et al 2021) to compute the mutual information between views in contrastive learning. We utilize a set of diverse real-world datasets, including CIFAR-10, STL-10, and ImageNet-100, with partially labeled subsets. We compare different metrics for measuring view similarity and estimate the MI between views.
CONTROLS: We include controls using I-p GetString metric from the original paper by contrastive learning; Strong baseline is SSL training.
COST: 1345.6
PREDICTION: We expect that utilizing semi-supervised meta-learning for MI calculations between views will resemble a better ranking for contrastive settings than SSL alone; But as least partially, it will fail against settings when the models' transformation are fairly diverse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical lower bound on the mutual information achievable by contrastive learning objectives under mild assumptions (sub-Gaussian noise, bounded data distribution). Utilizing results from recent literature on information-theoretic lower bounds for MMRE and WRE estimators, we prove that a family of contrastive objectives requires at least Ω(log(n)) mutual information across views to avoid trivial solutions, where n is the number of data points.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to existing analyses of contrastive objectives (Chen et al 2020, Tschannen et al 2020).
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Our analysis will demonstrate a lower bound of  Ω(log(n)) as a theoretical necessity, which is expected to no longer be reduced below in practice, even with epoch-wise exponentially increasing instance complexities

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Refining Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We extend our previous work on information-theoretic lower bounds for contrastive learning objectives by applying the Fano’s inequality to our mutual information formulation. This new bound allows us to more accurately quantify the fundamental "noise floor" in the information landscape, which is crucial to understanding the feasible and fundamental nature of different augmentations. We also detail an analysis of the maximum achievable mutual information under a variety of augmentation heuristics, including fixed and adaptive methods.
CONTROLS: In addition to comparing to existing results (Chen et al 2020, Tschannen et al 2020), we also consider contrastive models using a single augmentation scheme from (Wu et al 2020).
COST: 3654
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in our analysis's accuracy and can demonstrate the noise floor more accurately in practice. Still, we can reveal the cause behind trials where our former work showed curvature of choices.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation-Guided Exploration of the Information Landscape
PROPOSAL: We leverage the semi-supervised meta-learning framework from our first proposal to explore how different augmentation strategies affect the information gain between views. By systematically manipulating augmentation hyperparameters (e.g., kernel size, color-jittering), we seek to understand the curvilinear factors that influence the trade-off between semantic coherence and representational diversity. We analyze the resulting dynamics using our lower bound analysis from the second proposal.
CONTROLS: Ablations with random data augmentation strategies will be used for comparison to state-of-the-art baseline contrastive models (SimCLR).
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to identify key hyperparameters for augmentation schemes that significantly enhance information gain while maintaining semantic consistency; Yet, conversely, augmentation schemes should ultimately prove of limited balance given large offsets.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Dynamic Graph Construction for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive dynamic graph construction method, ADGC, to selectively sample high-information-gain augmentations and build a learned graph structure for each instance during training. The graph represents the relationships between different views and their augmentations, which allows for informed sampling and mitigates the need for large batch sizes. We incorporate the learned graph into the semi-supervised meta-learning framework from our first proposal to refine the representation learning process.
CONTROLS: Comparison to batch-hard negative sampling (Wen et al 2020) and evaluations on ImageNet-100.
COST: 9310
PREDICTION: We anticipate that ADGC will significantly improve the adaptive sampling strategy, resulting in a notable performance gap against non-adaptive settings; Still, the improvement may be expected to diminish when augmentations are randomly permuted or dissimilar.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Instance-Specific and Average-Pooling Metrics for Augmentation Evaluation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the performance of both instance-specific and average-pooling metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of augmentations in the information landscape. Utilizing the adaptive graph construction method from our fourth proposal, we examine how different metrics impact the learning dynamics and the resulting representations. We contrast instance-specific metrics, such as mutual information or Jensen-Shannon divergence, with average-pooling metrics, such as forward KL-divergence.
CONTROLS: In addition to state-of-the-art baseline contrastive models (SimCLR), we compare our results with "training diffusion" an average-pooling strategy.
COST: 10700
PREDICTION: We expect that instance-specific metrics will outperform average-pooling metrics in terms of information gain and semantic coherence; Conversely, performance may decrease in the metric when batch sizes approach large scale.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Multi-Branch Distance Metric Learning Approach for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel multi-branch distance metric learning approach to contrastive learning, MBL. MBL employs multiple branches to learn augmented views of an instance, leveraging the information gain from different hyperparameter settings and augmentation strategies. Each branch is trained with a custom distance metric, allowing for more nuanced and higher-fidelity representation learning. We combine the outputs from all branches to generate a comprehensive and informative representation.
CONTROLS: Comparison with other contrastive learning models, such as SimCLR and MoCo, utilizing ImageNet-100.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the multi-branch approach will improve upon state-of-the-art models by capturing complex relationships between augmentations, with significant performance gains, especially in low-shot, high-complexity scenarios; However, we also expect computational overhead for inference will be significantly higher.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Information Bottleneck Interpretation for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We apply the information bottleneck framework (TBFB 2014) to the contrastive learning setting, investigating the role of the information bottleneck in shaping the representation learning process. By analyzing the information-theoretic constraints imposed on the representation, we seek to understand the relationship between the information bottleneck and the mutual information between views.
CONTROLS: Comparison with current state-of-the-art contrastive learning models, using ImageNet-100.
COST: 16800
PREDICTION: We expect that applying the information bottleneck framework will provide insights into the fundamental trade-off between representation accuracy and efficiency, and reveal new constraints on representation learning that are essential for effective training; Yet, the information bottleneck interpretation might struggle due to the noise in diversity values.

TITLE: Evaluating Episodic Test-Time Adaptation Methods on CLIP
PROPOSAL: Compare CLIP's performance on image classification tasks before and after applying 5 well-known episodic TTA methods (such as coarse-fine attention, selective attention, multiscale features, Prospective Parsimoniousamer Understanding of Text, and Cross-modal Coupling and Plugging Model), using a consistent evaluation setup with a fixed pre-trained model checkpoint and evaluation protocol.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Reproducibility of Existing Episodic TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Run a set of 10 experiments on 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) with 2 different pre-trained checkpoints each, using the same text prompts and evaluation protocols, to isolate and evaluate the impact of checkpoint variations on the performance of existing episodic TTA methods. Use the ImageNet validation set and report accuracy, recall, and F1-score as metrics.
CONTROLS: Run the same experiments on a single pre-trained checkpoint, using the same text prompts and evaluation protocols, to serve as a baseline comparison.
COST: 330
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the choice of pre-trained checkpoint significantly impacts the reported performance of episodic TTA methods, with some methods showing larger variability than others. However, this may not lead to significant differences in reported progress over earlier methods. 

This proposal aims to address the issue of unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, and provide a controlled basis for evaluating the impact of TTA methods on existing VLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Test-Time Adaptation on Model Trustworthiness and Stability
PROPOSAL: Develop a custom evaluation framework to assess the trustworthiness and stability of VLMs under test-time adaptation, using metrics such as robustness against adversarial attacks, calibration error, and model interpretability. Apply this framework to 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) with and without test-time adaptation using 5 different episodic TTA methods, and compare the results to a baseline model not adapted at test time.
CONTROLS: Use a different evaluation framework focused solely on accuracy, and compare the results to the original baseline model.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect to find that some TTA methods may compromise the trustworthiness and stability of VLMs, particularly those that focus solely on accuracy, while other methods may have little impact or even improve these properties. However, this may not be the case for all models and adaptation scenarios.

This proposal addresses the issue of incomplete understanding of TTA methods beyond accuracy, and aims to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of their practical strengths and weaknesses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Existing Episodic and Online TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare 10 existing episodic and online TTA methods on 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) using the ImageNet validation set and report accuracy, recall, and F1-score as metrics. For episodic methods, evaluate their performance on 10 different test samples with varying data distributions. For online methods, compare their performance on a streaming dataset consisting of 1000 images with varying data distributions.
CONTROLS: Use a baseline model not adapted at test time, and compare its performance to that of the TTA methods.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect to find that some episodic TTA methods may outperform others, particularly in scenarios with significant data distribution shifts, while online methods may adapt better to gradual changes in data distributions. However, we also expect to find that the performance differences between TTA methods may be relatively small compared to the performance differences between VLMs and between different pre-trained checkpoints.

This proposal aims to provide a comprehensive comparison of existing TTA methods under consistent and controlled conditions, and assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Reproducibility of Existing Episodic TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Run a set of 10 experiments on 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) with 2 different pre-trained checkpoints each, using the same text prompts and evaluation protocols, to isolate and evaluate the impact of checkpoint variations on the performance of existing episodic TTA methods. Use the ImageNet validation set and report accuracy, recall, and F1-score as metrics.
CONTROLS: Run the same experiments on a single pre-trained checkpoint, using the same text prompts and evaluation protocols, to serve as a baseline comparison.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the choice of pre-trained checkpoint significantly impacts the reported performance of episodic TTA methods, with some methods showing larger variability than others. However, this may not lead to significant differences in reported progress over earlier methods. 

This proposal aims to address the issue of unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, and provide a controlled basis for evaluating the impact of TTA methods on existing VLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Test-Time Adaptation on Model Trustworthiness and Stability
PROPOSAL: Develop a custom evaluation framework to assess the trustworthiness and stability of VLMs under test-time adaptation, using metrics such as robustness against adversarial attacks, calibration error, and model interpretability. Apply this framework to 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) with and without test-time adaptation using 5 different episodic TTA methods, and compare the results to a baseline model not adapted at test time.
CONTROLS: Use a different evaluation framework focused solely on accuracy, and compare the results to the original baseline model.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that some TTA methods may compromise the trustworthiness and stability of VLMs, particularly those that focus solely on accuracy, while other methods may have little impact or even improve these properties. However, this may not be the case for all models and adaptation scenarios.

This proposal addresses the issue of incomplete understanding of TTA methods beyond accuracy, and aims to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of their practical strengths and weaknesses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Existing Episodic and Online TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare 10 existing episodic and online TTA methods on 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) using the ImageNet validation set and report accuracy, recall, and F1-score as metrics. For episodic methods, evaluate their performance on 10 different test samples with varying data distributions. For online methods, compare their performance on a streaming dataset consisting of 1000 images with varying data distributions.
CONTROLS: Use a baseline model not adapted at test time, and compare its performance to that of the TTA methods.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that some episodic TTA methods may outperform others, particularly in scenarios with significant data distribution shifts, while online methods may adapt better to gradual changes in data distributions. However, we also expect to find that the performance differences between TTA methods may be relatively small compared to the performance differences between VLMs and between different pre-trained checkpoints.

This proposal aims to provide a comprehensive comparison of existing TTA methods under consistent and controlled conditions, and assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison of Episodic and Online TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Revise the comparative study (proposal 3) to include a systematic evaluation of the performance ofishops episodic and online TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time, using a $350K \times 350K$-resized ImageNet validation set and report accuracy, recall, and F1-score as metrics. Specifically, fine-tune 5 types of VLMs (CLIP, VL-BERT, DALL-E, VisualBERT, and Flamingo) using 10 different training datasets with varying sizes and complexities, and then apply the episodic and online TTA methods to the resulting models.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the fine-tuned models with and without TTA methods, and evaluate the performance of the TTA methods on the pre-fine-tuned models.
COST: 3200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that TTA methods generally have smaller performance gains on models that have already been tuned at training time, as the models are more accurately adapted to the target task. However, some TTA methods may still provide significant value in certain scenarios, particularly those involving large data distribution shifts.

This revised proposal aims to address the limited evaluation of TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time, and assess their practical strengths and weaknesses in more realistic scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison of Episodic and Online TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Add a permutation test analysis to the comparative study (proposal 3) to assess the statistical significance of the performance differences between the episodic and online TTA methods, and evaluate the stability of these differences across different test samples and streaming datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of the permutation test analysis to those of a null hypothesis testing framework, where the performance differences are assumed to be due to chance.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the performance differences between the episodic and online TTA methods may not be statistically significant in some cases, suggesting that the observed differences may be due to chance rather than the adaptation methods themselves.

This revised proposal aims to provide a more rigorous evaluation of the performance differences between the episodic and online TTA methods, and assess the stability of these differences in more detail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Initializing Discrete Video Tokenizers with Image-to-Video Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate whether pre-training image tokenizers on a large image dataset can serve as a good initialization for discrete video tokenizers, and whether fine-tuning on a small video dataset can achieve high reconstruction quality more efficiently than training from scratch. We propose several pre-training strategies on large image datasets (e.g., ImageNet-21k) and fine-tuning on a range of video benchmarks (e.g., UCF101, HMDB51). Our goal is to minimize the gap in reconstruction quality between pre-trained and fine-tuned models, and to determine whether this approach can scale to high-resolution video tokenization.
CONTROLS: We compare our pre-trained and fine-tuned models against two baselines: a video tokenizer trained from scratch on the same video dataset, and an image tokenizer used directly without any fine-tuning. We also examine the effect of pre-training duration, fine-tuning duration, and dataset size on tokenizer quality.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in tokenizer quality when pre-training on large image datasets and fine-tuning on video data, with a modest increase in computational cost. However, the quality gap between pre-trained and fine-tuned models may persist, especially for high-resolution video tokenization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Fast and Accurate Long-term Video Generation with Temporally-Shared Models
PROPOSAL: We explore the feasibility of a temporally-shared model architecture that allows for efficient handling of long videos and extended interaction with users. The model is designed to learn a video representation that captures both the visual and temporal information, and is optimized for fast and accurate generation of future video frames. We propose a conditional spatial-agnostic Temporal Transformer block that aggregates previous frame representations, allowing the model to progressively update the video context without requiring sequential attention to the full history. This design allows for faster-than-real-time video generation and extended interaction.
CONTROLS: We compare our model against a baseline that uses a standard next-token prediction approach and against a state-of-the-art diffusion model. We also evaluate the impact of various hyperparameters, such as the number of past frames to condense and the number of iterations for each temporal step, on the model's performance and efficiency.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant reduction in generation latency and an increase in generation quality when using our temporally-shared model architecture, especially for longer videos. However, it may require a careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

TITLE: Improved Temporal Modeling with Hierarchical Discrete Tokens
PROPOSAL: We introduce Hierarchical Discrete Tokeners (HDTs) that divide the video sequence into intervals, and use a discrete tokenizer within each interval to capture both spatial and temporal features. This hierarchical strategy decouples the factorial growth of token count with increasing video length and reduces the need for expensive sequential denoising steps or long contexts. By iteratively predicting and combining tokens from selected intervals, HDTs  maintain temporal consistency while allowing for efficient generation and refinement.
CONTROLS: Compare to a ablation experiment with single-level discrete tokenizers and several state-of-the-art diffusion models (listed below).
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: This yields significant speedup while preserving high video quality and possibly outperforming diffusion models (tolerance for motion artefacts due to possible preference of continuous sampled additive noise in distortion measure). HDT might struggle to balance between high-detail refinement and temporal information, or when describing long-term motions in concise tokens. 

STATE-OF-THE-ART DIFFUSION MODELS: Visual VGDL, ProT, SAVAG, SDE-based wired vaeps

TITLE: Efficient Video Discrete Tokenizers via Inverse Decomposition
PROPOSAL: We develop a novel decomposition-based discrete tokenizer, IDE-Tokener, which learns a compact representation of discrete video tokens from coarse-to-fine scale decomposition of frames, seeded from a pre-trained static image tokenizer. This approach speeds up video tokenizer training, leveraging the Fisher information of the static image tokenizer and focusing the learning process on rapid deviation rationale recovering precise dynamic contents. IDE-Tokener also enjoys lighter storage and inference footprints through its structural compression of temporally sequential data into higher-discriminatory parallel stream tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare IDE-Tokener against (a) naively adapted single-frame static tokenizer, (b) static tokenizer with additional component learning to compress temporal dynamics, (c) parallel training strategies (space-or-time-sharing, chunking etc.) and (d) diffusion models such as for control.
COST: 12,000
PREDICTION: The efficiency improvement is expected to hold even for short clips (256 frame) and selections training costs could be narrowly outdone only by top-rank end-diffusion-scapes if optimized under sufficient minrecord and disk buddy synchronization but motion anticipation may sometimes degrade.

TITLE: Temporally-Sensitive Attention Mechanism for Long Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a Temporally-Sensitive Attention Mechanism (TSAM) to selectively focus on relevant past frames and adaptively adjust its contribution based on the current frame's importance in the video sequence. TSAM enables models to maintain a consistent temporal context and generate long videos without exploding context lengths. It is particularly effective when combined with proposals 1 and 3, as it can refine the trade-off between temporal coherence and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare TSAM against (a) fixed-weight attention, (b) naive concatenation of past frames, and (c) TSAM+HDT and TSAM+Hybrid VAR-Diff combinations.
COST: 27,240
PREDICTION: TSAM facilitates the generation of high-quality long videos by effectively managing temporal context, however its added computational cost for selective refinement may affect its adoption in scenarios demanding extreme efficiency.

PROPOSAL: We refine Hierarchical Discrete Tokeners (HDTs) by incorporating a top-down conditionally scattered convolution (CSC) block to strengthen the communication between neighboring intervals, enhance temporal coherence and capture intricate dynamics simultaneously. The CSC block learns to selectively share information between intervals, avoiding information explosion and enabling efficient generation of long videos.
CONTROLS: Compare CSC-HDT against the original HDT and several state-of-the-art diffusion models, as well as ablations of CSC components.

PREDICTION: This yields a significant improvement in video quality and temporal coherence, and possibly outperforms diffusion models in certain settings. However, the added complexity of CSC block might increase training time and make the model more prone to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying Visual AutoRegressive and Diffusion Modeling
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel model, Hybrid VAR-Diff, which combines the strengths of Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) and diffusion modeling. Our approach uses a discrete autoencoder to refine the latent representation learned by a diffusion model, and incorporates a VAR-style refinement mechanism to produce high-quality, coherent videos. Hybrid VAR-Diff unifies the advantages of VAR's efficient generation and diffusion models' high-quality outputs.
CONTROLS: Compare Hybrid VAR-Diff against the original variables from proposals 1 and 2, as well as state-of-the-art diffusion models (listed below).
COST: 55,000
PREDICTION: This approach shows a notable improvement in video quality and temporal coherence, and might achieve state-of-the-art results on certain benchmarks. However, the added complexity and interplay between VAR and diffusion components poses computational and debugging challenges as well.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Video Discrete Tokenizers via Inverse Decomposition
PROPOSAL: We further improve the IDE-Tokener by integrating a meta-learning approach to adapt the inverse decomposition to different video lengths and complexities. This Meta-IDE-Tokener learns to adjust its strategy for optimal trade-offs between training efficiency and tokenizer quality for varied inputs. By doing so, Meta-IDE-Tokener generalizes to unseen video lengths and compositions and enhances adaptability for newer datasets, serving as a valuable companion for discrete video generators.
CONTROLS: Compare Meta-IDE-Tokener against (a) naively adapted single-frame static tokenizer, (b) static tokenizer with additional component learning to compress temporal dynamics, (c) parallel training strategies and (d) a baseline using the non-meta version of IDE-Tokener.
COST: 45,000
PREDICTION: The efficiency and adaptability of Meta-IDE-Tokener should improve the performance and robustness of discrete video generators, but its meta-learning component might introduce new hyperparameters to tune and potentially increase memory requirement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporally-Sensitive Attention Mechanism for Long Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a Temporally-Sensitive Attention Mechanism (TSAM) to selectively focus on relevant past frames and adaptively adjust its contribution based on the current frame's importance in the video sequence. TSAM enables models to maintain a consistent temporal context and generate long videos without exploding context lengths. It is particularly effective when combined with proposals 1 and 3, as it can refine the trade-off between temporal coherence and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare TSAM against (a) fixed-weight attention, (b) naive concatenation of past frames, and (c) TSAM+HDT and TSAM+Hybrid VAR-Diff combinations.
COST: 82,000
PREDICTION: TSAM facilitates the generation of high-quality long videos by effectively managing temporal context, however its added computational cost for selective refinement may affect its adoption in scenarios demanding extreme efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Video Autoregressive Pipelines with Interplenning Diffusion Steps
PROPOSAL: We explore interpolated diffusion schedules as a backbone for discrete video autoregressive models. Borrowing from the stability benefits of correlated diffusion steps in image synthesis, we propose an inclusive step-size predictor that interplen the diffusion schedules of the direct autoregressive generation approach with a concurrently sampled diffusion step for some of the tokens in each frame, alternating this approach in a hybrid schedule composed of either stiff (strong alpha schedule) or adaptive interplenning predictions between two parameterschedules - slopes.
Meanwhile, video predictor, image infor and occupancy are estimated, and the current state of the video sequence learned simultaneously with key-frame / vanishing frame interplen lag analyses.
Controls: Compare against strong diffusion models like Stadim, EZD, RGB-Mixin. An ablation study will be conducted on the weights of cross predictor between the, in order to understand how it affects video quality against modelling complexity. Lastly, average self-supervised / weakly-supervised self-training validation can be used as alternatives that reduce upscratch training. 
COST: 15,120
PREDICTION: We anticipate significant latency reduction and promising image fidelity for long video sequences and relative independence to classical video tokenization architectures, primarily in our upstream correlate predictor of more visual blocks relative to image pixel level learnings.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Swapped Attention Traversal for Efficient Long-Term Context Management
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the explosively high sequence length and attendant high computational costs often present in standard transformer-style video-to-video models, we investigate a novel attention traversal strategy that swaps the typical left-to-right traversal order with a tailored bidirectional traversal of the video tokens, exploiting the inherent temporal coherence in video data. By incorporating a hierarchical attention structure, we adaptively allocate more attention to spatially and temporally distant tokens, facilitating efficient capturing of long-term contexts without explicitly attending to the full video sequence. 
Controls: Compare against baseline models with standard transformer attention, and ablate the effectiveness of the bidirectional traversal and hierarchical attention. 
COST: 14,350
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant reduction in computational costs while preserving, and potentially improving, the model's ability to capture long-term context in video sequences. 

Additional note: I corrected some of the proposal text in the 3rd item, based on my understanding of the context. I also made it clear what we're manipulating in the 'swapped traversal' approach

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Duration-Aware Video Synthesis for Realistic Long-Range Video Generation
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating coherent and realistic videos over long time horizons, we propose a duration-aware video synthesis approach that adaptively adjusts the attention span of the model based on the input video duration. By learning a probabilistic distribution over time steps, we can dynamically allocate more attention to critical periods in the video, such as sudden changes or key-frame events, while adapting to the overall pacing and rhythm of the clip. This allows the model to capture the nuanced temporal relationships in the data without requiring explicit annotations.
Controls: Compare against baseline models with fixed attention spans, and evaluate the effectiveness of the duration-aware approach on a range of video duration settings. 
COST: 16,200
PREDICTION: We anticipate an improvement in the realistic generation of long-range videos, with a focus on preserving the temporal coherence and dramatic arcs that are characteristic of human-created content.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Hybrid Video Autoregressive Pipelines with Interplenning Diffusion Steps
PROPOSAL: We refine the hybrid approach by replacing the traditional autoregressive generation with a conditional video diffusion model, which leverages the strengths of both paradigms to produce high-quality video sequences. The diffusion model is conditioned on the hidden states of the video prompt, allowing for more effective incorporation of temporal structure and coherent motion in the generated videos. We also investigate the use of progressive diffusion schedules, which adaptively adjust the number of diffusion steps based on the input video quality and computational resources available.
Controls: Compare against the original hybrid pipeline, and evaluate the effectiveness of the conditional diffusion model and progressive schedules on a range of video quality settings and computational constraints. 
COST: 21,000
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in video quality and computational efficiency, with the conditional diffusion model enabling more effective capture of temporal structure and progressive schedules allowing for adaptability to varying computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Stage Video Generation with Conditional Inference and Contextual Refining
PROPOSAL: To improve the overall coherence and realism of generated videos, we propose a multi-stage video generation framework that consists of three stages: 1) conditional inference, where the model infers the most likely video sequence given the input prompts and context; 2) contextual refining, where the model refines the predicted video sequence based on the contextual information of the input prompts and previous frame; and 3) output generation, where the final video sequence is generated. This framework allows for more sophisticated modeling of context and temporal relationships, leading to higher-quality video generation.
Controls: Compare against baseline models with single-stage video generation, and evaluate the effectiveness of the multi-stage framework on a range of video quality settings and applications. 
COST: 24,300
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in video quality and coherence, with the multi-stage framework enabling more effective capture of complex temporal relationships and contextual information.

TITLE: Adversarial Training for Video Generation Models with Temporal Consistency Loss
PROPOSAL: To improve the temporal consistency and realism of generated video sequences, we propose an adversarial training framework that incorporates a temporal consistency loss function. This loss function encourages the model to generate video sequences that are consistent over time, by minimizing the difference between the predicted frames and the ground truth frames. We use a temporal discriminator to evaluate the temporal consistency of the generated video sequences, and an adversarial loss function to encourage the model to generate more realistic and coherent video sequences.
Controls: Compare against baseline models without adversarial training and temporal consistency loss, and evaluate the effectiveness of the adversarial training framework on a range of video quality settings and applications. 
COST: 32,320
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in video quality and temporal consistency, with the adversarial training framework enabling more realistic and coherent video generation.

TITLE: Plug-and-Play Video Generation with Transferable Component-Based Models
PROPOSAL: To enable the plug-and-play integration of video generation models on new applications and datasets, we propose a transferable component-based model that decomposes the video generation process into a set of reusable components. Each component is trained on a specific task or dataset, but can be easily combined with other components to form a new video generation model. This framework enables the efficient reuse of knowledge across different applications and datasets, and reduces the need for extensive retraining and fine-tuning.
