ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Role of MoE in Reducing the Adversarial Robustness Gap in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether MoE architectures can help reduce the adversarial robustness gap in diffusion transformers, which arises due to the vulnerability of density models to noisy input. We will test the adversarial robustness of MoE and dense diffusion transformers using various attacks, such as FGSM and PGD, and measure their performance on adversarially perturbed images. We will also explore the effects of varying the number of experts, expert capacity, and routing strategy on the robustness gap, and compare the MoE models with dense diffusion transformers in terms of robustness. Additionally, we will investigate whether the MoE layers can learn to ignore or suppress the noise in the input data, and how this affects their robustness.
CONTROLS: We will include baseline models (e.g., dense DiT, tokenized DiT) and study several cases of expert pool crowd including large, small and median models
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect to find that MoE architectures can indeed help reduce the adversarial robustness gap in diffusion transformers, but the benefits will depend heavily on the chosen architecture, number of experts, and routing strategy, and that the MoE layers can learn to ignore or suppress the noise in the input data to some extent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Data-efficient Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will propose a data-efficient MoE framework that can be efficiently trained on smaller datasets, making it more practical for widespread adoption. We will design an MoE architecture that incorporates knowledge distillation, weight pruning, and expert clustering to reduce the number of parameters and computational overhead. We will evaluate the proposed framework on several text-to-image tasks, including COCO and LINDART-V2, and compare its performance with state-of-the-art MoE architectures on the same datasets. Additionally, we will investigate the effects of varying the number of experts, clustering strategy, and knowledge distillation temperature on the model's performance and data efficiency.
CONTROLS: We will include baseline models (e.g., dense DiT, tokenized DiT) and study several cases of expert pool crowd including large, small and median models
COST: 4249.2
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the proposed framework significantly reduces the computational overhead and storage requirements of MoE architectures, while maintaining their performance on various text-to-image tasks, and that the number of experts, clustering strategy, and knowledge distillation temperature play a crucial role in determining the model's data efficiency.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Temporally Consistent State Estimation for Episodic Offset Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: Investigate a model-agnostic state estimation approach that estimates the cumulative offset at the end of each episode and normalizes future observations during test time using this estimated offset, in order to align perceived and actual states. This offset correction will be used as input to the pre-trained offline model, ensuring a more consistent policy with the true environment. The corrected observations will be assumed to be generated from the pre-trained offline model, with the underlying environmental dynamics remaining unchanged.
CONTROLS: Use ablation studies and comparisons with a state-estimation-naive pre-trained offline RL model to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Evaluate on a range of episodic offset patterns, and on the robot navigation and manipulation simulations later in the proposal set.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: This approach should provide enhanced robustness and performance in non-stationary environments with episodic offset shifts, but may fail when the patterns of shift are extremely complex or show high frequencies within an episode.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Temporally Consistent State Estimation for Episodic Offset Non-Stationarity with Observational Autocorrelation
PROPOSAL: Revising proposal 1, incorporate consideration of observational autocorrelation in proposing an improved state estimation algorithm, specifically an AutoRegressive model (AR(1)) that leverages temporal dependencies in the observation function to estimate the offset more accurately, accounting for both the variance and autocorrelation of the observations to minimize misalignment between perceived and actual states. Consider a signal processing approach to explicitly estimate the autocorrelation of observations along with the offset transitions, to refine the learning of the offset history and improve robustness to complex shift patterns.
CONTROLS: Maintain comparisons with the baseline and ablations of the revised approach, implementing either without using autocorrelating observations during estimation in order to demonstrate the benefits of incorporating temporal dependencies. Simulation with synthetic and realistic autocorrelation patterns across the robot navigation and manipulation environments should validate the theoretical improvement.
COST: 7291.7
PREDICTION: This revised approach is likely to further improve the robustness of the offline model under episodic offset shifts and should demonstrate particularly good performance in domains where observations exhibit significant temporal autocorrelation, but may require higher compute resources for estimation and risk excessive overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Temporally Consistent State Estimation for Episodic Offset Non-Stationarity with Multi-Decoder Offsets
PROPOSAL: Revising proposal 2, adapt the AR(1) model to not only estimate the cumulative offset but also learn a multi-decoder structure to identify per-dimension offset patterns. Introduce a modified architecture allowing each decoder to focus on a subset of dimensions, thus allowing the model to learn distinct offsets for different components of the observation space. Consider running each dimension of the state space through its own decoder block, enabling improved robustness to non-stationarity across multiple aspects of the observation space.
CONTROLS: Similar to previous ablations and baseline comparisons, compare the performance of models with single and multi-decoder architectures and their respective AR models, to emphasize the benefit of joint per-dimension estimation. Empirically validate across various offset patterns, establishing the utility of a multi-decoder approach in real-world test episodes.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: This updated approach should demonstrate notable improvements in handling complex and diverse offset patterns, and its multi-decoder structure will make it particularly well-suited for scenarios involving multiple types of non-stationarity within a single episode, such as those seen in multi-modal robot perception or manipulation tasks.

TITLE: Temporally Consistent State Estimation for Episodic Offset Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: Investigate a model-agnostic state estimation approach that estimates the cumulative offset at the end of each episode and normalizes future observations during test time using this estimated offset, in order to align perceived and actual states. This offset correction will be used as input to the pre-trained offline model, ensuring a more consistent policy with the true environment. The corrected observations will be assumed to be generated from the pre-trained offline model, with the underlying environmental dynamics remaining unchanged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Adapt to Episodic Observation Shifts in Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the existing TRY-LESS algorithm, an offline RL method for learning to adapt to test-time perturbations, to handle episodic observation shifts. This will involve adding a novel neural mechanism that can predict the per-episode offset for each dimension of the state. We will initialize this predictor with a pre-trained feature extractor and fine-tune it using the stationary offline dataset. The adapted algorithm will then use this predictor to correct for the observation shift at test time. To control for the uncertainty around the offset prediction, we will use Monte Carlo dropout during inference.
CONTROLS: We will compare the adapted TRY-LESS algorithm with the original TRY-LESS baseline, as well as a modified version that uses a simple linear predictor for offset prediction instead of the neural mechanism. We will also compare our results against the current offline RL state-of-the-art on a set of robot navigation and manipulation tasks in simulation.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect our algorithm to outperform the baselines by at least 10% on the average return across episodes, but may struggle with highly non-stationary environments that require longer-term offset predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Imitation Learning with Robust Offset Estimation
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous proposal, we will investigate using imitation learning to train a policy that can robustly estimate offset values in the presence of non-stationarity. This will involve using a behavior regularization term in the imitation learning objective to encourage the policy to track a distribution of offset estimates that are consistent with the stationary offline dataset. We will use a VID2D actor-critic model, a state-of-the-art imitation learning model that can handle high-dimensional observations, to learn the policy.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with a standard offline RL method trained without imitation learning, as well as a version of the imitation learning method that is trained without behavior regularization. We will also compare our results against the adapted TRY-LESS algorithm from our previous proposal.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect imitation learning to improve robustness to non-stationarity, but may struggle with environments that require the policy to adapt to highly variable offset patterns during training.

TITLE: Imitation Learning with Robust Offset Estimation
PROPOSAL: To further improve the robustness of imitation learning to non-stationarity, we will modify the VID2D actor-critic model to incorporate a neural offset predictor, similar to the one proposed in our first experiment. This will allow the policy to learn to predict offsets directly from observations, rather than relying on behavior regularization. We will also investigate using a gradient-based method to regularize the offset predictions, such as gradient penalty or corrective gradients, to encourage the policy to output accurate offset estimates.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised imitation learning method with the standard offline RL method, as well as the version of imitation learning without neural offset prediction. We will also compare our results against the adapted TRY-LESS algorithm from our previous proposal.

PREDICTION: We expect the revised imitation learning method to outperform its predecessor by at least 15% on the average return across episodes, but may require additional training time to converge due to the added complexity of the neural offset predictor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Adapt to Episodic Observation Shifts in Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the existing TRY-LESS algorithm, an offline RL method for learning to adapt to test-time perturbations, to handle episodic observation shifts. This will involve adding a novel neural mechanism that can predict the per-episode offset for each dimension of the state. We will initialize this predictor with a pre-trained feature extractor and fine-tune it using the stationary offline dataset. The adapted algorithm will then use this predictor to correct for the observation shift at test time. To control for the uncertainty around the offset prediction, we will use Monte Carlo dropout during inference.
CONTROLS: We will compare the adapted TRY-LESS algorithm with the original TRY-LESS baseline, as well as a modified version that uses a simple linear predictor for offset prediction instead of the neural mechanism. We will also compare our results against the current offline RL state-of-the-art on a set of robot navigation and manipulation tasks in simulation.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: We expect our algorithm to outperform the baselines by at least 10% on the average return across episodes, but may struggle with highly non-stationary environments that require longer-term offset predictions.

PREDICTION: We expect imitation learning to improve robustness to non-stationarity, but may struggle with environments that require the policy to adapt to highly variable offset patterns during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline RL for Temporally Ordered Episodic Evolution of Observation Functions
PROPOSAL: Train a model-agnostic, episodic learning module on a synthetic dataset (e.g., MuJoCo environments with randomly generated, per-dimension additive offsets) with an asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) algorithm, using a neural network with multiple, parallel autoencoder branches that learn to identify offsets episode by episode, but store only such offsets, not state values or policy probabilities. 
CONTROLS:  Baseline experiments will include offline RL agents trained on standard datasets without any knowledge of the offset evolution, synthetically trained on scenarios without offsets, and standard state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: We expect this learning module to robustly identify and adapt to arbitrary, real-world-like time-series patterns of offsets, as it does not rely on knowledge of state transition dynamics, rewards, or action-space exploration. However, offline RL may fail to generalize well to real-world scenarios with additional, hard-to-predict non-stationarity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness of Offset Estimation Against Complex Time-Series Patterns
PROPOSAL: Investigate the estimation performance of the proposed learning module under various complex time-series patterns of offsets that may occur at test time, such as abrupt, sinusoidal, or trend-like changes in each dimension, and contrast this with state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms that assume stationarity or Gaussian perturbations. This will be done by generating synthetic test episodes with diverse patterns of offset evolution and computing the mean squared error (MSE) between true and estimated offsets.
CONTROLS: Experimental results will be compared to an ablation study where the learning module is trained to identify smooth, Gaussian perturbations, as well as state-of-the-art offline RL agents using stationary datasets and standard state-estimation techniques.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: We expect the learning module to robustly identify complex time-series patterns that may occur at test time, when trained on a diverse range of scenarios during training. However, the performance may degrade if these complex patterns significantly deviate from those seen during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline RL for Temporally Ordered Episodic Evolution of Observation Functions
PROPOSAL: Train a model-agnostic, episodic learning module on a synthetic dataset (e.g., MuJoCo environments with randomly generated, per-dimension additive offsets) with an asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) algorithm, using a neural network with multiple, parallel autoencoder branches that learn to identify offsets episode by episode, but store only such offsets, not state values or policy probabilities. 
CONTROLS:  Baseline experiments will include offline RL agents trained on standard datasets without any knowledge of the offset evolution, synthetically trained on scenarios without offsets, and standard state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms.
COST: 32400
PREDICTION: We expect this learning module to robustly identify and adapt to arbitrary, real-world-like time-series patterns of offsets, as it does not rely on knowledge of state transition dynamics, rewards, or action-space exploration. However, offline RL may fail to generalize well to real-world scenarios with additional, hard-to-predict non-stationarity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness of Offset Estimation Against Complex Time-Series Patterns
PROPOSAL: Investigate the estimation performance of the proposed learning module under various complex time-series patterns of offsets that may occur at test time, such as abrupt, sinusoidal, or trend-like changes in each dimension, and contrast this with state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms that assume stationarity or Gaussian perturbations. This will be done by generating synthetic test episodes with diverse patterns of offset evolution and computing the mean squared error (MSE) between true and estimated offsets.
CONTROLS: Experimental results will be compared to an ablation study where the learning module is trained to identify smooth, Gaussian perturbations, as well as state-of-the-art offline RL agents using stationary datasets and standard state-estimation techniques.
COST: 48600
PREDICTION: We expect the learning module to robustly identify complex time-series patterns that may occur at test time, when trained on a diverse range of scenarios during training. However, the performance may degrade if these complex patterns significantly deviate from those seen during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extend to Partial-History Settings with Future Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: Modify the learning module to take into account only limited past information about offsets, specifically the offset values over the previous episode or window of episodes, and investigate its performance under this constraint. This will be done using synthetic datasets with limited past offset information for each episode and evaluating the agent's ability to generalize to unseen future offset patterns.
CONTROLS: This will be compared against a scenario where the full history of past offsets is available, as well as an ablation study where the agent is only trained on known past offsets.
COST: 64800
PREDICTION: We expect the modified learning module to achieve satisfactory generalization performance in scenarios with limited past information, but potentially degrade in cases where the future offset patterns significantly diverge from those experienced during training.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Extend to Partial-History Settings with Future Uncertainty
REVISION: Instead of evaluating the agent's ability to generalize to unseen future offset patterns, modify the partial-history setting to evaluate the agent's performance under scenarios where it receives a discrete sequence of offset values at regular intervals during testing, such as daily or weekly updates, but not the offsets at the current or next intervals. This will be done using synthetic datasets with offset updates at regular intervals, and assessing the agent's ability to adapt to the changed environment without knowing the current or upcoming offset values.

CONTROLS: This setting will be compared against the full-history setting, as well as an ablation study where the agent is given access to the current and upcoming offset values.
COST: 64800
PREDICTION: We expect the modified learning module to adapt effectively to the changing environment with partial-horizon knowledge and estimate the current or upcoming offset correctly, but might struggle if the interval for updates is very long or there is a variation in a value at unknown intervals.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Offline RL for Temporally Ordered Episodic Evolution of Observation Functions
REVISION: In addition to the original learning module for episodic offset estimation, incorporate a novelty detection component to identify episodes with unknown, unseen patterns of offset evolution. This novelty detection component will utilize a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) or an autoencoder to capture the distribution of past seen offsets and flag episodes with offsets significantly different from this distribution.
CONTROLS: A baseline comparison will be made against the original learning module without novelty detection, as well as against an ablation study that omits the novelty detection component.
COST: 81000
PREDICTION: We expect the modified learning module with novelty detection to robustly identify episodes with unknown, unseen patterns of offset evolution and signal when it's safe to relearn, but the performance might be affected by the choice of GMM or autoencoder, and potential sensitivity to parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Offline RL Agents in Real-World Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Transfer the learning module and novelty detection component to real-world datasets in robot navigation and robot manipulation domains (e.g., GTA-Suite), with anecdotal offset evolution and episodes' history, using high-quality, multi-modal cameras.  We then will evaluate the performance of our agents against human expert policies recorded in these domains.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be compared against a set of state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms adapted to account for temporally ordered episodic evolution and against offline RL agents that access a full history of past offsets during testing.
COST: 97200
PREDICTION: We expect our offline RL agents to adapt to the new scenarios in real-world domains with complex time-series patterns, provided they are trained on a suitable set of synthetic and semi-realistic simulation data and configurations consistent with actual robots. The results will however likely vary based on the degree to which simulated training and real-world test settings parallel one another.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Transferability Across Domains and Observation Types
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether learning modules trained on simulated datasets from the robot navigation and robot manipulation domains can transfer effectively to other real-world or simulated domains with different observation types (e.g., multi-modal sensors such as ultrasound and depth cameras, 3D point clouds, or even rendering synthetic image observations), while maintaining their performance.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be compared against transfer learning approaches adapted for other offline RL settings with changing dynamics and observations.
COST: 129600
PREDICTION: We expect that learning modules for episodic evolution of observation functions will transfer effectively, with slight degradation in performance due to differences in observation modalities, especially when ground-based acquisition rather than hooked-up, hardware devices are used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Compensate for Unknown, Episodic Observation Shifts
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate the beta-VAEs (Variational AutoEncoders) with a compensatory scheme to detect and adjust for unknown, episodic observation shifts. Train beta-VAEs on a synthetic dataset based on the MuJoCo benchmark for robot manipulation, where each episode contains static transitions, noise, and a hidden additive offset in the observations.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline policies trained on stationary offline data using either Q-learning or Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients (DDPG) methods, without any offset compensation. Also, evaluate with various "ablated" versions of the beta-VAE where the compensatory adjustments are disabled or different forms of regularization are used on the beta-VAE's reconstruction losses.
COST: 516
PREDICTION: The proposed beta-VAE with compensatory scheme should outperform the baseline policies significantly by learning to robustly adapt to new episodes' observation shifts. However, in cases with drastically changing offsets, scalability and the agent's ability to accurately predict the new states from shifted observations may become its main adversary.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Offset Dynamics on Offline RL
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between the types of unknown, time-varying, episodic observation shifts and the performance of offline reinforcement learning (RL) agents. We will generate and analyze a varied set of synthetic datasets for a robot navigation task based on a simplified simulation environment with systematically changed offset dynamics, polynomial, sinusoidal, and a time-series forecasting task with complex patterns. Assess policy performance metrics, such as the average episode return and exploration. Consider the average offset size, duration, or frequency changes that most significantly affect the offline RL performance.
CONTROLS: Compare performance across various offset configurations within a fixed agent training procedure to identify trends and where exactly the failure modes appear. Include baseline agents without knowledge of any offset dynamics, to serve as an additional performance benchmark. Also, produce results with the Learning to Compensate for Unknown, Episodic Observation Shifts proposal (PR-1) in this dataset.
COST: 940
PREDICTION: This study should reveal that offline RL's robustness to test-time offset dynamics profoundly depends on the nature of those dynamics and uncover specific common patterns that agents typically struggle with. It might indicate cases in which the learning to compensate for unknown shifts is more, or less valuable.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Translation-based State Estimation for Offset-Affected States
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel state estimation mechanism that translates predicted offsets for an online agent to the offline RL domain. This translation-based estimation leverages an idea from the external data processing literature, utilizing empirical estimators, such as robust least-squares and generalized method of moments, to induce its predictions from historical data, thereby incorporating partially observable information in the offline RL setting. The approach minimizes the strain on current computing resources by taking full advantage of the given static offline dataset, whereas working entirely with hypothetical offset patterns at testing time is computationally inefficient and inaccurate as well.
CONTROLS: Compare translation-based state estimation with direct prediction-based beta-VAEs. Investigate the results using a real-world benchmark from the robot manipulation domain. Use this proposal paired with proposal-2's varied synthetic datasets for fairness.
COST: 1216.68
PREDICTION: This translation-based estimation technique will prove effective for estimating unseen offset dynamics under the given offline setup. Since this approach stands halfway between a prediction-based and an engagement-based solution, it is expected that within some conditions it may show significant performance boosts not seen in purely prediction-based models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Certified Robustness against Unseen Offset Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Design a model-agnostic certification approach that guarantee bounds on performance degradation due to unseen offset dynamics. This approach leverages techniques like interval arithmetics or probabilistic abstract interpretation to reason about performance under offset perturbations, and formal methods to bound the error. Apply this approach to Proposal-1 (Learning to Compensate for Unknown, Episodic Observation Shifts) and evaluate its robust performance against unseen offset dynamics on MuJoCo robot navigation scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare certification bounds obtained with methods such as worst-case value and robust optimization-based methods against observed performance degradation in realistic scenarios. Also, investigate combinations with learning-based offset compensation methods.
COST: 1345.6
PREDICTION: This approach should provide strong guarantees about performance under unseen offset dynamics, potentially paralleling learning-based methods in certain scenarios when unseen patterns are too specialized. However, robust performance may come at a computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Offset Detection and Compensation for Offline RL
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical approach that first detects the presence of offsets and then compensates for them. The hierarchy consists of a primary component, which detects the average offset pattern, and a secondary component, which adapts to changes in the offset pattern. Employ this hierarchical approach with the learning-based compensation methods proposed in Learning to Compensate for Unknown, Episodic Observation Shifts (Proposal-1) and evaluate performance on offline RL benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Compare the hierarchical approach against combination methods like Predictive Code Generation, Transfer Learning, or Certified Robustness in the context of offline RL.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The hierarchical approach should provide better detection and compensation of offsets, leading to improved performance in offline RL applications. However, potential challenges in identifying the causal relations between detected offsets may pose limitations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Masked Visual Encoding for Efficient Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We adapt the popular large language model XLM-R {21} to incorporate a masked visual encoder, specifically the vision transformer {mothadjetiou2015} applied to a visual token sequence representing the visual state transition, which is then masked and processed in parallel to the textual intermediates. We also experiment with separating the vision transformer's sequence length from the overall reasoning chain length by reusing the previously generated images in each step. This design allows us to leverage pre-trained weights and reduce sequence lengths while still modeling visual transitions.
CONTROLS: Train and evaluate XLM-R without visual encoding, a standard text-based reasoning baseline, and compare with the proposed model on the same reasoning-intensive tasks from the paper statement's experimental domains.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The masked visual encoding improves performance on visually-grounded tasks by 10-20% but may struggle to capture global structural transformations, potentially leading to underperformance on tasks like navigation and jigsaw solving.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Reasoning Step Length for Efficient Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose a adaptive reasoning step length mechanism that dynamically adjusts the number of textual and visual intermediates produced at each step based on the task's difficulty and the model's confidence in the current solution. Inspired by recent work on adaptive sampling for sequence generation {37}, we introduce a novel weight-sharing scheme between the reasoning step selector and the step predictor. By adjusting the number of steps according to the task's difficulty and the model's confidence, we aim to mitigate the effects of increasing sequence lengths and improve the model's ability to scale to complex visually-grounded tasks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the adaptive reasoning step length in combination with the model from proposal 1 (masked visual encoding), and compare to a fixed-step length baseline.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: This mechanism should reduce training and inference costs by 20-30% on complex tasks while maintaining high performance, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning through Image-Text Grounding
PROPOSAL: We compare the performance of a transductive CoT-M model trained on a unified image-text grounder dataset (e.g., Visual CC, Conceptual Captions, and Visual Genome) against a generative visual conditioner baseline on four reasoning-driven tasks: Adelaide-Street-View jigsaw puzzle solving, landscape generation from topographic contour maps, and human-evaluated image editing through instruction. Task metrics include jigsaw completion accuracy, Inception Score for landscape generation, and human evaluator ratings for edit quality and coherence.
CONTROLS: (1) Textually grounded (Tg) MLLM baseline trained on the single-modal version of Visual Genome, and the aforementioned generative visual conditioner; (2) Dynamic graph attention variation of top-performing model; (3) State-of-the-art visual-textual grounding model; (4) An ablation testing that utilizes textual-logic components alone instead of unified multi-modal components.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The transductive CoT-M model significantly outperforms baselines in reasoning-driven tasks, especially visual question answering and landscape generation. However, failure might occur for tasks requiring precise geometric reasoning, such as Adelaide-Street-View jigsaw puzzle solving.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: CoT-as-TurboCharge: Harnessing Visual Reasoning with Explicit Transformations
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether coupling an MLLM with a learned trigonometry module and an image generator can enhance coherent multi-modal reasoning. Specify intermediate steps using vectors (e.g., position, orientation, or scale), enforce consistency among the three modalities (image, text, and measurements), and promote progression through geometrically aligned modules.
CONTROLS: Baseline on original MLLM, and ablations without the trigonometry module and image generator.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reifying Chain-of-Thought for Explicit Visual Reasoning: A Representation Learning Perspective
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of learned node embeddings to reify intermediate steps in chain-of-thought reasoning, effectively injecting explicit visual and linguistic knowledge into the sequence. This reformulation allows for improved understandability, controllability, and transferability of the generated reasoning chains. Experiments will focus on comparison with original chain-of-thought generation and evaluation on real-world tasks such as visual question answering and instruction-based image editing.
CONTROLS: Baseline on original MLLM, ablation study on the impact of learned node embeddings and chain understandability abstractions.
COST: 6800
PREDICTION: By incorporating explicit knowledge representations into chain-of-thought reasoning, performance improvements are expected on tasks requiring nuanced visual understanding, but this may come at the cost of increased sequence complexity.

Experiments will focus on comparison with original chain-of-thought generation and evaluation on tasks such as visual question answering and reasoning-driven text-to-image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Design a novel transformer-based model, Multi-Modal CoT-XL, that combines the advantages of a CoT-based reasoning mechanism with an efficient attention mechanism to handle long-range dependencies in multi-modal reasoning chains. Specifically, we introduce a new type of attention, called Coarse-to-Fine Attention, that simultaneously handles textual and visual inputs, reducing the quadratic growth of sequence lengths.
CONTROLS: Model variants with standard autoregressive generation and a CoT-XL baseline without Coarse-to-Fine Attention, evaluated on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and landscape image generation from topographic contour maps. Additionally, a refinement process that masks a portion of the visual input to simulate the effects of reduced visual information.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Multi-Modal CoT-XL is expected to outperform standard autoregressive generation on tasks requiring long, compositional reasoning chains, with a 20% improvement in performance on jigsaw solving. However, if the refinement process is insufficient, the increased reliance on visual tokens may lead to performance degradation on tasks with reduced visual input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Training Stability Enhancement
PROPOSAL: Propose an instability-coping mechanism, Interleaved Neural Decay (IND), to minimize long-range dependency modeling and cross-modal dynamics issues during training. IND progressively introduces noise and regularization to the visual states in each reasoning step, reducing the dependency on preceding history and mitigating the impact of mismatched cross-modal dynamics.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments with IND and without it (Std Train) on MLLMs loaded with the Multi-Modal CoT-XL model from Proposal 1, focusing on training stability on visually grounded tasks such as navigation and rearrangement. Also, ablation studies assessing the effects of the noise strength, temporal regularity, and visual state decay rate.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: IND is expected to stabilize training for Multi-Modal CoT-XL on visually grounded tasks, achieving 30% fewer training failures compared to the standard training method, and enabling successful convergence on tasks previously difficult to train (2% improvement in final training accuracy). However, inadequate noise introduction may hinder performance (as much as 10% degradation in accuracy).

TITLE: Evaluating Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities
PROPOSAL: Develop a suite of standardized evaluation benchmarks for unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning on reasoning-intensive tasks, including visual question answering (VQA), instruction-based image editing, and geometry tasks. The goal is to create a unified evaluation framework that assesses both the accuracy and interpretability of the generated reasoning chains.
CONTROLS: A set of established baselines, including the recent VQA-XL model, and a new test suite called Rhyme, focusing on tasks like solving jigsaw puzzles, image transformations, and generating landscape images from topographic contour maps. In addition, we perform transfer learning experiments to assess the adaptability of our unified model across various tasks.
COST: 18000

However, we risk overemphasizing the complexity of our model, hindering human evaluation (1.5% accuracy degradation on simpler tasks).

PROPOSAL: Develop a method to prune the sequential reasoning process in Multi-Modal CoT-XL, utilizing attention-based pruning and state-of-the-art schedule-based pruning techniques to reduce the inference time while maintaining a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. By dynamically adjusting the sequence length, we can adapt the pruning strategy to the task's complexity and the model's capacity.
CONTROLS: Comparison of the baseline Multi-Modal CoT-XL with the pruning method on various real-world benchmarks, including VQA, jigsaw puzzle solving, and instruction-based image editing. PREDICTION: Pruning will significantly speed up Multi-Modal CoT-XL inference without substantial accuracy losses (15-20% speedup and up to 5% accuracy degradation), but more aggressive pruning might lead to accuracy decreases (up to 10% accuracy degradation on some tasks).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Design a novel transformer-based model, Multi-Modal CoT-XL, that combines the advantages of a CoT-based reasoning mechanism with an efficient attention mechanism to handle long-range dependencies in multi-modal reasoning chains. Specifically, we introduce a new type of attention, called Coarse-to-Fine Attention, that simultaneously handles textual and visual inputs, reducing the quadratic growth of sequence lengths.
CONTROLS: Model variants with standard autoregressive generation and a CoT-XL baseline without Coarse-to-Fine Attention, evaluated on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and landscape image generation from topographic contour maps. Additionally, a refinement process that masks a portion of the visual input to simulate the effects of reduced visual information.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Multi-Modal CoT-XL is expected to outperform standard autoregressive generation on tasks requiring long, compositional reasoning chains, with a 20% improvement in performance on jigsaw solving. However, if the refinement process is insufficient, the increased reliance on visual tokens may lead to performance degradation on tasks with reduced visual input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Training Stability Enhancement
PROPOSAL: Propose an instability-coping mechanism, Interleaved Neural Decay (IND), to minimize long-range dependency modeling and cross-modal dynamics issues during training. IND progressively introduces noise and regularization to the visual states in each reasoning step, reducing the dependency on preceding history and mitigating the impact of mismatched cross-modal dynamics.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments with IND and without it (Std Train) on MLLMs loaded with the Multi-Modal CoT-XL model from Proposal 1, focusing on training stability on visually grounded tasks such as navigation and rearrangement. Also, ablation studies assessing the effects of the noise strength, temporal regularity, and visual state decay rate.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: IND is expected to stabilize training for Multi-Modal CoT-XL on visually grounded tasks, achieving 30% fewer training failures compared to the standard training method, and enabling successful convergence on tasks previously difficult to train (2% improvement in final training accuracy). However, inadequate noise introduction may hinder performance (as much as 10% degradation in accuracy).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities
PROPOSAL: Develop a suite of standardized evaluation benchmarks for unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning on reasoning-intensive tasks, including visual question answering (VQA), instruction-based image editing, and geometry tasks. The goal is to create a unified evaluation framework that assesses both the accuracy and interpretability of the generated reasoning chains.
CONTROLS: A set of established baselines, including the recent VQA-XL model, and a new test suite called Rhyme, focusing on tasks like solving jigsaw puzzles, image transformations, and generating landscape images from topographic contour maps. In addition, we perform transfer learning experiments to assess the adaptability of our unified model across various tasks.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: This evaluation framework will reveal the strengths and weaknesses of existing models and guide the development of new unified reasoning frameworks, potentially identifying areas where CoT-based methods are superior (up to 12% accuracy boost on tasks such as VQA). However, we risk overemphasizing the complexity of our model, hindering human evaluation (1.5% accuracy degradation on simpler tasks).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Revise the Multi-Modal CoT-XL model to incorporate a hierarchical reasoning structure, consisting of two reasoning stages: 1) a local reasoning stage using Coarse-to-Fine Attention (Proposal 1) for handling short-range dependencies and 2) a global reasoning stage utilizing a hierarchical transformer encoder to capture long-range dependencies between visual state transitions. This hierarchical approach aims to balance the computational complexity and the need for coherent visual state transitions in the multi-modal reasoning chain.
CONTROLS: Revised Multi-Modal CoT-XL experiments compared to the original version, including the Coarse-to-Fine Attention and the hierarchical reasoning structure. Baseline experiments using the original standard autoregressive generation will be used for comparisons.
COST: 66000
PREDICTION: The revised Multi-Modal CoT-XL is expected to improve performance on tasks requiring intermediate-range dependencies, such as visual question answering (15% improvement), but potentially lead to increased computational costs (2.5% slowdown compared to standard autoregressive generation) and overfitting issues if the hierarchical structure is not properly regularized (5% accuracy degradation).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities
PROPOSAL: Revise the Rhyme test suite (Proposal 3) to include a TZ-Jigsaw subgroup focusing on tasks that require reasoning about visual transformations and spatial reasoning, consisting of assembly puzzles, image completion tasks, and visual analogies. Additionally, integrate human-annotated explanations for each task, enabling more comprehensive assessments of model interpretability and reasoning quality.
CONTROLS: Original experiment setup compared to revised Rhyme test suite with TZ-Jigsaw subgroup. A study on the utility of human-annotated explanations in model evaluation will also be conducted.
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: The TZ-Jigsaw subgroup will be found effective in challenging MLLMs, particularly those using CoT-based reasoning, on tasks involving visual transformations (improvements up to 18% accuracy and 25% interpretability), yet it might require precise tuning to avoid overfitting and relying too heavily on human-annotated explanations (3-5% accuracy degradation on simpler tasks).

CONTROLS: Compare performance to Visual-BERT, study impact of gaze information on Visual Transformer's performance
COST: 156,900
PREDICTION: Visual Transformer will outperform Visual-BERT, but the improvement might not fully translate when using estimated gaze information due to its increased sensitivity to initializations and training stability issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Egocentric Gaze Cues on Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of an egocentric video question answering model (VQA-EG) on the VQA-Ewhy benchmark when provided with access to simulated egocentric gaze cues versus when gaze information is withheld. The simulated gaze cues will be generated using a gaze estimation model trained on a publicly available eye-tracking dataset (e.g., EyeF) and will reflect the attention of the user on specific objects or regions within the egocentric video frame. We anticipate that adding gaze information will improve model performance due to its ability to focus on relevant aspects of the scene.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard VQA-EG model (no gaze information), gaze-estimation model (single-task trained for gaze estimation)
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We predict that the VQA-EG model with simulated gaze information will perform significantly better on questions that involve the user's focus or attention (e.g., "What am I looking at?"), whereas performance on questions that rely more heavily on scene layout or recognition may not be as strongly impacted. Gaze prediction performance could be jeopardized if the eye-tracking dataset introduces domain mismatch.

However, the model's reliance on real-world gaze data might lead to suboptimal performance in cases where the quality of gaze information is compromised.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding How Gaze Information Should Be Presented to MLLMs
PROPOSAL: To address the open question of how to effectively present gaze information to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for better understanding of user focus and intention, we will conduct an ablation study with the VQA-EG-Gaze model. The study will compare different modalities and formats of presenting gaze information, such as gaze heatmaps, gaze vectors, and text-based descriptions of gaze events, to determine which presentation format leads to the best model performance. We will also investigate the impact of gaze information presentation resolution and frequency on model performance.
CONTROLS: Ablations: different gaze presentation formats, presentation resolution, frequency
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the VQA-EG-Gaze model will perform significantly better when presented with gaze information in a format that closely matches the model's internal representation, such as gaze vectors, than when presented with alternative formats, such as static gaze heatmaps or text-based descriptions. However, this could potentially be dependent on the complexity and nuance of the gaze information being presented.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of MLLMs to Noisy or Inaccurate Gaze Information
PROPOSAL: To investigate how MLLMs (specifically the VQA-EG-Gaze model) handle noisy or inaccurate gaze information, we will introduce artificial errors or noises into the simulated or real-world gaze information and evaluate the model's performance under these conditions. We will also explore the impact of gaze signal accuracy on model performance and examine how different gaze information processing mechanisms in the model handle corrupted or inaccurate gaze cues.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard VQA-EG-Gaze model (with accurate gaze information), modified VQA-EG-Gaze model (with added gaze noise or inaccuracies)
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We predict that the MLLM will be sensitive to inaccuracies in gaze information and that performance will degrade as gaze signal accuracy decreases. However, we also expect to see a certain degree of resilience, particularly if the model has been trained with mechanisms for handling noisy or uncertain inputs. It's possible that the model might fair better with artificially introduced noise in lieu of real-world inaccuracies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Information on Proactive Personal AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: To investigate the potential benefits of incorporating gaze-awareness into proactive personal AI assistants, we will develop a new variant of the VQA-EG-Gaze model (named EG-ASP) that is specifically designed for proactive assistance in everyday tasks. We will evaluate the performance of EG-ASP in anticipating and responding to user needs compared to a standard model without gaze information. Additionally, we will explore the user experience and acceptance of an AI assistant that incorporates gaze-awareness for proactive assistance.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard VQA-EG model (no gaze information), EG-ASP model with gaze information
COST: 8640
PREDICTION: We predict that the EG-ASP model will provide more accurate and proactive assistance, leading to a better user experience and increased acceptance of gaze-aware AI assistants. However, we also anticipate that the added complexity of gaze-awareness may introduce new challenges, such as increased computational requirements or potential biases in gaze-related data.

TITLE: Egocentric Gaze-Augmented MLLM for User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: Develop an egocentric MLLM model that incorporates gaze-related signals from eye-tracking data and compare its performance on an egocentric video question answering benchmark against a standard MLLM baseline and a gaze-agnostic variant of the same MLLM.  The proposed model uses a gaze-conditioned attention mechanism to focus on regions of interest in the egocentric video, and it is fine-tuned on a specially designed egocentric gaze dataset.
CONTROLS: Standard MLLM baseline (e.g., RoBERTa on Places Video Standard+100K), gaze-agnostic variant of the standard MLLM baseline, and a multimodal baseline that combines the egocentric video features with gaze features.
COST: 1036.8 GPU hours
PREDICTION: The egocentric MLLM with gaze-augmentation should outperform the standard MLLM, and the gaze-agnostic variant should roughly match the standard MLLM performance. However, the prediction might fail if the gaze dataset is not representative enough, or if the gaze-conditioned attention mechanism does not adapt well to different egocentric scenarios.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Egocentric Gaze-Aware Multimodal Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We design and conduct controlled experiments to compare gaze-aware and gaze-agnostic variants of state-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on the Multimodal OBjection Reasoning (MOBOR) dataset, a egocentric video question answering benchmark. Particularly, we measure the MLLMs' performance when provided with and without ground-truth gaze data, using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and answer span overlap.
CONTROLS: We compare against a) a strong baseline (e.g, CLIP) without gaze information, and b) an ablation experiment where the gaze-aware variant's gaze decoder is substituted with a dummy decoder generating random gaze vectors.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect the gaze-aware variant to outperform the baseline by at least 10% in terms of accuracy on questions about the user's focus and intention. The result might fail if the gaze-data is noisy or the MLLMs' capacity to interpret gaze cues is limited.

Note: To our understanding, the MOBOR dataset offers bright angles for this experiment, including a rich set of questions easily adaptable to a customized vision of "gaze-aware" MLLMs that recognize accuracy and F1-score extensively called upon for supervised learning tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Gaze Signal Presentation for Improved User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: We explore how gaze information should be presented to an MLLM to effectively improve the model's understanding of the user's focus and intention. We analyze and compare different ways of incorporating gaze signals, including gaze embeddings as input to the MLLM, gaze-based attention mechanisms within the MLLM, and a gaze-driven schema for controlling the MLLM's output, using the Ego4D dataset, a large-scale egocentric video dataset collected from daily life and other activities.
CONTROLS: We compare against a) a baseline MLLM without gaze information, b) an ablation experiment where the MLLM's attention mechanisms are substituted with a gaze-agnostic counterpart, and c) an experiment where the MLLM's output is controlled by a hand-coded gaze-driven schema used as reference.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect that using gaze-based attention mechanisms within the MLLM yields the best performance in terms of user intent understanding, followed closely by incorporating gaze signals as input to the MLLM. However, the model's capacity to interpret gaze cues could limit its effectiveness, and the choice of presentation method might not always align with the user's actual intention.

Note: To further examine how gaze information should be presented in MLLMs, we decided to take a look at how MLLMs can first apply gaze attention weights, hence fitting the given real-world scenario and both setting a baseline as well as structuring counter scenarios, and further expanding feature vector length as free input.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Probing the Capacity of Gaze-Aware MLLMs to Interpret Gaze Cues
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to use synthetic gaze data instead of real gaze annotations from the GazeGPT framework, due to the challenges and limitations of annotating real gaze data. We generate realistic gaze data for the GIF dataset using a gaze simulation model and compare the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs on contrasting gaze-invariant and gaze-variant question answering tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare against a) a strong baseline (e.g, a gaze-agnostic MLLM) on both tasks, b) a model pre-trained on a dataset with gaze-annotated images and fine-tuned on the GIF dataset, and c) a version of the model where the gaze encoder is replaced with a different type of representation learning on the gaze data.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the models' performance on the gaze-variant tasks is not significantly better than on the gaze-invariant tasks, indicating a limited capacity to interpret gaze cues, due to the challenging nature of gaze simulation and the potential for the models to overfit to the synthetic data.

Note: By revising our proposal to use synthetic data, we are accounting for the challenges and limitations of annotating real gaze data, while still being able to evaluate the capacity of gaze-aware MLLMs to interpret gaze cues in a controlled and reliable manner.

TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Gaze Signal Accuracy on User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the impact of gaze signal accuracy on the performance of gaze-aware MLLMs in understanding user intent from egocentric videos. We manipulate the ground-truth gaze data in the GIF dataset to simulate gaze signal noise at different levels (e.g., simulation, mild, severe) and assess the degradation in performance using standard evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: We compare against a) a strong baseline (e.g, a gaze-agnostic MLLM) with perfect gaze signals, b) the revised model from proposal 3 with synthetic gaze data, and c) a version of the model where gaze-related parameters are fine-tuned to correct for gaze signal noise.
COST: 729.17
PREDICTION: We expect to find that even small amounts of gaze signal noise significantly degrade the performance of gaze-aware MLLMs, highlighting the need for robust gaze signal pre-processing and robustness against noise in real-world applications.

Note: By evaluating the impact of gaze signal accuracy on user intent understanding, we can better understand the challenges and limitations of using gaze-aware MLLMs in real-world scenarios.

TITLE: Evaluating Egocentric Gaze-Aware Multimodal Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We refine the evaluation protocol of our previous proposal to focus on a more specific and challenging subtask: identifying the target object of the user's attention from egocentric videos. CONTROLS: We compare against a) a strong baseline (e.g, a gaze-agnostic MLLM) with and without the new target object annotations, b) the model from proposal 3 with synthetic gaze data, and c) a version of the model where gaze-related parameters are fine-tuned to improve target object identification.
COST: 931
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the gaze-aware MLLM outperforms the baseline by a significant margin, highlighting the importance of gaze-awareness for target object identification in egocentric videos.

Note: By revising the evaluation protocol to focus on a more specific and challenging subtask, we can better understand the strengths and limitations of gaze-aware MLLMs in real-world applications.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that the gaze-aware MLLM is vulnerable to adversarial gaze attacks, especially when the attacker is aware of the model's internal workings, highlighting the need for more robust gaze-aware architectures.

Note: By investigating the robustness of gaze-aware MLLMs to adversarial gaze attacks, we can identify potential vulnerabilities and develop strategies to improve the model's security and reliability.

Particularly, we measure the MLLMs' performance when provided with and without ground-truth gaze data, using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and answer span overlap.
CONTROLS: We compare against a) a strong baseline (e.g, CLIP) without gaze information, and b) an ablation experiment where the gaze-aware variant's gaze decoder is substituted with a dummy decoder generating random gaze vectors.

Note: To our understanding, the MOBOR dataset offers bright angles for this experiment, including a rich set of questions easily adaptable to a customized vision of "gaze-aware" MLLMs that recognize accuracy and F1-score extensively called upon for supervised learning tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gradient Interference in Shared-Modality AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Train and analyze several baseline AR UMMs on text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing tasks using the DALL-E 2 model, CC3M dataset, and CLEVR dataset. We will compare model performance on these tasks with and without a modality-specific gradient penalty to mitigate inter-modal conflict. The penalty term will be computed as the L2 norm of the sum of gradients induced by the text and vision components of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare with a standard AR UMM without gradient penalty, and a gradient-penalized AR UMM variant that applies the same penalty term but only in the intermediate layers.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect the gradient-penalized model to outperform the standard model on tasks with high modal discrepancy, such as text-to-image generation, while exhibiting comparable performance on tasks with low discrepancy, like visual question answering. However, it may fail to correct conflicts in early layers due to the strong influence of the weight initialization on the gradient directions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Alternative to Gradient Penalties
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a variant of the AR UMM where the inter-modal conflict is addressed through adaptive synchronized learning rates for the text and vision components. This approach aims to balance the gradients from both modalities by adjusting the learning rates in a modality-specific manner, rather than penalizing them directly.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR UMM, and the gradient-penalized model from proposal 1, with a focus on testing the learning rate adaptation policy on different depth layers.
COST: 729.17
PREDICTION: The learning rate adaptation approach is expected to alleviate the gradient interference issue in the AR UMM, particularly when the modalities have significantly different optimal learning rates, and reduce the need for careful tuning. However, it may lead to variable optimization efficiency, and might suffer from an added risk of overfitting to the fewer parameters ( learning rates).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Data for Controlled Analysis
PROPOSAL: Generate a synthetic dataset consisting of paired text-image tokens using a combination of generative adversarial networks (GANs) and pattern language encodings. This controlled dataset will enable the evaluation of modality interaction mechanisms for AR UMMs under precisely curated conditions, allowing us to isolate and analyze the effects of text-image similarity on modality conflicts.
CONTROLS: Use the synthetic dataset to investigate the effects of gradient variance on training efficiency and modality collaboration, and compare the findings with results from the real-world datasets used in proposals 1 and 2.
COST: 1345.6
PREDICTION: The synthetic dataset analysis will provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms of gradient interference in AR UMMs, and help identify specific patterns or properties of the text-image pairs that influence modality interactions in AR UMMs, potentially freeing research for zero-shot generalization. However, handling complexity of real models and numerous parameters can often take a toll due to computational challenges for GAN training.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimizer for Modality-Specific Weights
PROPOSAL: Develop a modality-specific joint optimizer that learns distinct optimizer schedules for the text and vision components of the AR UMM, separately. This approach aims to enable more effective learning of modality-specific weights and to address the issue of gradient interference without direct gradient penalty or adaptive learning rate adjustments.
CONTROLS: Compare with the adaptive learning rate adaptation from proposal 2, and the gradient-penalized model from proposal 1, with a focus on assessing the impact of optimizers on convergence rates and modality collaboration.
COST: 1263.593
PREDICTION: The modality-specific joint optimizer will likely improve the effectiveness of AR UMMs on tasks involving significant intermodal conflicts, and provide more robust optimization compared to adaptive learning rates or gradient penalties. However, developing a robust and efficient modality-specific joint optimizer may add considerable complexity to the overall optimization pipeline, challenging existing gradient clipping techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gradient Interference in Shared-Modality AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Train and analyze several baseline AR UMMs on text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing tasks using the DALL-E 2 model, CC3M dataset, and CLEVR dataset. We will compare model performance on these tasks with and without a modality-specific gradient penalty to mitigate inter-modal conflict. The penalty term will be computed as the L2 norm of the sum of gradients induced by the text and vision components of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare with a standard AR UMM without gradient penalty, and a gradient-penalized AR UMM variant that applies the same penalty term but only in the intermediate layers.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect the gradient-penalized model to outperform the standard model on tasks with high modal discrepancy, such as text-to-image generation, while exhibiting comparable performance on tasks with low discrepancy, like visual question answering. However, it may fail to correct conflicts in early layers due to the strong influence of the weight initialization on the gradient directions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining Gradient Interference Analysis in Shared-Modality AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: REVISE 1: To gain deeper insights into the inter-modal conflict, we will add an attention-based layer to the baseline AR UMMs to visualize and decompose the magnitude and direction of gradients induced by the text and vision components at different depths. This will enable us to identify how conflicts between the gradients vary along the network architecture. 
CONTROLS: Compare with the results from the baseline experiments (1), and analyze attention distributions for state-of-the-art non-autoregressive architectures on the same tasks.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: The attention-based visualization is expected to reveal that early layers are dominated by trivial gradients, while intermediate layers experience more significant conflicts between text and vision gradients, indicating that these layers are most critical for improving the modality sharing in AR UMMs. However, achieving high-quality, interpretable results using attention may be demanding for computationally complex models, posing a risk of  substantial training-time increases.

This will enable us to identify how conflicts between the gradients vary along the network architecture. Additionally, we will train a new set of baseline models that only have a small number of attention heads (e.g., 2-4) to determine whether the success of attention-based approaches is due to the added capacity or the attention mechanism itself.
CONTROLS: Compare with the results from the baseline experiments (1), and analyze attention distributions for state-of-the-art non-autoregressive architectures on the same tasks.
COST: 3500

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Alternative to Gradient Penalties
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a variant of the AR UMM where the inter-modal conflict is addressed through adaptive synchronized learning rates for the text and vision components. This approach aims to balance the gradients from both modalities by adjusting the learning rates in a modality-specific manner, rather than penalizing them directly.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original AR UMM, and the gradient-penalized model from proposal 1, with a focus on testing the learning rate adaptation policy on different depth layers.
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: The learning rate adaptation approach is expected to alleviate the gradient interference issue in the AR UMM, particularly when the modalities have significantly different optimal learning rates, and reduce the need for careful tuning. However, it may lead to variable optimization efficiency, and might suffer from an added risk of overfitting to the fewer parameters ( learning rates).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Data for Controlled Analysis
PROPOSAL: Generate a synthetic dataset consisting of paired text-image tokens using a combination of generative adversarial networks (GANs) and pattern language encodings. This controlled dataset will enable the evaluation of modality interaction mechanisms for AR UMMs under precisely curated conditions, allowing us to isolate and analyze the effects of text-image similarity on modality conflicts.
CONTROLS: Use the synthetic dataset to investigate the effects of gradient variance on training efficiency and modality collaboration, and compare the findings with results from the real-world datasets used in proposals 1 and 2.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The synthetic dataset analysis will provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms of gradient interference in AR UMMs, and help identify specific patterns or properties of the text-image pairs that influence modality interactions in AR UMMs, potentially freeing research for zero-shot generalization. However, handling complexity of real models and numerous parameters can often take a toll due to computational challenges for GAN training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimizer for Modality-Specific Weights
PROPOSAL: Develop a modality-specific joint optimizer that learns distinct optimizer schedules for the text and vision components of the AR UMM, separately. This approach aims to enable more effective learning of modality-specific weights and to address the issue of gradient interference without direct gradient penalty or adaptive learning rate adjustments.
CONTROLS: Compare with the adaptive learning rate adaptation from proposal 2, and the gradient-penalized model from proposal 1, with a focus on assessing the impact of optimizers on convergence rates and modality collaboration.
COST: 3800
PREDICTION: The modality-specific joint optimizer will likely improve the effectiveness of AR UMMs on tasks involving significant intermodal conflicts, and provide more robust optimization compared to adaptive learning rates or gradient penalties. However, developing a robust and efficient modality-specific joint optimizer may add considerable complexity to the overall optimization pipeline, challenging existing gradient clipping techniques.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improved Modality-Specific Joint Optimizer
PROPOSAL: REVISE 4: Enhance the modality-specific joint optimizer by incorporating a meta-learning component to learn a mapping between modality-specific loss landscapes and optimizer parameters. This will enable the optimizer to adapt its schedule in a more informed way, potentially leading to improved modality collaboration and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original joint optimizer from proposal 4, and evaluate the impact of meta-learning on convergence rates and modality-specific weight outputs for different deep architectures.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: The revised joint optimizer should provide a substantial boost to modality collaboration in AR UMMs by enabling better adaptation to modality-specific loss landscapes. However, incorporating meta-learning may increase the risk of overfitting to the optimal trajectories or leading to an overly complex optimizer that is computationally expensive to train.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate task-aware and modality-adaptive architectural components for AR UMMs that learn to adaptively shift between modality-specific layers or select the most effective layer combinations for a given task, aiming to mitigate the challenges of fixed modality-sharing architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Inter-Modality Gradient Conflicts in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the visual-linguistic dataset COCOCaptions to experimentally investigate the inter-modal conflicts in a modality-shared AR transformer. We propose to compare the gradient directions and magnitudes between text and vision modalities at different layers of a pre-trained AR UMM, using a variant of the information bottleneck principle and gradient norms. To control for differences in modality embeddings, we will add an ablation in which the vision embeddings are projected into the text embedding space before next-token prediction.
CONTROLS: We will compare to an unprojected baseline for vision embeddings. We will also perform an ablation studying the effect of number of modulation layers on gradient conflict.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: We expect to find that gradient conflict is higher in mid-level layers where text and vision representations start to diverge in significance and gradient norms. We predict that projecting vision embeddings into text space can reduce inter-modal conflict but also has the potential to diminish neural activation, where performance might suffer in certain real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Gradient Alignment in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the layer-wise gradient conflict between text and vision in an autoregressive transformer by training a model on the COCO captioning dataset, Clevr VQA, and Conceptual Captions, and monitoring the gradients' alignment at different transformer depths using the Jaccard similarity coefficient as a metric. This will be done by competing the standard autoregressive model with two variants: one uses a smaller embedding dimension for vision tokens to reduce the modality conflict, and the other adds an auxiliary contrastive loss to encourage gradient alignment.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the baselines against the two variants on the original test sets, and ablate the reduced embedding dimension and contrastive loss components individually to understand their relative contributions.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the variants to show improved alignment of text and vision gradients, especially in intermediate layers, and comparable or improved performance on the evaluation metrics, mainly due to the reduced gradient conflict.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Comparison of Gradient Conflicts in Modality-Shared AR Transformers
PROPOSAL: Use a comprehensive suite of self-supervised, image+text, and text-to-image benchmarks such as CLEVR-VQA, Conceptual Captions, Flicker30k and COCO, to compare the empirical severity of gradient conflicts in modality-shared versus modality-separated autoregressive transformers. The comparison will be done by computing the average norm of the gradients in each modality across a set of layers. Additionally, we will quantify the effect of gradient conflict on model performance by comparing modality-shared models with modality-separated ones.
CONTROLS: The baselines will include standard modality-separated models (both autoregressive and cross-modal attention-based) and explore the impact of different SVT tokenizer-based adverse conditions to see how the gradient conflict varies, along with analysis on how much the gradient conflict contributes to performance difference between standard vs modality-separated AR models.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that gradient conflicts vary significantly across tasks, datasets, and layer depths, and that modality-separated transformers can alleviate some performance losses due to inter-modal conflicts, but may also struggle with capturing the multimodal generalization capabilities of modality-shared transformers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient Conflict Diagnosis in Inter-Modal AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Identify and measure the inter-modal conflicts between text and image gradients in a modality-shared AR UMM across different transformer depths, utilizing the layer-wise attention weights and feature normalization of the multi-modal transformer architecture. Specifically, we'll employ the singular value decomposition (SVD) to analyze and compare the singular values and vectors of the product between the attention weights and the features from each modality. This will provide a principled and quantitative measure of the disagreement between text and vision gradients.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline of standard layer-wise feature analysis and controlled ablation studies on different sampling strategies for analyzing attention weights.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to uncover insightful layer-wise patterns of gradient conflicts, and possibly to identify critical depth ranges where these conflicts significantly hinder the training process. The technique may fail to capture more subtle, high-dimensional conflicts, or struggle with representations where features become increasingly abstract and semantic.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Modality Biases on Gradient Conflicts
PROPOSAL: Explore the relationship between the statistical properties of modality-specific data and the manifestation of gradient conflicts in modality-shared AR UMMs. We will generate synthetic datasets with explicitly controlled biases, such as different token distributions, sequence lengths, or vocabulary sizes, for both text and image modalities. Then, we will train and evaluate our AR UMM on these datasets to systematically analyze how modality biases affect gradient conflicts, attention patterns, and overall performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluate performance on both biased and unbiased versions of natural-language and natural-image datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and COCO Captioning.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expects to reveal how the statistical properties of modality-specific data influence gradient conflicts, which may guide the development of more effective AR UMMs by tailoring their design to the characteristics of specific datasets or tasks. The analysis might also identify robustness issues in AR UMMs across disparate domains, particularly where modality biases significantly diverge.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Gradient Conflict Diagnosis in Inter-Modal AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Extend the layer-wise analysis of gradient conflicts in inter-modal AR UMMs to account for the influence of depth-specific weights and the asymmetric information passing between text and vision modules. Specifically, we will incorporate the output of the vision branch as input to the text branch at each depth, and assess whether this asymmetric path contributes to alleviating or exacerbating gradient conflicts.
CONTROLS: Compare the performances of standard layer-wise feature analysis with the revised framework, and evaluate the effects of including / excluding asymmetric information passing between vision and text modules.
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide deeper insights into how gradient conflicts evolve across the transformer depth, potentially identifying key layers and modality interactions that contribute to or mitigate conflicts, and informing the design of more effective modality-sharing strategies in AR UMMs. However, the revised framework may struggle to generalize across different tasks and domains due to its highly customized nature.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Asymmetry-Aware Modality-Sharing AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate an asymmetric modality-sharing strategy for AR UMMs, where the text and vision branches are designed to operate with different levels of reciprocity, based on their respective statistical properties and task requirements. We will employ a two-level architecture, where a global modality-agnostic component makes high-level decisions and a modality-specific component refines the outputs. This approach aims to reduce gradient conflicts by allowing the text and vision modules to exploit their respective strengths while minimizing their respective weaknesses.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard modality-sharing AR UMMs, and evaluate the effects of varying the degree of asymmetry in the architecture.
COST: 2700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expects to demonstrate improved performance and reduced gradient conflicts in AR UMMs by adaptively tailoring the interaction between text and vision modules, particularly in tasks where modality-specific knowledge and expertise are crucial. However, the design might struggle to generalize across disparate tasks and domains, where the optimal level of asymmetry may differ.

PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework for understanding the impact of modality-sharing on the optimization and generalization of unified multimodal models.
